div.p: pottrp.

- NEW EVERY HORNING. Every day is a fresh beginning, Every morn is the world made new. Tod are weary of sorrow and sinning. Here is a beautiful hope for you; A hope for me and a hope for you. All the past things are past and over. The tasks are done and the tears are shed. Yesterday's errors let yesterday cover; Yesterday's wound's, which smarted and bled, Are healed with the healing which night has shed. • Yesterday now is a part of forever; Bound up in a sheaf, which God holds tight, With glad days, and sad days, and bad days which never , Shall visit us more with their bloom and their blight, Their fulness of sunshine or sorrowful night. Let them go, since we cannot re-live them, Cannot undo, and ca3inot atone; • God in His mercy receive, forgive them; Only the new days are our own. To-day is ours, and to-day alone. Here are the skies all burnished brightly, Here is the spent earth all re-born, Here are the tired limbs springing lightly To face the sun, and to share -with the morn In the chrism of dew and the cool of dawn. Every day is a fresh beginning; Listen, my soul, to the glad refrain, And, spite of old sorrow and older sinning, And puzzles forecasted, and possible pain, Take heart with the day and begin again. SUSAN COOLIDOE.

Monkeytown is the name of a new post-office in Yazoo County, Mississippi. Doubtless the postmaster could unfold a tale. It was a family gathering, called to name the baby. The name proposed was "William." The jury retired, and in two minutes returned and reported, "No. Bill." "Here," said the salesman. waving his hand, "is a full line of our celebrated spring beds." "Yes." replied Mrs. Malaprop; "they were very nice for the warm weather, but I want to see some of your autumn beds." "Your plot is ingenious," remarked the manager to the young play-writer, "but there is rot enough of it. How do you expect this fragment to stretch over thiee hours ?" "Oh, it will stretch all right," was the reply. "I'll make fifteen years elapse between acts one and two." "Mr. Editor, did you read that article I hassled you yesterday?" "Yes, sir." "What would you think after reading that, if I told you that I had but one year's schooling In my life ?" "I would think that you must have wasted your time most abominably." "Mamma," said a, beautiful maiden, in tender tones, one morning at breakfast, "Henry is coming around to- morrow night." "Well, what of that ?" replied mamma, with in-concealed disappointment. "He's been coming every Sunday:night for two years." "Very true, mamma, but neither of them was leap year," and a cold, hard, determined look spread over her lovely features. President Cleveland is a model husband. Waited upon by a committee from Cincinnati and requested to go to that city and "bring Mrs. Cleveland with him," he replied, "I will come myself, but as regards Mrs. Cleveland I can say nothing, as I never • control her actions and wishes." The advocates of women's rights and suffrage in the States say they shall vote for Cleve- land next election. Some European ladies passing through Constantinople paid a visit to a certain high Turkish functionary. The host offered them refreshments, including a great variety of sweetmeats, always taking care to give one of the ladies double the quantity he gave to others. Flattered by this marked attention, she put the question through the interpreter—" Why do you serve me more liberally than the rest ?" "Because you have a larger mouth," was the straightforward reply. Aunt Madge was entertaining a friend from the city, and little Gertie had come with her mamma to spend the day. Miss Kate, the visitor, made herself a favourite with children, and Gertie was soon her devoted admirer. i When mamma was ready to go home Miss Kate asked Gentle to stay. "If you go now you will not see me any more," she said impressively. Gertie, who was pull- - ing a tiny mitten on her dimpled hand, immediately answered, to the surprise of a 11—" Well, I've seen 'oo enuff." MURPHY'S WELL.—Cotonel Stokes, a wealthy cotton planter of Madison County, Miss., employed Jimmie - Murphy to dig a well. When the work was completed Jimmie called for his pay, and the following colloquy occurred How deep did you sink the well ?" "Phortv phutt, sue." "How much water is there now in it ?"' "Bate phutt. sun." "Is it good and clear ?" "Slum an' it was, sur, until the tadpoles and wagles got into it, but some of the nagers towld sue to put a couple of fish in the well and they would desthroy the divils, an' I have done it. The tads and svagles are as ded as me spade, but shure an' the waster tastes pow'ful of the fish." Upon investigation it was discovered that Jimmie. instead of putting live fish into the well, had placed therein a couple of pickled mackerel. At the last session of the German Reichstag, Herr Wichmann, it is said, was calling the roll, and coming to his own name, called it without getting any response. He repeated the name again in a louder tone. Still no answer, and he spoke it for the third time at the top of his voice, upon which the laughter of the House brought him to his senses, and he =irked himself present. To match this there is an anecdote in Mrs. Leslie's "Recol- lections of llify Msther," concerning an old Northampton stage driver. He had a phenomenal memory, to which he trusted implicitly, receiving and executing all sorts of commissions daily without ever making any memoran- dum. Once his wife went to Boston with him, and on the day when it had been agreed that she should return, ' the man was troubled all the way to Worcester with the feeling that he had forgotten something. He tried in vain to think what it could be, till just as he was whip- ping up his horses to leave that town. Then it suddenly came to him, and he exclaimed, "Oh, it's my wife! I've left my wife!" THE ADVANTAGES OF REST.—There is DO better preven- tive of nervous exhaustion than muter, unhurried, muscular exercise. If we could moderate our hurry, lessen our worry, and increase our open-air exercise a large proportion of nervous diseases would be abolished. For those who cannot get a sufficient holiday the best substitute is an occasional day in bed. Many whose nerves are constantly strained in their daily vocation have discovered this for themselves. A Spanish mer- chant in Barcelona told his medical man that he always went to bed for two or three days whenever he could be spared from his business, and he laughed at those who spent their holidays on toilsome mountains. One of the hardest worked women in England, who has for many years conducted a large wholesale business in England, retains excellent nerves at an advanced age, owing, it is believed, to her habit of taking one day a week in bed. If we cannot avoid frequent agitation we ought, if pos- sible, to give the nervous system time to recover itself between the shocks. Even an hour's seclusion after a good lunch will deprive a hurried, anxious day of much of its injury. The nerves can often be overcome by stratagem when they refuse to be controlled by strength of will. THE SLOWEST YET.—IL is well known That the Texas street cars do not travel quite so fast as a comet. An illustration of how slow they travel occurred the other day in A Texas city when a car-driver was discharged for a crippled man. The man who made the complaint had been in the habit of riding on the street cars before he was laid up with paralysis. The first time he was able to get out on crutches he signalled to the street car-driver, but the latter drove on. The car-driver owned that he saw the man, but didn't know that he wanted to ride. The cripple proceeded to the office of the company and made complaint. The driver was ordered to appear before the the president of the com- pany. "Did you see that crippled man ?" "Certainly, I saw him." "Did he signal to you/ with his crutch to stop?" "I saw him shake his crutch at me and heller something or other." "Why did'nt you stop the car ?" "Because I didn't think he wanted to ride on the car, for he could gd faster on crutches than the car. When he shook his crutch I thought he was making fun of me for going so slow. I thought he was bantering me for a race, so I put the whip to the mule and made the car go as fast as I could, and somehow I won the race." —Texas Siftings. HAWTHORNE AND THE YANlEE.—Nathaniel Hawthorne was a kind-hearted man as well as a great novelist. While he was Consul at Liverpool, a young Yankee one day walked into his office. The boy had left home to seek his fortune, but evidently had not found it yet, although he had crossed the sea in the search. Home- sick, friendless, nearly penniless, he wanted a passage home. The clerk said Mr. Hawthorne could not be seen, and intimated that the boy was no American, but was tryiag to steal a passage. The boy stuck to his point, and the clerk at last went to the inner room and said to Mr. Erawthorne—" Here's a boy insists upon seeing you; he says he's an American, but I know he isn't." Haw- thorne came out of his room and lopked keenly at the eager, ruddy face of the boy. "You want a passage to America?" "Yes, sir." "And you say you're an American?" "Yes, sir." "From what part of America ?" "United States. sir." "What State?" "New Hampshire, sir." "Town ?" "Exeter, sir." Hawthorne looked at him for a minute before asking the next question. "Who sold the -best apples in your town?" " Skim- milk Folsom, sir," said the boy, with glistening eyes, as the familiar by-word brought up the dear old scenes of home. "It's all right," said Hawthorne to the clerk, "give him a passage." THROAT IRRITATION AND COUGH.—Soreness and dryness tickling and irritation, inducing cough and affecting the voice. PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE.
XIV.-THE SCHOOL BOARD.

There was for a long time an appreciable vacancy for a useful institution in this country. Such great and noble institutions as the Long Parliament, Chief Justice Jeffreys's Special Commission, and the Antedeluvran Order of Buffalos have executed glorious things, and their respective merits have been justly appreciated ; but after all none of them filled the gap. Ever since Sing John signed Magna Charta England has agitated for and obtained inch by inch such a degree of freedom that it became necessary for its own welfare that a check should be put upon its unlimited liberty. Par-seeing men began to recognise that the pride developed, and the conceit engendered, by such total emancipation might ultimately lead the nation astray by feeding its head-strong pro- clivities, and the embryo of a magnanimous institution began to grow slowly, but surely.

We will not enter into the particulars of detail connected with its early life; suffice it to say that to-day it stands abft—a mighty and ever-increasing powerful institution. We call it the School Board.

The reason I haven't gone more into its antecedents is that I freely confess my technical ignorance of boards generally. I can tell a pitchpine board from a mahogany one, after which I am literally at the mercy of all boards, the School Board included. With this apology I shall proceed to dissect the School Board, after requesting the reader not to jump on me if I don't follow the beaten track. It will be readily understood by tracing the prin- ciples that first brought it into existence that the chief object of the School Board is to instil into the mind of , every Briton the lessons that the School Board is the nation, and that his children are more the property of the Board than his own; and when you come to a close , examination of the subject it is reasonable that the Board, selected from the-best possible intellectual sources, should dictate the requirements of each child to the ex- clusion of the father's wishes.

I feel sure in seating (so sure in fact that I will make the statement upon my own responsibility) that every member of every School Board can read and write; and in these days of education that is something to be proud of,. and fully entitles the Board to its authority. Suppose your place of residence has been selected on account of its being near your work, and both are over a mile from any school; suppose also that you have a little girl between five and six years of age who has the unfortunate tendency to get wet when she walks over a mile in the rain, have you to keep her at home? Not unless you are prepared for the full meaning of "five shillings and costs.' Your proper course is to make application to the Board, and it will probably inform I you that no sane marrwould thinlc of living and working over a mile from a school. According to rule 4 of the School Board regulations, when you keep a child from school in consequence of sickness, a medical certificate should (except in very temporary cases) be obtained and furnished to the Board. Of course you should I always have a medical man in the house instantly a child shows the least chance of being detained from school, and however simple the ailment you ought not to think of prescribing for it yourself; but if you don't know your duty in this respect you may at least procure a I medical certificate. You can get them for nothing that is if you are a medical man; the alternative 3s Jive shillings and costs.

Under the head of " employment " there is a rule that I am going to shy at; but before you venture to think that I am easily daunted, I beg you to consider that very old and very wise heads have meditated long before building that rule. I have put it before one school- master, but he couldn't enlighten me in the slightest degree. My dictionary being a cheap one, only gives the following simple definition of the word "employed." "To have the time, attention, and labour occupied ;" consequently it doesn't help me. I will quote this rule verbatim and leave you to study it. "(1) No child under 10 years of age may be employed IN ANY WAY wmarEvaa (at home or otherwise)." There is nothing makes a man feel more ignorant than to be utterly unable to under- stand two lines of a paper that is pushed under every door, and I can now see with regret the effect of there being no School Board when I was a boy. Why you have only to make the most casual observations in every- day life to be convinced that a beneficial influence has been wrought upon the youth of this generation. might Oita to many examples, but I will content-my- self with simply alluding to the progress of the pro- fession of football. which is so generally acknowledged that ir doesn't need any comment. Not the least feature of the School Board is the mighty engine, the inspector. A description of this official trom the point of view of the small boy wouldn't enable you to kick him out in the street. He is about ten feet high, and broad in proportion; stern beyond all description; the most noticeable part of him is his eyes, which may be compared to a mixture of field-glass and microscope; he can see small boys through walls and round corners; and he has a large pocket-book the size of an average ledger, in which he writes their names. When this official has, in a moment of thoughtlessness, patted a small boy on the head, and said, "good boy," the said boy never again looks behind him, so to speak. Now it is generally thought that small boys don't in- terest themselves about th* School Board, in fact they never heard of such a thing'. With a view to testing his knowledge of the institution I asked my youngest boy, aged six, what a School Board was and how many inspectors there were to one School Board. His answer was long and the details many, but I found that the following is a paraphrase of his idea of the School Board. The board was kept at the Police Station. and when the inspector wrote down any small boys' names in his great, great big book he went to the Police Station and copied the names from his book upon the board, which a policeman read, and immediately went off to fetch the small boys and to cast them into prison. It was useless for me to try and explain what a School Board really was; he wouldn't believe me; and there is only one person on this cold planet who could convince him, that is the inspector. The School Board is, of course, useful in a variety of ways, one of which is that you can lodge complaints against schoolmasters and schoolmistresses, and this is taken advantage of chiefly by doting mothers who don't believe their cherubs could do anything to irritate their teacher. For my part I think it more reasonable to write the teachers for an explanation in the first in- stance, which I have always found satisfactory. But there are odd cases where the bare thought of such a course takes the padding out of a man. I will give you my own experience of one. The youngest male issue of the line of Bette one day came home in the middle of school hours, walking as if he had seven corns on each foot, and shedding crocoolle tears. When he was full ten yards from the house he began his explanation, "Teacher wouldn't let me dow out. A very superficial examination proved that he had blotted his metaphorical copy-book, and the, out- raged Mrs. Bette insisted that I should write to the Board instanter; anyway I must write to someone, or somewhere. But look at my position. On principle, I don't like to write over the mistress's head to the Board, and to write to the schoolmistress—reader, I tremble at the recollection, but I did it, and by a manly determina- tion not to swerve from the path of duty, I received a most gracious reply, and saved the School Board Clerk a task. which I guess would have made his hair stand on end.
-N-.B.—The fine of five shillings and costs is not pressecl in cases of this sort.

BUILDING SOCIETY MEETING AT WARRINGTON. On Monday evening the - annual meeting of the members of the Warrington Workingmen's Perman- ent Benefit Building Society was held in Golborne- st. Schoolroom. Mr. John Hatton presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. - The Sec, rotary (Mr. Peter Dalton) read the managers 18th annual report and the balance sheet. The report read as follows : " The managers have pleasure in laying the eighteenth annual statement of accounts before the shareftelders as shown in the annexed statement. The sum of £1,586 7s has been received as subscriptions during the year, and £2,033 9s for repayments, making the total receipts £3,619 les. The withdrawals during the year amount to £843 Os 7d. The sum of £1,625 has been sold to members during the year. There are• 184 subscribers holding 289± shares, and 32 borrowers holding 110 f shares, making a tOtal of 215 members holding 380 shares. The profits for the year, including £29 18s lid from last account, after deducting working expenses, amount to £359 3s sd, out of which the managers recommend a dividend of four percent, which will take £294 3s sd, leaving a balance of -£B5, which they direct shall be dealt with as follows: £3O to be carried to the con- tingent fund, and the remaining £35 to be carried for- ward to next year's accounts. The reserve fund amounts to £350, and the contingent fnnd to £BO. The whole of the managers retire. Messrs. Harding, Wallington, Fen- ton; Isherwood, Bouchier, and Baxter are eligible and offer themselves for're-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the register in rotation." The.CHamximr remarked that he might congratu- late the members on the fact that in every branch there had been an increase, except in the case of withdrawals which were less.—Mr. POTTER moved, and it was seconded, that the report and balance sheet be accepted.—Mr. WALLINGTON, in support- ing the adoption of the report, pointed out that there was a sum of £1,718 in the bank, and he re-, marked that the directors would be very, glad to see some of the members come forward at the sales of money and take this out of the bank. He thought that if they considered, the advantages the society offered them they would be ready to do this.—The report and balan& skeet were adopted.—Mr. PEN- TON moved, in accordance • with tha recommenda- tion of the managers,- that a dividend of 4 per cent. be paid for the past year. He should- have been I glad, be said, if some of. the money they had in the ba,nk bad beep sold, for then' their dividend would have been larger. He also urged the desirability of people getting houses of their own to live in.—Mr. ISHERWOOD seconded the proposition, which was agreed to.—On the motion of Mr. HAVIOUR, Se-' conded by Mr. RUSSELL, Messrs. Harding, Walling- ton. Fenton, Isherwood, Bouchier, and Baxter were re-eleoted managers.—Mr. J. E. Wright was re- appointed surveyor, together with Mr. W. Bodle, jun., in place of Mr. Doraville, resigned.—Messrs. W. Ford and J. Leeson were re-elected auditors of the society.—Mr. LoNGLAND proposed that the sum of .E 3 12s 6d be paid the managers for their services during the past year. He said that if the money they had in the bank had been sold it would, have made a difference of 2 or 3' per cent., and if they did not get it sold he was afraid they would not have so large a dividend next year.—Mr. Iliviourif in seconding the proposition suggested that money might be lent out to members without their having to wait for the sales to buy.—Mr. WALLINGTON ex- plained that members who wished to borrow need not wait for the sales, as they could have money ad- vanced at very, short notice on the usual bonus.— The motion was agreed to.—A vote of thanks to the chairman, moved by Mr. Issznwoon, and se- conded by Mr. FRNTorr, brought the proceedings to a close.

The Duchess of Edinburgh, while passing the summer at Coburg with her children, will occupy Rosenau, a " Jagd Schloss," which the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha has presented to the Duke of Edinburgh. Rosenau, which lies four miles to the north of Coburg, is interesting aA baying been the birthplace of the Prince Consort, and the Queen has twice stayed there. The interior is beautifully fur- nished, and is remarkable for a very fine collection of hunting trophies.

The monthly meeting of the Committee•was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. Mr. J. Ry- lands presided, and there were also present Messrs. Blackhnest, Greening, Jolley, Balharry, Ratcliffe, Clark, W. Long, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Owen, J. Houghtlih, Pennington, and J. C. Sutton (clerk.) .ComursnaE Mims. On behalf of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Mr. R. Davies appeared before the committee td appeal against the assessment of Cockhedge Mills £3,436 gross; £2,665 rateable. In the course of some remarks Mr. Davies pointed out that Messrs. Armitage and Rigby paid 10d in the £ lass on their Manchester works than in Warrington. In Manchester the rates were 4s 4d in the £, and in Warrington 5s 2d, while they ,get their gas in Manchester at 2s Bd, and it was really a. matter of importance that these expenses should be kept down.—lt was agreed that the matter should be referred to the valuer, Mr. Owen, who will report at the next meeting of the committee. VALUER'S REPORT.—Mr. OWEN reported as to new valuations he had made. The fustian cutting works of Mr. John Platt in Carlisle-st., were reported to have been closed on the Ist September last, and were still closed ; for partial occupation as a store only the premises were valued at gross £l2, rateable £lO. The Cockhedgepre- raises were also closed on the Ist September, and were opened 6th of February of the current half-year, were assessed at gross £2O, rateable £l7. Rylancls-st. pre- mises closed Ist September- and opened 6th February, assessed toi the current half-year at gross £9 103, rate- able£B„ Additions to the -Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, works were assessed at gross £lO, rateable £76 lOs ; additions to Messrs J. H, Flem- ing and Co.'* tannery, Fennell-st., gross £79, rateable £65 additions to Messrs McCorquothle and Company's works, Newton, gross £lB9 10s, rateable £l5l 103 ;addi- tions to Messrs Gillespie and Mason's paper works, New- ton, gross £59, rateable £53: With regard to Messrs Horton and Walker's works, Dallam-lane, Warring- ton, Mr. Owen suggested that the assessment, whilst the works were unoccupied, and used simply a store for engine and boiler, .be gross £54, rateable £3O, one third of the assessment.— he Beidgewater Canal : Mr. OWEN reported with respect to the Manchester Ship Canal Bridgewater Canals Under- taking that he had had an interview with Mr. W. H. Col- lier, who its now manager of this undertaking. He (Mr. Owen) gleaned from Mr. Collier that although the busi- ness of the canal was better last year than the two pre- ceding years, it was not better than it was at the date the committee fixed the assessment at gross £420 per mile, rateable £370 per mile. He also learned that the increase made in the assessments of the canalin the Run- corn Union was only in the township of Runcorn, and not on theyout township of that Union. The appeal against the raising of the assessments in the township of Runcorn is to be held at Chester on the Bth July next, when all the facts and figures on the whole working for the year 1886 would-be given in evidence. He ascer- tained that the assessments in adjoining townships of other Unions compared with the township in their own as follows :—Appleton had an assessment of £350 per mile rateable, whilst Grappenhall was £370 per mile; Lymm had an assessment d £4ll per mite rateable, while ThelwaU was £370 per mile. As the whole of the figures of the working of the year 1886 and other infor- mation would be published at the appeal on the 6th of July, he had concluded it would be best to leave the present assessments unaltered until, after that date, when he could report further on the matter.--1- Newton Appeals: Mr. OWEN reported with regard to the Willows, Newton, the residence of Mr. McCorquodale, that the overseers had raised the assessment of the house from gross £265 to gross £275, but he had been over the premises, and was of opinion that the assessment of gross £265 was sufficient. The assessment of Park House, Newton, the residence of Mr. T. J. Gillespie, had also been raised by the overseers from gross £l4O to gross £l5O. but he was of opinion that the assessment was sufficient to cover this, and that it should remain gross £l4O, rateable £ll9. The report of the valuer was adopted. This was the principal business.'

WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held at the IV orkhouse on Friday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Jolley, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Grange, Kilshall, Humphries Owen, W. Long, J. Rylands, S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Humphries, (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). , ALLEGED POLLUTION OF A BROOIC.—The matter of the alleged pollution of the brook near their tannery, Thel- wall-road. by Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant, again came before the authority, and it was mentioned by the medical officer and inspector that the pollution was still very bad.—The CHAIRMAN said Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant contended that as there was no general system of drainage for the district they could not be expected to provide thorough drainage in the absence of such sys- tem.—ln the course of some conversation it was men- tioned that the brook was polluted to some extent by some cottages before it reached Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant's tannery, and it was decided to require the owners of these cottages to prevent the pollution, and that if this requirement was not complied with proceed- ings should be taken against them and also against Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant if they failed to comply • with a notice previously served upon them. PENKETH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—At a meeting of this committee, held on the 29th May, Mr. Routledge laid be. fore the meeting tenders received for the supply of pipe to flushing tank, and it was decided to recommend acceptance of that of Mr. T. H. Thomas, of Widnes, for the sum of up per lineal yard. Mr. Routledge also reported that the brook had been cleansed as directed, and that the cost was £3 18s 10d, which he had paid, and for which he produced axeceipt. The same was ap- proved, and it was decided to recommend a cheque for the amount to the Rural Sanitary Authority. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Sephton reported for the month ending May 31st—Births, males 71, females 20; deaths, males 13, females 16. The death rate from all causes was equal to 24-6 per 1,000, against 19, the average of the last three months. The cowsheds and dairies in Latchford, Grappenhall, and Thelwall have all been visited and found on the whole fairly satisfac- tory, and any defects noticed were pointed out and im- provements suggested. SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—The Surveyor reported that a sketch plan for new hospital for accidents only at the corner of Cross-lane and Thelwall-road, Thelwall, had been submitted by the Manchester Ship Canal contrac- tor.—The report was adopted. RE-APPOINTMENT.—On the motion of Mr.W.Houghton, seconded by Mr. Jolley, Dr. Sephton was re-appointed medical officer for the ensuing year.—An application was made by the inspector (Mr. F. Kerfoot) for an increase on his salary of £BO a year. On the motion of Mr. Pen- nington, seconded by Mr. Jolley, Mr. Kerfoot was re- appointed at £9O a year. This was the whole of the business.
RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. A PLAIN STREYTFORRITD NON Aw've trodden t' rooadp' life a while,

Un pept i' different skoos, Till aw've fun eawt as th' world's med up 0 romigues un honest foos. Aw'm one o'th' foolish sooart Sooa, as aw travel on, Aw'm fain to greet whene'cr aw meet A plain streytforrud mon. Them chaps ut's starched slap up to th' een, They bod seem med for show, Donned eawt i' broadcloth, cheons un rings;
Sum's goWd seet-lamps un 0! This world's a big uh, wheer a fop l'th' rook ceawnts nobbut one;

Un sitch as me wod rayther see A plain streytforrud mon. Ther's sum as keer for nobry else Iv they con fill ther peck; They'll nab ther needs, hi fair or feaw, While foo's are howdia' t' seek. Ther pet ambition seems to be To diddle o they con. Vi' wod ill grace they look i'th' face, A plain streytforrud mon. Sum look so meek Un fiddle-faced, Un shap t' saint 'boon a bit; Bud fooak Wr e'en con see streyt tbro' A smooth-tongued hypocrite. Wod hollo'-hearted things they are As try sitCh trickery on. Aw'd send 'em o wheer they'd ne'erkn)yr A plain dtreytforrud mon. Ther's sum thad preawd, till ackshully, They dorn'd know heaw to tawk ; They'll any ther nooases up tort' sky, 4 I Un waggle as they wawk. Hey! dorn'd thEy favver summat big, As, swaggerin' like a don, They glare wi' scorn on th' lowly-born Un plain streytforrud mon. Aw reckon nowt o' sitch like fooak, They do no good for ti:' world, Bud live too fast, un act too slow, Ther life-streng's soon untwirled. They wern'd gie Poverty a lift, Nor put id meyt th' pon ; • Ther's nooan tit lot as keers a jot For th' plain, streytforrud mon. Gie me a chap as tells his thowts P blunt and hooaroly speech, As shows, wi' deeds ov honesty, He'll do, as weel as prevail. A chap ut's gradely jannock, too, His word 'll allus ston ; Thad's mon for me, he's teed to be A plain, streytforrud mon. Ole me a mon wi' th' common sense To know- woe's reight fro' wrong, As never lets a nasty slur Or lie slip fro' his tongue. Un gie me th' grip o' th' hardy bond, As feels when Friendship's won; For t' true heart knows t' best friend ov o's A plain, streytforrud mon.
JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.p: CHAPTER XX.

HEADING THE WILL. If Simon Knight had been a man in an elevated position and a millionaire, there could scarcely, have been more interest about the opening of his will than was shewn by those people about Wandsworth who happened to be acquainted with him, Mrs. Knight and Phyllis excepted; and yet natnrally they should have been the most interested. It was not that outsiders expected any legacies from thq Wandsworth builder; only curiosity was aroused by a sort of impression that existed to the effect that Simon Knight's will was an unusual one; and that if, as report said, he had been started at Wandsworth by Mr. Stanhope, likely enough all the money would now go back to the Stanhopes, and perhaps his widow and daughter would be mere paupers. The arrival of Mr. Stanhope on the day of Simon's death had somewhat increased this view, which be- came to most people an absolute certainty when it was hinted about that he intended to be present when the document was read.
It was on this account, probably,that Geoffrey was absent.

----- The little party assembled in the room where the lawyer sat with the important parchment on the table before him consisted only .of Mr. Stanhope the widow and child of the deceased, Tom Chilton, and Greaves, the foreman, who did not expect to be wholly forgotten. • To a physiognomist Henry Stanhope's face was a study. "Did he fear lest his money should not be restored to him, or why that anxious, troubled look? Surely if it was his own he could claim it without wanting any will to be drawn up in his favour?" So thought Tom Milton, who, only there as a friend of the family, and looking for notliing him- self, devoted all his attention to the perusal of Mr. Stanhope's face. _ Ha little guessed that it was the fear lest a reason should be given for money having been advanced that was troubling Mr. Stanhope so deeply. At last Mr.Pettigrew, the solicitor,having adjusted his spectacles and cleared his throat, the reading

began. People were right when they looked for an un- expected will; but no one had in the very least hit on the exact arrangements that Simon Knight wished to have carried out. There was no mention in it from first to last of Henry Stanhope, nor of the souxce,ns far as the Wandsworthbusinesswas concemed,whence Simon Knight's money had been derived, the whole of which he left absolutely, to his daughter,Phyllis,with the understanding that, having a head on her shoulders, she would carry, on the business and. strive to double the money he left her at his death. If she were unmarried at the time she was not to marry for two years or she wonld forfeit every penny, which, would, in that case, go to a distant cousin of Silnon Knight, of whom no one there assembled had ever heard before. A breathlessness fell on the whole party while the provision was being read, and they waited in some suspense for the namingof the sum of money left to provide for the now somewhat ailing Hannah, who ' had been a true and loving wife to her quarrelsome and overbearing spouse. But not in any way was she mentioned—even as though she had never existed had he left her out. Not exactly out of unkindness, if the truth be told,but because Simon Knight never for a moment expected Hannah to survive him and his sole care was to arrange for the future of the'busi- ness which had been nearer to him than kith or kin. He believed in Phyllis's practical habits and natural acumen, and be would confide the business to her care being unmarried. If she married he would re- frame his wi 17 and that .he would have done so at on on the ciscovery of her engagement to Geoffrey Stanhope there is little doubt, had not a sterner decree than he• could control summoned hiin obedience.

._„ Greaves—yes, Greaves was not wholly disap- pointed ; his was the only legacy—" a 'hundred pounds. to Abel Greaves—fifty for faithful service in the past, and fifty as prepayment for good work i to be done for Phyllis Knight u the future." This Was the only actual sum mentioned; all, ia one sweeping monosyllable, was to go to Phyllis; but till day-books were gone into and ledgers totted up, no one could exactly tell what that all conveyed. Mr. Pettigrew had lard the document once more Oil the table, and had taken off his spectacles, replaced them in their case, and put the case in hia pocket; still, not one *Ord had been uttered in that room. Phyllis had risen from her seat, and kneeling beside her mother, her head buried in her lap, was sobbing convulsively, while poor fragile-looking Mrs. Knight, with a sort of• dazed expression on her face, down which the tears were slowly trickling, was softly stroking with on& hand the girl's thick curling hair. Mr. Stanhope was the first to speak; he tried to raise Phyllis from her crouching position and bade her not cry, or she would make herself quite, ill. Relief seemed to have come to Henry Stanhope by the reading of that will. Strange, too, since he had , not been mentioned in any way. He looked a ' brisker and younger man than he had looked when , he enkred the room. _ .._•

In an unusual course, the individual who had obtained the most was the most indignant. "It is a shame, a crying, burning shame," ex- claimed Phyllis, rising to her feet, and pushing her hair back off her weeping face, "such a good kind wife and mother as she has always been ' • but never mind, darling," and she took the thin, white hand between her strong brown 'fingers, "it is only on trust fOr you that, I shall keep to the letter of that un- just will; you shall have every luxury, every penny that you can possibly want out of the concern. Keep heart, my own mother. Father'must have known how to trust me when he left you to my care; but he shouldn't have risked it all the same." _ -

A murmur of applause fell from the lips of everyone present when they heard Phyllis's words. Only Mrs. Knight's lips were still pinched and white; she could not accevt the situation as readily as Phyllis would, have wished. Poor body, how could she be expected' to do so? She murmured something about charity, and not troubling any- one long," which almost angered her danghter ; who strong in her resolve that life, if she could make it so, should be a bed of rosea for the mother she loved, was scarcely pleased at finding her in of more than making up for her father'. re- missness met by a sort of unbelieving coldness. "'u have no right to talk so," she said, turning shortly on Mrs. Knight; "have I ever led you to think you trouble me ?" "No, child, no. You have been aye good. I scarce know what I should have done without you ; but all this is a heavy trial, and him that's gone seems to have laid a doubt on me, as if I was a worthless woman."

• These words stirred Phyllis once more to the depths of her warm heart. "You are the best and purest. Mr. Stanhope and Lady Fedora can vouch for that ;". and Phyllis's arm was round her mother's fragile frame, while Henry Stanhope came forward to say is well-turned phrase of condolence, and assure Mrs. 'Knight that no one could possibly blame her for this glaring omission of Simon s,

Mr. Sianhope,howevor,seemed so well pleased at the omission of his own namarom the will that he scarcely sympathised con, amore with Mrs. Knight, but very soon after he took his leave, promisin,g to send Irene dver in the carriage to give the needful comfort to her old nurse, in aflording which he felt that he had utterly failed. Mr. Stanhope gone, and Grea,ves having returned to the yard to begin, as he expressed it, a period of faithful service to Miss Phyllis, Mrs. Knight sat on in her arm-chair very silently with wide open oyes, as though she were looking into space for counsel, and Pfjyllis was left to a practical con- versation with Tom Chilton and Mr. Pettigrew. And very practical and determined she looked, very un- like the haunted nightmare dreaming Phyllis who had talked horrors with Geoffrey on the morning of her father's death.

And yet it was scarcely a week ago ; what had changed her? Circumstance—which has a potent influence in changing most of us. For the last week she had been in authority, giving orders, and seeing that work was properly done, after a fashion that had not a little astonished those who had witnessed how utterly crushed she had been at first by the suddenness of her father's death,

The fat was that Phyllis, through the kitchen window, had seen that meeting between the two StanhOpes and Tom Chilton in the yard. She had heard no .spoken word, but she had drawn her own deductions, and these deductions changed he; as no persausion, no hints, would ever have done. Simon Knight was right; he knew Phyllis to be a young person who could see clearly and would act straightforwardly according to the wisdom bestowed on her.
What she saw in that yard was that Tom Chilton was preparing to assume the position of master, and was under the impreadioz that neither Mrs. Knight

aor herself would be able to do without him. That he had been kind, most useful and kind, during the terrible and trying time they had gone through, *he readily acknowledged to her- sell; but he must not be allowed to get the thin end of the wedge too far, decided .practical Phyllis. There could not ,be two masters m that yard, and unless the business was sold, as Geoffrey had suggested, she would, with Greaves's counsel, manage it herself. Nothing she knew would have given her father greater pleasure than to know that she was carrying it on. She owed him a reparation; that reparation should be—work. Before the two Stanhopes—father and son—had strolled away again, Geoffrey not venturing to irritate his father by returning to the house, but only look- ing and kissing his hand to her in farewell, she had come to a decision. When Tom Chilton returned it was shining in bet eyes but she did not tell him or anyone what she had 'decided, only when he was not standing by she bade Greaves to take orders from her till affairs were settled, and said she would keep the order book and accounts, as she had done once before when her father was ill. Greaves was nothing loth; he had no love for Toni Chilton or any intruder; so business, what little business there was.while Simon Knight lay unburiedl drifted into Phyllis's hands; and now that the will was read, and she was left sole mistress, she felt hoW right she had been in taking her place at once. , Mr. Pettigrew, who had drawn up the will, had more than once tried to dissuade Simon Knight frog' making it; he did not believe in giving power to women, and how could any girl carry on such a boi: nese as that, it was absurd to expect such a thinig Before he had left the brickhouse at Wandswortht was, however, beginning to change his opinion. There was a practical knowledge of working matters and reliance on her own judgment about Phyllis which he had never thought to find in any woman, least of all in a beauty. But then, Mr. Pettigrer had in his youth married a pretty fool; "if only he had had a wife like Phyllis he would have been e richer man," he grumbled to himself as he went back to his office: Tom Chilton was not so thoroughly convincea of Phyllis's powers as was Mr. Pettigre*, prinei" pally, perhaps, because he did not wish to be se• He had a strong inclination to have a finger that business pie, and lie wished to think the; Phyllis would not he able to find good meat for lv and bake it without him. He lounged about the pre' mises, his hands in his pockets, whistling softlY, his mind full of thought, while Phyllis took her Mother to her room to lie down a bit, and the! busied herself as she ever did with her many sine° domestic operations; she seemingly paid no atten: tibn to Tom Chilton, though there was little doubv she was thinking the while that if the perpetual in" tmsion of this man's presence was to be stopped, et understanding of some sort must be come to betweee them. Even as she was conning over the how', TO Chilton spoke— " Your father's will has taken us all a little by suf. prise, eh, Phyllis ? " "Not me, except as far as mother is concerned." "You gave him credit for believing, in you?" "Aye. He always taught me all there was learn about the business." ." Wise • man; the only pity is your learnh4 wasn't confined to the business."

"What do you mean Tom?" "I mean the fine things you've learnt at t-a, Stanhopes ; they haven't lone you any goo Phyllis. , • "The more knowledge • you can get the better' knowledge never hurts anyone, Tom." "Knowledge as is out of one's sphere ain v good, take my word for it ; it breeds dissatisfactioP lass!" "I'm not dissatisfied. I shall • have no time to dissatisfied with all the work I have to do." "You won't have so much time t go to Eate'r square, and that will be good," he • aided. "I wonder what difference it wt.. make to gdo whether or not I go to Eaton-square. I have br in the habit of going to the Stanhopes all my But it's only of late you've took to sNyeetheartw° tith .Mr. Geoffrey." " Tom!" And the waN s;ich anger in her tone,such wrsl in her eyes, that Chilton ought to have but he he went on in a grumbl:44 voice, "Well, in two years that sort of nonsense have worn itself out, that's one blessine • Phyllis did nct speak ; she looked as if she workmfr herself, up to a fierce answer; but prevailed, and She remained, silent, only threw., window up suddenly, and tossed a panful ?f bread -and potatoes to SODIC fowls that were gathe`" about the door. Chilton watched the fowls fighting over t.l. precious morsels they preferred,. and waited stourof mg by Phyllis's side a., the window till every Se, ti had been devoured, ,and the birds: had return& their usual wanderinss. Then he 'said- slowly : "I've been 4 thinkiv, Phyllis, that I might be o 01, to help you somewhat. " How ?" niOP •The short answer was not espechilly moura, but he went on— lao "You know I've got a bit of coin, some' of "- is lying loose at this moment." " I" "If I was to, put that into this concern of yours, 0 might work it up, together into a rare big businc•9Biir A sudden flush came to Phyllis's brow at this Ped pof!al and she answered at once, sneaking quickly— ••••—•:• • • • "No, thank you, Tom ; I would rather be indeP dt.it. I can manage pretty well with what therl; I think.. Though father's will mentions no O haven't had the 'books in my hands for nothing'„.eA I know within a few pounds what the incomings "But whatever they are,they may be doubled,,'' in the young man. "They are enough for me and mother's Wo' _4O "Butryou will not always be as you are now--' will marry one day, Phyllis, and--" "I must wait two years, you know, and th 1,00111: blgssing, as you yourself have just observed, interrupted, half laughing. sett He was a little taken aback by her quick 05" but he said, "I wonder if, at the end of those two yearsl,o "Look here, Tom,we won't look so far ahead, T 4 0,0 please. The illness of Mr. Bright forms a topic of general and anxious conversation. Never in his long life has he been so popular in the higher society of Lon- don. No man in public life has been famous for so many years. Nearly ten years before Mr. Gladstone's first Budget, in 1853, Mr. Bright's name was one of terror to Tories and Protectionists, yet his habits are so little known that the " Standard " speaks of his rare appearances at the Reform Club. He has actually spent more than a score of afternoons there this spring, and about a fortnight ago he might have been seen there playing billiards with Mr. Illingsworth or chatting with the editor of the "Times" rind other Unionist friends. Since the long and serious illness he has some twenty years ago, Mr. Bright has been a fetal abstainer from all intoxicating drinks, but he had never ' wavered in his liking for an after-dinner cigar. In no place is he so much seen as the Reform Club. It has been the habit of Mr. Bright's Liberal friends of late not to intrude their opinions upon him, and to take with all kindness and respect, after• Mr. Gladstone's ex- ample,his ready remarks on the wickedness and folly and criminality of Home Rule. Somehow or other, by some personal charm or by the influence of his great career, Mr. Bright has seemed to lose no friends by these unsparing attacks, and to-day if the knowledge of an apparently universal sympathy could hasten his recovery he may accept the assur- ance of its fullest and immeasurable existence. All his friends wonder at his all-night journey to Roch- dale, for which there was no urgency. The 109th Derby-day opened with what a talen- ted writer in a London evening paper called an "auspicious morn." He also remarked that the "lowering welkin" of the day before, "which had threatened us every moment with the outpourings of the vials of its wrath," disappeared, and "sun- beams glaunced from Plcebus' face outright." lam not prepared to endorse all. this, which is evidently classical and smacks of Oxford and Cambridge, but —it was a very fine day on Wednesday, and the favourite won. The Prince of Wales was all on the Downs," and the Princess, with her eldest son arid three daughters, attended by a brilliant company of lords and ladies'and gentlemen and their dames. There was just dust enough to make one blink when on the road, and just wind enough to keep the dust pretty well on the go. For the rest, I don't think there were more people than usual at Epsom, and it struck me that, as on the last Blue Ribbon day, the omnibuses and waggonettes did not meet with the . patronage that the classic occasion deserves. In the evening the mild dissipation of the day showed its , traces on many of the returning travellers, and, as a , French journalist said last year, there were several people in town in good black broadcloth who looked 'careworn and sick."

A beautiful lady in Paris, belonging to the diplo- matic circle, lately met with a most peculiar acci- dent at a ball, to the intense delight of her "bosom friends" of the fair sex. The lady in question wore a low-bodied dress of artistic design which attracted general admiration, but what mrst riveted the atten- tion of the ball guesls were her shoulders of dazz- ling white. Suddenly her brooch, a splended cameo, became unfastened, dropped to the ground and broke to pieces. In her alarm, the fair owner quickly stooped to pick up the fragments. But this rapid "movement caused something still more valu- able to fall to the ground, viz„ a portion of the charming white shoulders of the lady, a piece of a mass resembling porcelain, delicately touched up in blue and pink. The gentlemen gazed in blank astonishment at the damaged beauty, while the ladies giggled in their pocket handkerchiefs, and the husband ran for a shawl to conceal the misfortune. (Tableau). I learn that a certain peer has recently become a traveller for a wholesale house in the city. We now possess aristocratic milliners, dressmakers, bonnet makers, perfumers, photographers, cab proprietors, private detectives, actors, social entertainers, curi- osity shopkeepers, coal merchants and money lenders', touts. There are besides but a few out of the many I could easily mention. Let me now propose a new trade. It is an acknowledged fact that many men and women, through constitutional nervousness, cannot unsupported parade the park. !I would therefore suggest that impecunious but well-known smart young men skould station themselves under the clock at Hyde Park corner, and hire themselves out at, say 5s an hour, to anyone desiring a companion. I really thiuk that a degent, respectable, and not over-wearying livelihood could easily be made out of this, and I therefore hasten to recommend it. A lady requires an accompliehed governess, but she can give no salary, because all her rev, hus- band's vestments are very costly, so she offers "a comfortable home; washing, and Church privileges." Another audacious flea-skinner requires a finishing governess, who is a thorough mistress of French, German, music, singing, and drawing, and she has 'the inconceivable effrontery to offer £l2 a year, as she "cannot afford more, having a son at college," but she can promise "full Church privileges." Another wants a lady help, who is to be a proficient in all work, and in many accomplishments, and she is offered .£lO a year, and the inevitable "Church privileges," which it is really too preposterous to hold out as a bait.

An inamrer has arrived at the important fact that out of the 658 members of the British House of Commons 410 are married men with -wives still living, 29 have been married twice, but are never- theless widowers, whilst one honourable member has lost three wives in succession. Altogether it seems that 504 of our elected representatives are or have been married; from which it would appear that our legislative bachelors form the somewhat unexpectedly large minority of 154. Both Mr. Bright and Mr. Joseph Chamberlain have been twice married, whilst Mr. Childers and Sir William Harcourt have not only married twice, but married widows at the second time of asking. Everyone who knows Mr. James Payn, the nove- list, is aware that he is as good a story-teller in society as he is novelist and whist player. One of his recent anecdotes relates to a popular astronomer, who, like Payn himself, is a Member of the lAthenasum Club. The astronomer paid a visit to America, and in the course of his travels reached the chief town of :I State well-nigh wholly devoted to agriculture. There were, as usual, a reception committee, with an official reception, a general levee of hand-shaking citizens, and so on. Presently the chairman of the board of reception, who had bided his time, came up. and addressing the distin- guished visitor, said, " Wal, sir, we have no acade- mical distinction to offer you, but allow me to say we bave done our level best to honour science in your person. Yes,sir, we have named our champion trotting pony after you, sir." The "Daily News" says the horror of the com- pensation scheme, and no milder term can be used, grows in extent and intensity every hour. Some of the religious bodies will certainly pronounce against it by large majorities, and there is every reason to believe that the Opposition will know of no dis- tinction of creed or sect. Cardinal Manning and Archdeacon Farrar are at one in their disgust with the licensing clauses. For this feeling the Govern- ment has in every "way only itself to blame. The 'compensation proposals are not only objectionable in themselves, but the manner of thekintroduction constitutes a most offensive challenge to general opinion throughout the country. The backwardness of legislation, which somehow or another does not come to be realised until mid- summer, is complicated in this instance by an ab- solute uncertainty as to the proposals which the Government intend to press, It is still uncertain what Mr. Goschen will do about his tax upon not only champagne, but cheap wines imported in bot- tles. His wheel tax is still hanging in the balance. The wheels do not seem to be greatly greased by the tax upon them. And the licensing clauses are generally admitted to be impossible in their present shape. The Cabinet on Saturday must, therefore,

RE-ASSEMBLING PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIRSDAY. The House re-assembled -niter the Whitsuntide holi- days. The Speaker, having recovered from his indis- 'Position, to& the chair silently after three o'clock. There was a small attendance of members. Peririolas.—A numbex.of petitions were presented, In- 'Oluding else by Mr. Handel Cossham, from Bristol, in favour of Women's Suffrages, and one by Mr. Sweten- ham agairist the licensing clauses of the Local Govern- Ment Bill from various goodies of Calvinistic Methodists in Wales. QuasaioNs. These were fifteen queations on the Paper, but several were not put in the absence of mem- bers responsible for bliem, and the remainder 'were not Of general interest. TEE ORDER OF NIBLIC BUSINESS:4\ft. SMITn, reply- ing to Mr. Baumarn, said the Governnaent intended on thisalay week to centimence the committee stage of the Local alovemment.Bill by moving thatlhe Speaker leave the chair. They 'would proceed with the bill on Govern- inent nights—Monday and Thursday :a 'and on Tuesday Sad Friday it was proposed to hold morning sittings' so that all available time should be devoted to the bill. Mr. Smith, in answar to Mr. Bradlaugh and Mr. Biggar, stated that the first order of the day on Monday would be the Imperial Defence Expenses Bill, to be followed by The introduction of bills f6r the improvement of the 'drainage of the areas of the Bann, the Barrow, and the '''Shannon. The third order wouldbe the Under Secretary 'for Ireland Bill. BALLINASIGE GUARDIANS.—On the report of Supply of May 17, Mr. A. O'CoNwort moved to reduce the vote on accouht bylo,ooo, protesting against the action of the Irish Local Government Board with regard to the Baffin- asloe Guardians.—Mr. BALFOUR said the Local Govern- ; Inent Board would have failed in its duty if it had allowed the continuance of suchdisgraceful sceees.—Mr. J. HARRINGTON and Mr. J. O'Coasioil also complained of the extreme course taken, the latterasserting that there 'as a design on the part of the Government to bring local representative bodies in Ireland into disrepute.— The amendment was negatived -without .a division, and the report of the Committee agreed to.—The House went into Committee of Supply. ADMIRALTY BUILDINGS.—On the vote of £4,200 for the extension of the Admiralty buildings, there was opposi- tion on architectural and economical grounds, and Mai Seaw-LEFEVRE also objected from an administrative Point of view, holding that if the money was spent it lessened the probability of bringing the Admiralty and the War Office under one roof.—Mr. PLUNEET replied, ,and explained that the scheme of 'extension put forward by the Government would cost LlBB,OOO, and could be completed in two and a half years. The vote was agreed to on a division. GOVERNMENT POLICY Di AFRICA. On the vote of £46,073 for salaries and expenses of the Foreign Office, Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL asked if England had abandoned the Soudan, and wished for inforination as to the fight- ing missionaries and traders who had established a quasi- dominion near the Great _Lakes in South-east Africa. Were the Government, he asked, encouraging annexa- tions there ? In order to elicit information he moved the reduction of the vote by £5OO. Sir J. FaaansoN Pointed out that Suakim was the only point now' held by Egyptian troops, but it was necessary to hold it to keep a check on the slave trade. Admitting the neces- sities of the situation in the Soudan, there was noireason why the rest of Africa should remain closed to European enterprise. There was 'little hope for the trade of this country except by opening up new markets, and English merchants would justly reproach the Goverment if they neglected to encourage any effort made in this direction. East Africa was perhaps the most hopeful district north of the Equaterwith which they were ac- quainted. The Consuls only took up, arms there when % European settlement was attacked and in a position of %oasiderable danger, and he need not defend the mis- aionaries from the imputation cast upon them—they were carrying on a goodwork with great courage and at much risk, and they totikaip arms only in self-defence. It was, he added, eminently desirable that where British Nerchants were willing to undertake considerable risks In pushing trade into the interior of Africa the Govern- Ment should give them all the assistance they could. Ultimately the Committee divided, and there were—for the amenament, 55 ; against, 103; majority against, 48. "-Discussion followed on the foreign policy of the Go- vernment, and Mr. ANDERSON moved the reduction of the vote by £l,OOO, as a protest against the treatment of Ring Ja. Ja.—On a division there were for the motion 62, kgainst ; majority against, 49.—After further dis- Mission progress was reported, and the House adjourned at thirty-five minutes past twelve o'clock.

The Spalding Board of Guardians, on Monday, decided, teethe casting vote of the chairman, against memorialising' 1 the Government against the pauper maintenance clauses Of the Local Government Bill. The Local Government Board has issued circulars to the Clerks of the Peace of Counties, Town Clerks of ,Boroughs, and Returning Officers drawing attentien to - 'the provisions of the County Electors Act, 1888, which renders it necessary that supplemental precepts should be issued to overseers informing them of the action to be taken by them for the registration of county electors with a' 'view to the election in the future County 1 Councii,s. Sir F,d, Clarke, speaking at Dartmouth, on Monday, said the Government was quite prepared to make con- cessions to the opinion which prevailed in the House of Commons on questions of importance affecting the Local Government measure, but some of the amendments pro- trsed were intended to delay the passing of the bile The, only part of 'he measnre Which raised a serious challenge-was the i ~.nsing clauses, but the question et • compensation would receive greatconsideration.
