div.head: WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING.
div.p: THE WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING.

The Duke of Cambridge presided ea a general meeting of the National Rifle Aseobiation, in London, on Tuesday, and, iii opening the proceedings, said that the prize meeting would be opened on the 9th July. He then read out the list of wit- including several additional ones, to be offeredattbe meeting. A question was then asked as to securing Wimbledon for future meetings. The Chairman intimated that he wished to ref* during the discussion as to a site. Accordingly he witadrow. Major Mc:lie-mow erged that Parliament should be asked to deal with the matter, as with a railway bill, and purchase the land. Lord Wantage replied that the Council were pledged to give up the land when called upon, and, under the circumstances, the proposal would not be entertained by Parliament They might, therefore, consider Wimbledon out df hand. Inquiries had been made in reference to sites at Rasing, Epping Forest, Purbright, and other places in the vicinity of Brighton, at Staines, the Berkshire Downs, and Richmond Park. The latter possessed all the advantages now enjoyed at Wimbledon. The Queen 'had intimated her willingness,to allow a portion of it to be used by the Association. The Duke of Cambridge, howevetwithheld his sanction, on account of interference with public access, and on the ground of the unsuit- ability of the ground for the new rifle. The site was, therefore, at present undecided. Sir Henry Fletcher spoke in favour of a site to the north-west of Brighton. Colonel MACFIR (Liverpool) said he had been deputed With others by the County of Lancaster Rifle Associa- tion to attend that meeting and move a resolution Urging the claims of Altcar. He pointed out that there were more Volunteers in the North and in Scotland than there were in the Southtif Ensland, and Northern Volun- teers were, in his opinion, entitled to some consideration on the score of convenience. At Abner the camping ground was ample. • Last week there were 3,000 regulars and Militia encamped there. The soil was sandy, and the water supply was ample. Besides that there was no disadvantage with regard to spent-bul- lets which would go out to sea. They would not have to buy two miles of land in order to get the ranges. There were now over 100 targets availible, and 100 more could easily and cheaply be added{ ForßB years the meetings of the association had beck held at Wine*, bledon, and metropolitan Volunteers 'bud been able to send their full complement to shoot for the Queen's and St. George's prizes. It cost them nothing to send three men per company, but the cost from the North of England involved a great outlay. In addition to the railway fare there was the board for the week, or, if the men were successful, for a fortnight, and there was also lodging money, beceuse some men did not like to live in tents. For 27 years the Northern Volunteers had been handicapped to that extent He submitted that it wouldbe only reasonable, for one year at any rate, that the meeting should be held at Altcar, and the cost df fencing would not be more than £lOO. The rail- way facilities were most convenient They had sent a memorial to 'Volunteers north of Birmingham for signa- ture, and 450 approvals had been returned. In the North there were 133,000. Volunteers, whilst eolith of Birming- ham, and for the rest of the country, the number was 94,000, and ho, therefore.-urged that the North should be convenieneed if only for a year. Colonel Brideman had arranged to second the motion, but he was unavoidably absent. Major RUIN, in seconding the -motion, said the Meet- ing must have learned -with some astonishment that, whilst the Queen had given permission for the use of Richmond Park,- there-were objections raised elsewhere. It certainty ought not to be thought that they were a body of-men seeking their own pleasure. Their motives were those of patriotism. • (Hear hear.) Sir HENRY HALFORD said if Richmond Park were ob- tainable it would be by -far the 'best place for their national meeting, but if it were not obtainable, then he thought it would be wise in the interests of the Volun- teers generally that they should go to Altcar for one year. (Hear, hear.) He inspected that site on Monday. It was thoroughly suitable in every way except that it was out of the way. It was perfectly flat and sandy, there was plenty of camping ground, and abundance of water, and the railway accommodation was excellent. He thought that Brighton was too far south. It was on the wrong side of London. The Berkshire downs had many advantages; but he preferred Altcar next to Richmond. Sir' HENRY WILMOT said that unless they could come to some arrangement about Richmond they would be driven to Altear. (Hear, hear.) If the negotiations were thrown into the autumn he did not believe they would be able to get a range ready anywhere except at Altcar. At any rate, for one year he • thought the Northern Volunteers deserved some consideration. The Hon. ALGERNON EGERTON, speaking as a member of the County of Lancaster Rifle Association, endorsed the remarks of Colonel Mactie. Be had been informed, on most excellent authority, that not only would the National Rifle Association receive the most cerdial re- ception from Liverpoel, but they would also receive a very handsome contribution towarijs their funds. As far as the range was concerned, the#fin Lancashire knew it to-be a most excellent range. He agreed with Sir Henry' Wilmot that there did not seem td be any alterna- tive but to go to AtMar for one year. Major WALLER supported Colonel Macfie's proposal, in the event of their not being able to get a range ready at Richmond. Referring •to the reasons given by the ranger for refusing the permission which her Majesty leid given, he mentioned -that the line of fire was 2,060 -tar& before reaching the confines of the park, and there was, therefore, no possible public danger. He (Fel not think it was possible for any bullet to break through the screen of trees, Which were-very thick Indeed. As to eeptiving the people -of the use of the park, re did not -lank there would be any public objection under that head for a fortnight-esel. year. Private LOWE thought the association ought to have a r•ermanent home, which must be in the neighbourhood of London. If they once went to Altcar, and invested money in targets- there,- they would have to stop. He minted out that southern Volunteers had, by reason of their attendance at "Wimbledon, provided the prizes Which the northern 'Volunteers had -carried off, and islted whether Liverpool \ Volunteers vould flock to ihcar in sufficient numbers to provide prizes for the -nu-them Volunteers? i"Yea.") If they could not find a ,ite neat London in 1889 he would prop/Ise to suspend "alerations for one year—(" No, no ")—instead of extend- e the range at Altcar for the benefit of the Liverpool Vo!unteers. Mr. W. WELLS suggested- that by means of a debate in -he House of Cemmons•the Government should be ',reseed- to contribute towards the expenses of rifle -ergots. Colonel BMW said that as it was necessary the meeting ~-ould be held in a Volunteer centre, and as there was a lifficulty about Richmond Park he would support the woposal of Colonel lYtacfie. Major APKenner.t. objected to the meeting being held ei a ground which for the rest of the year would be a !ractising range for the Lapeashire Volunteers. Colonel Macrae said the intention was to erect 100 , -sirs targets at an angle across the prose-at range, so • hat it would be entirely new to the competitops. He understood that the cost of the transfer of the present e imp material from Wimbledon would be borne by a ?uhlic authority. Lod WANTAGE promised that the subject should be eigiously and carefully coesidered by the Council. It would not be proper to vote upon the proposal, as the responsibility rested upon the Council to decide these
:•,atten3. • The proceedinas then terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1888.
GEItTERAL NEWS.
The Court wifl not, return to Windsor Castle until after Ascot Races, about Pane 28th. ' •

131•3 steamer Cecile, from Bordeaux, in entering the Mersey on Sunday, picked up with her lifeboat five men and three'buys in exhausted condition. The Leeds police, on Monday arrested the landlord of the flarewood Arms Inn, and two alleced bookmakers on a charge of betting. Thtaccused was remanded. - -
SMALLPDX AT WAREFIRLD.—On Monday, no less than six smallpox patients were removed to the Wakefield Infectious Hospital, making 31 since last Wednesday. - • •

An athlete, named Jackson, of Loughborough (Leices- .ershire), died on Sunday,'from the effect of internal injury, produced by overtraining for the Whitsuntide sports. A strike of 3,000 Jewish tailors' at Leeds, for shorter hours and the recognition by the masters of the trades union system, has collapsed. The men returned to work on Monday. Between twelve and one a.m. on Saturday, Mr. Charles Handcock, J.P., son of the late Hon. Charles Handcock, and cousin of Lord Castlemaine, of Moydrum Castle, Athlone, was thrown from a side car which he I was driving, and killed, his neck being broken. MORE GOLD DISCOVERIES IN WALES.—Rich gold quartz has been discoveredtin Gaegwernog, three miles from Dolgelly. It lay near the surface. Relays of workmen have been put•to work the ore. Quantities have been taken to London for analysis, and pronounced to be excel- lent. At a conference of delegates of the United Plumbers' Association, representing nearly 4,000 members in all parts of the kingdom, held at Sheffield on Saturday, a resolution was passed favouring the system of registra- tion of qualified plumbers as established by the Com- pany of Plumbers, London, and urging the extension of the system. A telegram from Dnnkirk says that four fishing schooners of Dunkirk and Gravelines are fully believed to have gone down with all hands in the great storm last month off the coast of Iceland. As each cf these boats carried 18 men' and 30 more are positively known to have perished, the total loss of life in this great disaster is brought up to 102. The Warwickshire police are scouring the district of Tamworth for a gamekeeper named Joseph Payne, in the employ of Mr. Fisher, of Amington Hall. One night last week Payne was at a friend's house at Shuttington Common, leaving about midnight. since which thine nothing has been heard of him. There are suspicions of foul play, as the gamekeeper was disliked by a certain class of persons in the neighbourhood. A young man VMS shooting at a target, at Treorchy fair, *Rhomidda Valley, on Monday, when a shot went astray, and, entering the forehead of a girl standing near, caused fatal injuries.—A waterman, named John Cole, attempted to doss the railway at Twickenham station, in front of an advancing train, on Monday night, and was,instantly killed. A porter, who tried to rescue him, had a narrow escape. ARODT TO EcorE.—At Greenock. on Saturday, a young married man named Win. Hunter, lately cashier with Messrs. Poynter and Son, chemical manufacturers, Greenock, was committed for trial on a charge of for- gery and embezzling over £2OO. The accused, when apprehended, was in company with a young female teacher, with whom, it is said, he intended to elope. On him were found two tickets for America.

Mr. Ruskin having been questioned by a correspondent as to whether he partook of Holy Communion, replies from Bmntwood, Coniston, "I gladly take the water, wine, and meat of the Lord's supper with the members of any family or nation who obey Him, and should be equ'ally sure it was His giving if I were myself worthy to receive, whether the intermediate mortal hands were the Pope's, the Queen's, or a hedgeside gipsy's." BIGAMY PREVENTED: SCENE AT A SHEFFIELD CHURCH. —At Sheffield Parish Church, on Monday, a plumber, named Charles Richmond, presented himself for marriage to a widow, named Widdle, but the marriage was stopped by a solicitor, acting on behalf of his iawful wife, from whom he separated seventeen years ago. Mrs. Richmond attended church on Sunday, heard the banns published, and obtained legal advice. Richmond was hooted as he left the church, and sought refuge in a public-house.

A MURDERER'S SYMPATIITSERS.—.-. A. public meeting, ief the inhabitants of Monk Bretton and neighbouring col- liery villnes was held on Monday, and passed resolu- tions further recording their opinion that of the two South Yorkshire murderers James William Richardson, who was hanged, was less culpable than Dr. Burke, who was reprieved, and urging that the question of the course taken by the Home Secretary -should be , raised in Parliament. THE SALFORD Gas Scam:lat.—Samuel Hunter, lately the gas manager of Salford Corporation, was on Mon- day taken from Strangeways Prison to London, to be brought up at the Central Criminal Court. Hunter, it will be remembered, pleaded guilty. and sentence was deferred‘in order that he might make restitution to the Corporation in respect of commissions he had wrong- fully received. It is understood that he has refunded a large sum of money. Sanas; CloansEtrre ox a RAILIAAT Cours_wv.—Colonel Rich, in his report to the Board of Trade respecting the railway disaster at Hoylake on the 7th ult., ascribes the collision to a total disregard by the company and by several of their officers and servants of the regulations under which the line has been worked. If it had been worked on the block system in connection with the train staff, as agreed to by the secretary in a letter to the Board of Trade dated let April, 1878, the collision could not have occurred.
SAD CASE OF Stumm—The Manchester- Coroner,

on Monday, held an inquest on the body of a youth (18) named Albert Edward Lancaster. Deceased lost his mother some weeks ago, and since then he had been in very low spirits. On Sunday morning he was found dead in an upper room of the house where he lived, hay- ing hanged himself with a clothes line. On the floor of another room he had written, "What is home without a mother? Good-bye.—Ted Lancaster." The jury found "That he hanged himseif whilst of unsound mind."

EXPLOSION OF A BOILER ON STELNER.—ItteIIi• genco reached Queenstown on Sunday morning by the Cunard steamer Servia, from New, York, that on the 17th inst. the boiler of a passenger steamer, Robert Henry, exT lodel while she was proceeding up the Elk river, Parkersburg. with 25 persons on board, of whom six were killed, including two passengers. Eight others were so terribly mutilated that they are not expected to recover. Only three persons escaped injury. The steamer was completely wrecked. ANTI. SWEATING DEMONSTRATION.— On Saturday, street parade of Jewish and English workers ~was ar- ranged by the London Tailors' and Machinists Society, in order to make a collection in aid of the Jewish tailors on strike against the sweating system at Leeds. The procession was beaded by a black flag, with the words "Down with sweating.. Help the Jewish strikers at Leeds," and when upon its return it reached Mile End Waste a meeting was held and the following resolutions were submitted and approved :--,-"That this meeting ex- presses its deep sympathy with the men and women who are the victims of the sweating system, and urges them to organise so that they may be able to win better terms for themselves by presenting an undivided front to those who oppress them," and "That this meeting, recognising the unjust conduct of the sweaters of London and else- ' where, urges in the strongest manner the London work- ' men to boycott the shops and warehouse where sweating takes place or where goods made by sweaters Ire sold." EXTRAORDINARY SCENES AT DOUGLAS.-1,000 EAS- Ski:GP:RS ALL NIGHT ON THE ,Pszrz..—One thousand visitors were left all night on the pier at Douglas, on Saturday. Owing to tthe New Many line run- ning only one steamer between Douglas and Liverpool, and many passengers whom they had brought during the week having delayed their departure from Douglas until Saturday, a terrific cruela ensued upon the steamer Queen Victoria arriving In the afternoon. The vessel landed 1,500 on Saturday, and the struggle to get on board the steamer was simply frightful, women and children being trampled on, and their clothing torn. One woman who endeavoured to jump on board fell into the water, and was with difficulty rescued. The steamer sailed crammed full, and there werell,ooo persons left clamouring on the pier fops boat to take them to Liver- pool. They had to watt on the pier, however, until four o'clock on Sunday morning, when .the Queen Victoria arrived, amidst groans,"and conveyed them to Liverpool. r INTERESTING TO NATURALISTS:A rather curious epi- sode in natural history occurred the other day on board the French steamboat Abd-el-Kader during the passage from Marseilles to Algiers. Just as the \vessel was about two hours out,ethe skies became quite black with swal- lows. It was then about six o'clock bathe evening. The birds alighted imthousands on the assilsoropes, and yards of the Abd-el-Eadsr. After a surrey of the deck from their eminences .aloft, they desceeded 'coolly on deck, hopped about among the sailors and passengers, and eventually found<their way into the cabins both fore and sit. The birds were evidently fatigued .after a long fright, and allowed themselves to be caughtby the people of the ship, who 'gave them a welcome reception, and pauvided them with food, which they enjoyed heartily. Theilittle winged strangers remained all night on the vessel, and in the ;moriung, at seven o'clock, the head looklaut bird had, no doubt, .sighted the Balearic Isles, for the whole flock made for land, after having spent a comfortable and refreshing night on board ship. LORE, JAMES DOUGLAS COMMITTRD TO PRISON: In the. Chancery Divisiort, London, on Tuesday, before Justice CAlitty, Mr. Romer, Q.C.. moved to commit Lord James Douglas to prison, for breach of an undertaking. The learned counsel said thrtt the motion was by Miss Mabel Edith Scott, by her mother, and was the third motion that had been made for committal. He now asked that Lord James Douglas should be absolutely committed to prison, in order to show that the order of the court might not be disregarded with impunity. Miss Scott was an infant of considerable means, and Lord Douglas had made proposals of marriage which were de- clined. In consequence of alleged persecution Miss Scott sought the protection of the court, and ultimately Lard James Douglas was restrained from communicating with the lady. It was now, however, alleged that he had disobeyed the order of the court. Counsel for the defendant tendered a psofound apology awl regret for what had occurred, but Justice Chitty, in making an order for committal, said the former leniency had appar- ently been thrown away,

div.head: RE LAND.
div.p: RE LAND.

Archbishop Walsh left Rome on Saturday afternoon, on his return journey to Ireland. A large number of friends assembled at the railway station to bid him fare- welL He is in good health. A subscription has been opened on the Kingston estate for the purpose of 'Presenting a testimonial to Mr. T. J. Condon, M.P., in recognition of his-efforts on Kingston estate in directing the Plan of Campaign movement. A man named Michael Staunton has been arrested in Glasgow by l`rish detectives, on a charge of being con- cerned in a inurdenti in county Mayo ten years ago. Staunton was on Monday remanded at Glasgow Police Court for two days. It is supposed Staunton had. since the alleged crime, gone to America, and recently returned. On Sunday afternoon, five boys, none ot them over 15 years of age, hired a boat and rowed down Belfast Lough. After they had gone a short distance the boat got capsized. The boys were thrown into the water, but one of them managed to get to a buoy floating a short distance off. Some boys who were bathing near swam over to the boat, but they only succeeded in rescuing one of the four lads. The other three were drowned. Last night the bodies of two of the lads were recovered. Information reached Belfast, on Sunday, of a terrible encounter between two farmers, near Banbridge, county Down. The combatants, named John Pren- tice and Alexander Guiney, were neighbours, and quarrelled on Saturday night. Provoked by junior members of both families, the quarrel resulted in a hand-to-hand conflict between the two men, who, having armed themselves with long knives, hacked each other in a frightful manner. Prentice is not expected to re- cover, and Guiney has been remanded in custody.

THE PAPAL RESCRIPT. GREAT MEETING IN LIMERICK. • The demonstration convened by the Mayor of Limerick on Sunday to adopt the resolution of the Irish Parlia- mentary party in reference to the Papal Rescript was attended by about twenty thousand people, fewer clergymen than usual being present. Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., was the principal speaker, and said he would not be deterred from his duty by threats, the .rashest and most disgraceful that ever appeared from the pen of an Irish ecclesiastic. They would not forget the respect due to Dr. O'Dwyer's sacred office, though he had forgotten it himself when he singled himself out from the trusted bishops of the Catholic Church, and rushed into pelt at the moment when his sacred brethren were remonstrating at Rome. He left Lime- rick the previous day, tatiirm care to supply his manifesto to every Orange paper In the three kingdoms. He did not forget the London Tins, but did not send a copy to the clef magitrate of Limerick. They knew the weight to be attached to the political opinions of Bishop O'Dwyer, who had a special faculty for being on the wrone. Ode in politics all his life. He dared to invoke Mr. wrong assistance, but when the Irish leader wanted his assistance he had done his worst to blacken Mr. Parnell's character. The constant disposi- tion of officials at Rome to tamper with Irish political affairs at critical moments was a source of apprehension and shame to the best priests and bishops in Ireland.

div.head: IRELAND AND THE VATICAN,
div.p: IRELAND AND THE VATICAN,

The Freeman's Journal says: The national idea of self- government in Ireland, indicated by Sunday's meet- ings, will never stand foreign enthralment. Their independent spirit feels it to be degrading, but the people will please neither the enemies of the Pope by disrespecting his spiritual authority, nor the enemies of Ireland by permitting any foreign political authority in Ireland. The existence not only of Irishmen, as individuals, but of the Irish people as a nation, is involved in the struggle of which the present agitation is a period and a phase; and the ropes— themselves the highest exemplars of morality and right —have resorted, for instance, to a system of boycotting the most extreme against the landgrabbers of their patrimony. The King of Italy, in the Quirinal, is more effectually boycotted by Pope Leo XIII. in the Vatican at the pre- sent time. Then, to ccmpare small things with great, any Irish land grabber is banned by his neighbours. It should be the policy of the clergy to guide the spirit of the people, rather than hold aloof; and this is the opinion and the judgment of the ecclesiastics best qualified to judge. They are all Irish- men, and the sheet-anchor of the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland—the unswerving and devoted patriotism of the priests, linked through weal and woe with the people, out of whose loins they have sprung. But, as Mr. Dillon said in Kildare, if Home Rule in Ireland were to mean Rome Rule in Irish politics, no man could ask an Irish Protestant to lift his hand or voice to win it. We say, authoritatively and un- falteringly, it would mean nothing of the kind. Irishmen would die rather than desert their faith, at the bidding of England or any other power; but Irishmen would die, too, rather than desert the country's cause, at the bidding of Rome- In establishing this, the Rescript, or Decree, has done a splendid service.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM.

The inaugural meeting of the new Liberal Unionist Association for Birmingham was held in the Birmingham Town Hall, on Monday night. The association has been formed in opposition to the old Liberal Association, from which the Liberal Unionists have seceded, and the objectef the meeting was the adoption of the laws of the new association. There was a large attendance, and among those present were Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P., Mr. George Dixon, MP., Mr. Kenrick, M.P., and the principal members of the Liberal Unionist party. Mr. Bright was also expected to be present, and considerable disappoint- ment was felt at the absence of the right bon. gentleman, from whom a telegram had been received by Mr. Cham- berlain stating that he was unable to attend in con- sequence of indisposition. Letters of apology for non- attendance were also read from Mr. Powell Williams, MP., and others. Mr. Dixon was voted to the chair pro tent., and the laws and constitution of the association were read. The CRAITVIAN moved their adoption. In doing so, lie explained the working of the new organisation, and de- plored that it was necessary to form such an association, but they were, he said, compelled to do so owing to the action of the Home Rule party, and in order to prevent the establishment of a separate Parliament in Ireland, and to show Mr. Gladstone or any other leader of the Home Rule party that no such result must be at- tempted. They were • told that the effect of sup- porting a Conservative Government meant that all Liberal legislation VMS to be stopped, and that we were to wait until the Irish question was put on one side. What had the Conservative Government, which it was said would do nothing—what had it done? It had passed the great conversion scheme of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, which would save millions a year to the naxpayers. It was not forgetful of the working classes, as was evidenced bythe Coal Mines Regulation Bill and the Employers Liability Bill. This Conservative Govern- ment ought also to be supported by the commercial classes because of their action with reference to the Rail- way and Canal Traffic Bill, and on the ground of general politics. Though Conservative in name, it was in reality a Liberal Government, because a Conservative Govern- ment knew that the democracy had now got all the political power owing to household suffrage and equal electoral districts. ,(Cheers.) The motion was adopted, and Mr. Chamberlain was afterwards elected president of the Association. Mr. CHAMBERLATN, having taken the chair, said he regretted this departure had been forced upon them, but it was rendered necessary by the surrender which Mr. Gladstone had made -to a faction whose policy for the greater part of his life he had denounced. For himself, he preferred alliance with the present Unionist Govern- ment to the great political revolution proposed by Mr. Gladstone. He regretted Mr. Gladstone's policy of mys- tery in reference to his method of dealing with Ireland, because he (Mr. Chamberlain) thought the present was a good time fot •considering this great problem. He had always held that if the land question were settled the difficulties attending local government in Ireland would almost entirely vanish. What was now unsafe, difficult, impossible, would then become per- fectly natural and reasonable. Therefore the settlement of the land question must precede reform, of local go- vernment. There might be some diYergence as to Ow exact form which local government should take, but the one great point upon which he would insist was that he would never recognise a separate political nationality in Ireland. In conclusion, he called upon Gladstonian Liberals to make 'known to the nation their alternative Vice-presidents and other officers having been duly elected, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Chamber- lain for presiding. Mr. CIIANTEMILATN. in responding, said: I thank you very much. The sight of this meeting, the sense "of your enthusiasm, are to me more than a sufficient reward and a great encouragement. Liberal Unionism in Birming- ham has hitherto been on the defensive. Now the time has come--it has been forced ripen us by our opponents —when we must assume a more aggressive mood— (cheers), and, gentlemen, you will remember the words of Shakspere-- Beware Of entranee to a quarrel; but being in Bear it that the opposer may beware of thee. (Cheers.) I have just received a telegram from Roth- dale to the effect that Mr. Bright's indisposition is of a somewhat serious character—(a voice: "Very sorry to hear it ")—and I thought you would like to send to him, under these circumstances, a resolution of sympathy— (cheers)—the assurance of the affectionate regard of his constituents, and your earnest hope for his speedy restoration to health. (Cheers.) I propose that I should be authorised in your name to send such-a resolution to Mr. Bright. (Cheers.) Mr. Dixox. M.P., seconded the resolution, remarking that he could assure the meeting from what he knew of Mr. Bright that it would be one of the greatest consola- tions in his suffering that could possibly be offered to him. The resolution was carried unanimously, and the meeting then terminated.

Five persons were drowned, on Saturday, by a tidal wave on the Clare coast, near Goleen Bay, half-way be- tween Kilkee and Carrigaholt. The unfortunate people were collecting seaweed, when the wave suddenly over- took them, and carried them out to sea. They were Michael Lynch, hisNeou and daughter, and Michael Odea and his son; both mon tk.shlg, farmers. The bodies have not yet been recovered.

div.head: TOWN BEGGARS.
div.p: TOWN BEGGARS.

BY A WARRINGTON TOWNSMAN. As the half-way house between two populous and contending cities, the link between two important counties, and a stage upon a national highway, Warrington receives, retains, and sustains more than itb full quota of beggars. Whether from the gullibility, the soft-heartedness, or the timidity of its inhabitants, certain it is that in this busy and expanding town beggars thrive to such an extent that they are loth to leave its hospitable boundaries. Watch the four main avenues leading into the borough any evening, summer or winter, and you will see entering the town with every conceivable Variety of gait, such a motley assortment of weather- beaten, travel-stained individuals, as will fill you with astonishment as to how they will find food and shelter. But follow carefully, for a short time, any one of these weary wayfarers and your astonishment will be of short duration. The eld hands, of course, have been here before, and know their way about. With the familiarity born of previous acquaintance, they betake themselves direct to the tramps' haven, where they report their arrival, and, if they have money, set about preparing their evening meals. If without funds, they learn very soon the residences of "generous givers," and are not long in obtaining sufficient "browns " to provide themselves with a night's "doss" and a good supply of victuals. The "greenhorns" may be seen, about six o'clock in the evening, in Indian file along the outer wall of the ' Police Parade Room waiting their turns for tickets of admission to the Vagrant Ward of the Work- house. Being insufficiently versed in the arts of "cadging," and loving liberty too much to court being "bagged," these junior members ot the beg- ging fraternity think discretion decidedly the better part of valour, and consequently seek a night's lodging, gratis, in the local " Worlthus." The granting of tickets is a severely business-like affair. The applicants, afraid of making too close an acquaintance with the establishment, steal sus- piciously into the spotlessly clean police office, pol- luting the very atmosphere of the place with their unwashed and unkempt persons. On the counter of the office lies the ticket book, and over it stands the "Officer in Charge," with as forbidding a coun- tenance as he can command. Scant ceremony is shown to the dusty travellers, as may well be imagined; and in applying for tickets a dialogue, somewhat after the following, ensues : Officer ( gruffly) : What's y our name ? Applicant: Michael Muldoon. 0.: What's your age? A.: Thirty-five. 0. : What's your height? A.: 5 feet 6 inches. 0.: What's your complexion? A.: Fresh. • 0.: Colour of your hair? A.: Brown. 0.: What's your occupation? A.: Labourer. 0.: Where were you born? A.: Ballyhaunis. 0.: County? A.: Roscommon. 0.: Where are you last from? A.: Manchester. 0. : Where are you for?

A.: Liverpool. All being apparently satisfactory, the ticket is granted, and the bearer hastens out, and with quickened steps makes for the "Union." But our business is not so much with this class of I beggar as with the professional cadgers, who make a good halt in our town while on their passage. The haunt of these individuals was formerly the low lodging-houses on Town lull; and some amusing examples of the hypocrisy practised by the har- dened deceivers were there to be witnessed. On Sunday mornings, the whole company congregated in the back yard of the house, and displayed to the I edification of their confreres the roles by which they avoided work. How many times have we chuckled over the " hard " lot of the one-armed man who maimed himself daily by first inserting his elbow in his sleeve instead:of his hand. How we have laughed, too, over the trials of the "poor crip- ple," as he has hobbled round the yard with a sym- pathy-moving limp, which has periodically changed legs! What mariners we have come across who have never been on board a ship in their lives, and what miners who have never seen the inside of a coal-pit! On Saturday nights, Town Hill swarmed with men "on the road,' and afforded splendid opportu- nities for the study of human nature. Far-reaching odours emanated from the lodging-houses, and told of the good times the birds of prey were having— times far different to those of the genuine poor who fail to elicit the substantial sympathy the profes- sional beggar knows se well how to obtain. As tpwn improvements have swept away the nest of dilapidated dwellings that stood on Town Hill, the beggars' colony has migrated to Dolman's-lane, ' the policeman's happy hunting ground, off Bridge- street. Here, any morning from nine to twelve o'clock, may be seen the gentry who are "working" the town, taking an airing, previous to commencing the day's operations. The men lean lazily against the pillar that blocks the entrance of the lane to carts, and take whiffs from stumpy clays with the air of self-satisfied persons. The women hang in groups about the lane cerner, or stand about the footpath, and gossip with the vivacity of people who have a lot to say and little time to say it in. After dinner, the company sally forth to earn their living, and they do it with numerous artifices and innumerable lies. There's the man who is "just a halfpenny short of his night's lodging money." So successful has this wail proved that the man has been known to unblushingly commence collecting his halfpence at breakfast time ! Then there's the fellow that tries "the confidence trick." "May I speak to you a moment, sir?" he asks appealingly. "Oh, certainly, as long as you like!" Theh he goes en to lie as fast as he can, asserting that begging is a thing he is totally unaccustomed t o, but through lack of work he has been forced to it, and he continues in this strain until he shows unmistakably to those who "know the ropes" that he is a transparent fraud. Another man pro- fesses to be at the end of his tether. He has no money, no acquaintances, and knows not where to go. His whole get-up is woebegone and calculated to excite pity, and he puts on the most fetching facial aspect. This individual generally turns up on a wet day, when the thought of a man with "no where to go" is sufficient to draw unstinted help. Such a man as this I like to get hold of, just for the fun of the thing. " Nowhere to go ?" say I; "why I pay so many pounds a year to find such as you with food and lodgings." "The Union, I suppose you mean?" "Yes." "Well, go there yourself!" savagely exclaims the man preparing to depart. "I have been there, and still would. go," I retort before he gets out of range. A third man will have a mania for walking, and will tell you he has tramled an impossible number of miles and nothing has passed his lips. Never- theless, the man's appearance betrays him, as he seems far from falling with fatigue. I remember a woman who tried this game on for a whole week. She came up to me in Rylands-st., remarking most earnestly that she had walked "all the way from Warrington!" "Is that so?" I queried. "It is in- deed," responded the old hypocrite. " Why you are in Warrington now !" said I. "Oh, excuse me, I meant Liverpool ! " "What have you come from Liverpool for?" "To look for my son who's joined the militia," she said, but all the consolation she got was, "Your son shouldn't have been so soft." Women are the most persistent of beggars. I re- call one bloated old creature who affected a limp, who had a daily round in Bold-st., Wilson Patten- st., and Sankey-st. Her constant cry to passers-by was: "Please could you spare a copper "--. "She's here yet," I remarked one day, when she immediately replied "And likely to be; I've as much right to live as you!" A very plausible old woman used to haunt the streets, attired in a dirty grey shawl and dress, shabby bonnet, and white apron. She invariably carried a hand-bag, in which was a number of knitted articles. She told a tale of former gentility, and how since her husband's death she had come down in the world. She was a wily old creature, and completely got over a gen- • tleman who takes a friendly interest in the deserv- ing poor. For weeks together, she kept in the good graces of this benevolent gentleman, until the , latter, happening to mention her to a relieving officer, found to his disgust that she was a rank im- • poster. This little, smooth-tongued woman would ' buttonhole any respectable woman she could, pour out her piteous story, and if she failed to obtain money would assert that she had got an order for some knitting from a lady. She had been with the ' work home but the customer was not in, and she consequently did not know where to turn for the next meal, as all her money was exhausted. She would beg the woman to advance her a trifle on the articles, which she would leave and fetch next morning. If she got money she faded to return, as the bag and contents were not worth near the sum ' she had obtained. I Other women are perpetually under bereavement.

They usually have dhildren dead and nothing to bury them in. The gift of an old garment would be thankfully received, but once obtained, it is forthwith „packed off to the pawnshop. The fact is; charity is wasted on beggars. If people have anything to,spare, they should send it to someone they know, and not bestow it on the that person that asks. From long experience of beggars, I can safely say I have never known a really necessitous person to ask for anything. It is the dissolute and shiftless who get the gifts ,of the benevolent, as they have implicit confidence in the scriptural 'in- junction "they that ask shall receive." It may seem hard advice, but the only safe course respect- ing beggars is to give nothing.

div.head: HORRIBLE TRAGEDIES.
div.p: HORRIBLE TRAGEDIES.

STABBING A PRINTER TO DEATH. The police have succeeded in arresting seven of the eight men who were together when some of their num- ber attacked and killed Joseph Rumbold iu Regent's Park on Thursday week. Deteotive-insnector Hobson with Inspectors Bannister and Rare arrested Peter Lee, Graefe Renshaw, and another, on Saturday night, and soon after three more of the men wanted appeared at the police-station and offered to give evidence in the case, but they were detained, and will lee charged this morning with the other four with parMipating in the crime. One man is still at large. At the Itre,Oebone Police-court, before Mr. De Ihrtzen, on Monda2. eight young men, Ren- shaw, Peter Lee, George Gallatley, William Joseph Graefe, Edward Gobrien, Frank Cole, Michael Doolan, and William Elvis, were charged with being concerned in the murder of Joseph Rumbold, in Regent's Park, on Thursday evening. Elizabeth Lee gave evidence as to the attack, but said she did not see who stabbed her sweetheart, nor could she identify any of the prisoners. Inspectors Robson, Bannister, and Hale deposed to. arresting four of the prisoners. The others surrendered, one being taken to the station by his mother to make a statement. Peter Lee, when arrested, said, "The man that did it had my knife, but I do not know his name." Only four of the prisoners had legal advisers. Graefe's solicitor urged that there was no case against his client, but all were remanded for a week.

The inquest on the body of Joseph Rumbold, who was stabbed to death in Regent's Park, on the 24th inst., was held on Monday, before Mr. Danford Thomas, coroner for Central Middlesex.—Eli7abeth Lee, who was with the deceased when he was attacked, gave similar evidence to that she gave at tjle police court.—Alonzo Byrne, who was walking behidd the last witness and Rumbold, deposed that he spoke to two of the lads who attacked Rumbold, and they said they thought Rumbold came from the Seven Dials. They further said they had been beaten by some lads from the Dials.—lnspector Robson said there were eight persons in custody charged with the crime. There was sufficient evidence to make a distinct charge against one of the prisoners.—The jury at once brought in a verdict of wilful murder against some person or persons at present unknown.

STRUGGLE WITH A DERANGED WORKMAN. A workman named William Davies, in the employ of Mr. Gilten Owen, builder, Bala. Merioneth, fired a gun at his master on Saturday morning. The shot missed and lodged in the chest of Evan Jones, a blacksmith. Mr. Owen struggled with Davies, took the gun from him, and beat him about the head with the stock. He was then secured and removed to Bala lock-up, where he was examined by the asylum doctor, who pronounced him to be utterly deranged. Jones lies in a dangerous condi- tion. SHOCKING MURDER BY A FATHER.

Late on Saturday night a man, named William Alfred Pierpoint, residing in Neate-street, Camberwell, who, with his wife, was about leaving there for a house in Runham-street, Walworth, seized his little boy Sidney, aged two years, by the legs, and dashed his head on the pavement with great violence. The little lad was picked up and taken to a local surgery, where he was found to sustafned such serious injuries that his removal t ily's Hospital was rendered necessary. He died about 20 minutes after his admission to the insti- tution. The father, who had run off after committing the deed, was afterwards arrested and taken to the rolice station. He will be charged with murder at the Lambeth Police Court to-day.

div.head: SUICIDE AND ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER..
div.p: SUICIDE AND ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER..

A shocking tragedy was discovered at Bristol on Sun- day evening, in Church-lane, Temple. An army reserve man, named Henry Clements, and his wife, recently took lodgings in the house of Charles Cole. Since Thursday nothing had been seen of them, and about eight o'clock last night the landlord caused the door to be forced, when it was found that Clements was dead, having stabbed himself with a knife in the heart. The woman-was lying on the floor terribly hacked by a hatchet on the forehead and arm, but was still living and groaning. On Thurs- day last screams were heard by the neighbours, but no particular notice was taken of the matter. The woman is likely to recover.

A POLICE SUPERINTENDENT MURDERED. A terrible tragedy was committed on Thursday morn- ing in Silver-st., Durham. Superintendent Joseph Scott, of Jarrow, was conveying a prisoner to Durham shortly before eleven o'clock, when a man who was fol- lowing suddenly took a gun which he was carrying from its case and deliberately shot the officer through the back. He then threw the gun away, and, drawing a revolver from his pocket, put it into his mouth and fired, part of his head being shattered, and a bullet pass- ing out at the back of his head. Scott fell dead in- stantly, and his murderer died within a few minutes. The latter has been identified as Benjamin Wright, an ex-sergeant of police, who had served under Scott at Jarrow, and who had been dismissed from the force for bad conduct. Both bodies have been removed to the police station.

div.head: MURDER OF A WARDER.
div.p: THE MURDER OF A WARDER.
FUNERAL OF HE VIGTIAL

The funeral of Ralph Dyer Wilk, the murdered warder, took place during Saturillsy forenoon. For some time before the hour appointed for the corage to leave the prison, large crowds of people were assembled in the streets. The hearse was followed by several mourning coaches, in one of which Major Preston (the governor of the gaol) rode, and the mourners included a brother-in-law and other relatives of the deceased. in addition to a number of the prison officials. The in- terment took place at the Salford Cemetery, and the prison chaplain &the Rev. Mr. Dreaper) officiated. Both at the cemetery and on the way thither considerable crowds of people had gathered, from whom expressions of sympathy with the widow of the murdered man were heard on every hand. Four of the gaol warders acted as pall bearers.

div.head: POLICE STILL BAFFLED.
div.p: THE POLICE STILL BAFFLED.

Several persons whose movements excited suspicion, and who were supposed to resemble in some degree the official description of Jackson issued by the police authorities, have been arrested on suspicion of being the murderer, but in nearly all the cases satisfactory evid- ence of identity has been tendered by the persons so arrested, and they have been forthwith discharged.

An extraordinary statement is made whtcn ;terms to confirm the alleged premeditation of Jackson's fetal attack on the Strangeways prison warder and his sub- sequent escape from gaol. It is that on the day previous to the murder, another warder who had him in'eJaarge noticed him locking the door, and promptly reprimanded him for doing so. At the inquest it was disclosed that Jackeon had been occupied some hours daily for three days with work which could very much sooner have been accomplished, and that when an alarm was raised after suspicion, the door of the room was found locked. Everything tends to prove that the crime was deliber- ately planned, and not the result of a sudden impulse, as was at first imagined.

div.head: STRANGE POLICE BLUNDER.
div.p: A STRANGE POLICE BLUNDER.

A mistake was made by the metropolitr police On Saturday. They received a report that Jackson was in custody, and they accordingly printed in the Police Gazette an intimation to the effect that the police need take no further notice of the matter. The bills de- scribing Jackson were accordingly taken down. On Monday they were renewed, but the difficulty of identi- fylng the murderer is increased by the absence of any photograph of him in London.

div.head: CHASE AT ROCHDALE.
div.p: A CHASE AT ROCHDALE.

On Saturday, some men found a stranger concealing himself in an outhouse on the farm of Mr. Sidebottorn, which is situated between Rochdale and Castleton. Fancying that he bore a great resemblance to the de- scription given of the escaped murderer from Strange- ways Gaol, they decided upon capturing him. However, the stranger soon perceived their design, and bolted with all speed. They nave chase, but he soon out-distanced them, and escaped. They gave information at the Roth.. date Police Office, and Detective-inspector Challon made full inquiry into the circumstances, and the personal app-arance of the stranger and his dress, and came to the conclusion that he was not the missing prisoner' but a tramp who had resorted to the outhouse for a night's rest.

div.head: HIS REAL NAME.
div.p: HIS REAL NAME.

Further disclosures have been made with regard to the murderer "Jackson." It is now stated with confi- dence that'his real name is Charles Wood Firth, that he is a native of Birstal, Yorkshire, and is "wanted" by the police of that county on charges of forgery and rob- bery. Five years ago Firth broke out of Wakefield Gaol but was recaptured. A photograph of the criminal has been obtained, and copies will be circulated very widely.

div.head: IMPORTANT ARREST.
div.p: IMPORTANT ARREST.

Late on Tuesd;Tnight-iKe-atTenii—o-nOf Inspector Hol- lingworth was drawn to a man in the Junction Hotel, Sheepbridge, near Chesterfield, on account of his extraor- dinary likeness to the escaped Manchester convict, Jack- son. He promptly effected his arrest, and took him to Chesterfield lock-up. When arrested he had in his pos- session a mason's trowel similar to one Jackson was said to have been carrying, and was wearing a pair of con- vict's braces. He appeared very uneasy, and is closely guarded by the police. His description tallies in every particular with those circulated, with the exception that he has no small lump on his fore fin-
ger. but has on his smallest finger; a mark on the grow also, not on the right but on the left. He has a small scar ob one side of his nose. He appears to have walked some _ .

distance, and admitted having been several times in a convict prisoner. He was brought up before Mr. E. A. 3. Maynard, charged with being a convict failing to re- port himself, and was remanded until Saturday. He - gave the name of John Kemp, plumber, Nottingham, but is extremely reticent, as are the police; but it is firmly believed by all who have seen the prisoner that be is the man wanted. The Nottingham police have been communicated with. SUPPOSED VISIT OF THE MURDERER TO ST.

div.head: HELENS.
div.p: HELENS.

Considerable excitement Eas-been occasioned at St. Helens by a rumour that Jackson was seen there on Tuesday. Inquiries have elicited the factthat in Febru- ary last a man giving the name of Graham applied for work as a painter and plumber at Messrs. Beecha.m's new pill works, and about that time the house of a Salvation Army captain, Emma Burton, was broken into and thirty-five shillings stolen. Mr. Andrews, manacer for Messrs. Beecham, declares that he met Graham in the town on Tuesday. They recognised each other, and Graham who was walking rapidly, stepped into the middle of the road and made off. He was wearing an old black suit, elastic boots, and cap. Mr. Andrews was hurrying to catch the train, and it only flashed upon his mind that the man was Graham when he had gone. Mr. Andrews further asserts that the description of the matt Graham corresponds exactly with that of the missing murderer. Diligent search is being made by the police.

div.head: CCHRENT rOLITICS.
div.p: CCHRENT rOLITICS.

Mr. W. Leathim Bright, M.P., addressing a meeting at Northan, in the Rye Division, Sussex, on Saturday night, said the Local Government Bill was less Radical than at first supposed. He strongly objected to the compensation clauses, and declared his intention of moving an amendment to the effect that the compensa- tion should be based on the income-tax returns made by publicans during the labt three:years. The fourth quarterly conferesce ot the Midland Union of Conservative Associations was preceded on Monday, at Derby, by a meeting of the Ladies' Auxiliary Council. Lady George Hamilton presided, and after a resolution had been rronAsed in favour of the extension of the Par- liamentary ranchise to women, Lord George Hamilton made a short speech, in which he said there WAS, no doubt, considerable difference of opinion on the question, but his mind was very open regarding it. He was almost persuaded to be a believer by the way the ladies' claims had been urged, although certain doubts suggested themselves to his mind. He spoke of the aid he had derived from his wife in his election contests. He con- sidered women's influence in political life tended to soften its asperities. The resolution was carried. Later in the afternoon Lord George was present aty the conference. The vacancy in the Ayr Burghs, caused by the death of Mr. R. F. F. Campbell, a Liberal Unionist, will lead, writes the London correspondent of a contemporary, to a very interesting contest. Ayrshire is the one county in Scotland which is undivided in its allegiance to the Unionist cause. The Ayr Burghs returned a Unionist Liberal at the last election by 1,175 majority. In North Ayrshire the Hon. H. F. H. Elliot was not even opposed. In South Ayrshire, though the majority was only five, the Liberal Unionist got the seat. Mr. Campbell, whose seat is now vacated, was a , local representative much given to hospitality, popular throughout the county, and a difficult candidate to heat at any time. But the Ayr Burghs are Liberal, and a Unionist majority of nearly 1,200 is hardly likely to be repeated. In fact, the Home Rulers believe that they will be able to wrest at Ayr another seat from Lord Hartington's grasp. Captain Sinclair will pro- bably be again the Liberal candidate.
Liberal

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE PAST_ PRAYING FOR.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE PAST_ PRAYING FOR.

Mr. Joseph Chamberlain received, at Birmingham, oft Tuesday, a deputation representing the wholesale brewers and retail licensed victuallers, in reference to the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill and the special revenue for compensation. The deputation said that they were willing to concede local option and in- creased license duty if security were given for compensa- tion; and Mr. Chamberlain, in replying, said that he had always advocated compensation for disturbance of legi- timate interests brought into existence by the Legisla- ture; and he was very much astonished to see that Mr. Gladstone had now gone back on that principle, and was apparently past praying for. He was not influenced by judicial decisions on the point, but was in favour of compensation as a matter of equity. ROCHDALE LIBERALS AT HAWARDEN.—SPEECH _ _ .

div.head: BY MR. GLADSTONE,
div.p: BY MR. GLADSTONE,

Several hundred excursionists from Rochdale, Little- borough, and Smallbridge paid a visit to Hawarden, on Saturday. In the course of the afternoon they gathered close GO the terrace in front of the castle, and warmly cheered Mr. Gladstone as he walked forward to speak to them. On the terrace at the time were Mrs. Gladstone. the Rev. S. Gladstone, Mr. H. Gladstone, M.P., Professor Stuart, M.P., and the Rev. H. Drew and Mrs. Drew. Mr. GLADSTOME said he was induced to depart from his usual rule of not speaking by the announcement that a candidate, whom he would not name, was to appose their old and trusted friend, Mr. Potter, at Roch- dale. He was not, however, in the least afraid of what Rochdale would do on the. occasion, for there was no constituency in which the self-governing, self-regulating, and seiecontroling, principles were better developed. He looked to them to maintain the character which they had hitherto upheld. Southampton had taught Rochdale a lesson. Their victory there had been attributed to the licensing clauses, and he, therefore, felt justified in alluding to those clauses, to which he was opposed. The Local Government Bill, whether it was a good bill or not on the whole, undoubtedly contained many things that were good, and one of the things that were good was in the licensing clauses. It contemplated the trans- fer of the power of licensing from a body which was ' purely nominated to a body which would be elective and representative, and they ought not; therefore, to disguise from themselves that something had been gained by the proposal of those clauses. Notwithstanding that, he was altogether opposed to these clauses, because although they were good in so much as they introduced the principle of popular control over licenses, to which he was friendlyeyet they introduced along with it a principle which in his opinion was quite intolerable, the principle of converting a license into an estate. Mr. Ritchie had been asked whether he would withdraw the clauses, but he held rather high language, and intimated that the Government would press the clauses and pass them as rapidly as they with propriety could. In considering whether, after what had happened at Southampton, the Government would press the clauses, they must recol- lect that the Government looked to the possessors of these licenses as the great mainstay, the foundation, and the backbone of their political party throughout the country. He was afraid that if the Government chose to press the clauses they would be passed in the House of Commons, and if they were carried in the House of Commons it was not to the House ot Lords that the people would look for redress. If England was con- demned to be saddled with these licensing clauses it would ,be lest Ireland should obtain the benefits of Home Rule. If all the gentlemen who called themselves Liberals were to unite with the other Liberal members they would have the aid the Irish Nationalists and the clauses would be thrown out by a fair majority. But the Liberal Unionists dare not vote against the Govern- ment, and if the Government announced that they would stand or fall by the clauses, the majority of the Liberal Unionists would vote for the clauses. Even if these chums became law, however, he had very great doubts whether anything that might be founded upon them would become a permanent institution. Referring to the Present position of the Irish question, he remarked that while within the walls of Parliament there had been nothing but retrogression, outside the walls of Parlia- ment the question was going forwards instead of back- wards. Two years ago the majority against them was 110; now it was somewhere between 8Q and 90. The nation was showing at every opportunity its disposition and determination to back up the Liberal party, and if anything could be certain in the future it was that the nation would bring the blessed result for which the Liberal party was labouring to a happy accomplishment. Mr. Gladstone addressed another body of excursionists at Hawarden on Wednesday, pointing out to them that the responsibility for Irish policy rested ultimately upon the constituencies, and urging that if a change were to be made individual electors must feel the responsibility and act accordingly. As to the "plans" published at Birmingham for the nineteexth or twentieth time, it was only for the Government to say that they must be rejected or the Ministry go out, and the Dissentient Liberals would pass whatever the Government desired.

A Sittmgbourne telegram states that reports to hand from the principal growers indicate that this year's crop of Kentish cherries will be above the average. Wire MUR,DER.-At Chipping Norton, in Oxfordshire, on Wednesday, a labourer named Robert Upton, 61 years old, was committed for trial for the murder of his wife. The evidence showed that the prisoner, after telling a fellow-workman that there would "be a rum job pre- sently," went home and beat his wife about the head with, an iron bar till she was dead.

DERBY -DAY...T:71;6 Derby was won on Wednesday by the Duke of Portland's Ayrshire, Mr.Vyner's CrowbeTry being second, and Mr. Rose's Van Dietnan's Land third. Gautby led for some distance, but Van Die- man's Land afterwards came to the front. At a quarter of a mile from home, however, Ayr- shire took up the running, and won easily by two lengths. The Prince and Princess of Wales were among those who witnessed the race. The Epsom High Weight Handicap was taken by Devilshoof, the Stanley Stakes by North Star colt, the Juvenile Plate by Corbellle, the Chetwynd Plate by Padua, the Headley Stakes by Fast and Loose,. and the Epsom Town Plate by Sweet Alice.

1 ----- 1! MR. CHAMBERLAIN is finding that he has got himself in a queer corner by turning his back i'llen the Liberal party ; and the worst of it is he does not as yet see his way out. He and his friends have been beaten out-and-out in the elec- tiens at Birmingham of the members of the Liberal Caucus; and, as he cannot play second fiddle in tha.t part of the country, there has been nothing ler it but getting together a fresh orchestra in order that he may have something to lead. The k*st united meeting of the newly-formed Liberal thdoniat Association was held in the Birmingham .evi.n Hall on Monday evening, and Mr. CHAM- .r: 1.44LA1N gave an address as the president. He ii,ad a good many nice things to say of the Tories; 1 411 fact he made it out that there were no Tories 4tit all. Old Toryism, he said, had died out; and he Present Government were just as anxious as _ the Liberal Unionists "to promote all reasonable aad safe reforms." Mr. CHAMBERLAIN did not say that the present Government were ready to carry i'•°tit such features of the unauthorised programme as Free Education and the Disestablishment of tile English Church ; and it must be inferred, we anPPose, that he has of late changed his mind and to the conclusion that these are not " safe teferms," It seems that while the Tories have karched forward, the Liberal Unionists have ataPPed backward, so that now Righteousness and r eaee can embrace and kiss each other. The I: Inealber for West Birmingham says there are ' 1:411Y two parties, though there are three political ssrganisations ; but he ought to see that it is hard 12.11 the Party to which he has admittedly allied anuself, that, whilst it is united as a party, it aheuld be split in two as to its political organisa- cin. It is a little ochr that the President 44 the new Unionist Association had nothing to 3' On. either of these topics, particularly as they tio 1 a 1 accord with the chief features of the un- ,4,4ltherised programme. However, as to compen- ou, he has since made up for the omission by Lihng a deputation of licensed victuallers that he ,e—ct afraid Mr. GLADSTONE is past praying for, be- he is opposed to the compensation clauses of " Local Government Bill. We are thus left to e°llelude that he thinks the KING-HARMAN and L'clmilliPensation measures are to be classed amongst at he described as "reasonable and safe reforms:. K.-4r. He recognises that, like himself, 1:bl:still unsettled; and it is not a little curious to erve that, notwithstanding his attachment to the Unionist policy of the Unionist Government, lie leeks forward to a settlement being effected— by the Unionist, but by the Liberal party. "eed, he asks for a declaration ef policy from :the man who claims to be the leader of the -t,i Q beral party." Liberals will take note of Mr. 4ANIBERLAIN'S sneer; but, happily, Mr. GLAD- IiT°NE has no need to " claim "—he is the leader .?!..the Liberal party; for, unlike the member for 4764 Birmingham, he has been tested a thousand ;'rees, and he has never been found wanting. ,Mr. kfAZYIBERL.IIN had a good deal to say of the kherne for dealing with Ireland, which was pro- -I)olinded, last week, in the columns of the " fir- !aingham Daily Post." He did not deny that he a. 14 the author of it: he almost, in fact, went so far ~,,,-'tz) admit its authorship, for he said—" We have b'qi t forward for discusssion and criticism our Unfortunately, the " our " in this case ;1144Y mean nothing more than the Chamberlain /41:14Y group. There is no evidence at all that the t 11, such as it is, meets with the approval of HARTINGTON OE of Lord SALISBURY. Surely, 4h4r. CHAMBERLAIN knows of "only two parties," ql ,CI does not reckon himself as belonging to the 1470steman party, he ought to address himself to rd SALISBURY rather than to Mr. GLADSTONS. Now that he is acting with the Govern- that are so anxious to promote " all reason- and safe reforms," there should be no diffi- Dl.,tY about getting them to accept this wonderful n which he so eagerly commends. And, once a•ate el)ted' what is there to prevent its being imme- -l' jat. , Y carried out ? The Tories and the Union- the nave combined: they are in a majority in the ' /louse of Commons; they are backed up by hold 10115 e of Lords: and, more than that, they AA/ the reins of Government. \\rill,Ar last issue, we gave some account of artington Cairo-street Chapel, which has a. story extending over two hundred years that a IWays Ler and intellectual progress. This week we lay 00 °re our readers a report of the proceedings in illrle,ection with the celebration of the centenary 'airo-st :A. A centeßary is tt ; for, however stead-

fast people may prove to be as to their princi- ples and objects, it is almost a matter of course to say that there will be great changes in the method of carrying them out in the cycle of a hundred years. Thus we find as to Cairo-street Sunday School that it was designated, at its foundation, as "an institution establithed by certain Protest- ant Dissenters in the year 1788 for the charitable instruction of poor children in the town and neighbourhood of Warrington." Need we say that that instruction included the simple elements of knowledge such as are taught to-day to the first standard children of our national schools? There were no day schools at that time for the masses. Indeed, it was considered questionable whether they would be any the better for book learning; and thus it happened for many many years that the children of the poor had to rest contort with such meagre instruction as could be got at the Sunday Sehool. Mr. W. D. HOUGHTON, in an interesting address which he delivered on Monday evening, referred to his own recollection of read- ing, writing, and arithmetic being taught in their Sunday School some fifty years ago. This was a common practice at that period, not only at Cairo-street, but at almost all other Sunday Schools. Let the children at present attending our day schools question their grand- fathers and grandmothers on this matter, and they will hear them lament that in their young days their oi.portunities for learning were confined to such instruction as they were able to obtain at the Sunday School. It will perhaps make the youngsters thankful that they are born in better times, though it is just possible that, if they are of the class described by Shakespeare as "creeping like snail unwillingly to school," they may think their lines would have fallen in pleasanter places if they had had to go to school on Sunday only. The Sunday School is no longer what it was originally—an institution for "the charitable in- struction of poor children." The civilised world has outgrown the need of furnishing rudimentary instruction on a Sunday, or of supplying it either on Sunday or week day as a charity. But, a hundred years 'ago, it was a noble and charitable thing to do, and it is fitting by such celebrations as that at Cairo-street, that a tribute should be paid to the memory of those who were so long ago engaged inthe work. They were the pioneers of their day, and if they had been born in this generation they would be amongst those who see the need of Free Education, and of national provision for Techni- cal Instruction. The Sunday School has had its day; its function is at an end so far as primary education is concerned; and, as was mentioned the other evening, there are people who think there is now no need at all of such an institution. But is this the right view to take? We note that one of the rules framed for the conduct of Cairo- street School one at its origin required that care should be taken "to instruct children on Sundays in the great and fundamental duties of religion," and, amongst other things, " to.warn them of the evil consequences of idleness, profane swearing, drunkenness, lying, and stealing." Surely there is need to-day to instruct and to warn as to these matters; and, as there is likely to be need for a long time yet, there is still plenty of work for the Sunday School. It is true that the tendency of the time is to make the day school teacher re- sponsible, in a large degree, for the moral as well as the mental condition of his pupils; but the teacher justly pleads that the requirements of an iron-bound code leave him altogether too little time to play the part of the moralist. He looks upon that as essentially the function of the Sun- day school teacher. Sunday schools are of im- portame, too, from a denominational point of view, as nurseries of the various churches. Chil- dren are sent to work early, and if it were not for the Sunday School they would often be lost sight of after leaving the day school. It is at this period that boys and girls are most susceptible to in- fluences which may make or mar their future; and we regard those men and women as nobly em- ployed in the Sunday School, who, without think- ing over-much of theology, teach and practico the simple truths which "make for righteousness." Cairo-street Sunday School has ever been an insti- tution of this kind; and the celebration of its centenary is, therefore, honourable as well as hon- ouring.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

There was an important discussion in the House of Commons last evening on Trustee Savings Banks. It resulted in the Chancellor of the Ex- che9uer undertaking to take steps to prevent Savings Banks representing themselves as Govern- ment institutions.

Lori Stanley of Alderley is opposed to a reform of the House of Lords; and complains that "Two Prime Ministers have filled it with the rubbish of the House of Commons." This is doubtless hard on the lords; but the House of Commons must shoot its "rubbish" somewhere.

At Frodsham, a labourer has been fined 40s. and costs for assaulting a farmer upon whose field he was trespassing. As the assault resulted in a broken rib, it cannot be said that the penalty is a great one. The value of a rib seems to have sadly depreciated since the creation of Eve.

Now that the Rev. F. W. Willis has been insti- tuted as Rector of Warrington people are wonder- ing what he will proceed to institute. When he has arranged his cards, will he play for high, low, Jack, or game. The opinion is already abroad that it will be "high," and that it will be the par- ishioners who will prove " game "

A flatman named Abraham was fined 20s. and costs at Runcorn, on Monday, for cruelty to "a harmless, necessary cat." He had broken it% leg with a kick, and caused it to fall into the canal. His defence was that the cat flew at his ouppy; he "merely kicked it away, and it rolled into the canal." Merely kicked" is as good as " mobbled 'queen," as old Polonius would say.

St. Helens men are again to the fore at the an- nual prize meeting of the Lancaster Rifle Associa- tion. ThQre is no withstanding them. The total of prizes won represents £l6O in money, three challenge cups, and a field glass, value in all £l7l 6s, besides three aggregate badges. Last year the St. Helens rifle corps won £145 in money, three chal- lenge cups out of the four offered, and two badges and medals. Bravo St. Helens

Two Ship Canal navvies have been fined lOs and costs each for trespassing, in pursuit of game, in the neighbourhood of Acton Grange. Navvies are commonly said to know the delight of a shiny night, and the happy lot of a boiling pot wi+l. big rabbit in it. Rabbits are 4--i. sure, a nuis- auee to the far,— anu the navvy may therefore brie farmer's friend. The navvy is in this particular a keen nuisance inspector, and, besides, he does his own scavenging.

In another column, there will be found an in- teresting sketch on "Town Beggars" by a Towns- nan who knows "Who's Who," and "What's AN'-at." Some particulars are also given of the Print', of Idlers, who renewed his acquaintance with t.e magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on 'Tiursday. He goes to the Workhouse not to wor but to have an easy time of it, and to gaol because ~7„ likes even prison life better than honest labour.

A young man named Thomas Oakes has been committed for trial for breaking into the offices of Messrs. Pilling and Co., contractors, Golborne, and consuming between £3 and £4 worth of cham- pagne, whisky, gin, port, and sherry. It is a won- der that he survived his extraordinary spree. He ' must be a man of "an unbounded stomach," as Wolsey is said to have been. Oakes states that he was "put on the job." There is no doubt that he went to work with a will; but it is not un- likely that the next job he will be put on will be the treadmill.

The " Standard"—Tory though it is—takes the Duke of Cambridge sharply to task for his med- dling and muddling in the matter of the place of meeting for the Wimbledon Rifle Association. It has not to be held at Wimbledon because it may depreciate the house property of his Royal High- ness; and he puts his foot on the proposal to hold the meetings in Richmond Park because he, as "George, Ranger," does not think the place suit- able. The latest suggestion is to try Altcar. This is good news for Lancashire men. It would be central, too, for the whole country.

Ashockingcase of wife assaultat Widnes exampli- fies the terrible curse of drunkenness. The poor woman, the wife of a labourer named Dug- gan, was so brutally beaten by her hus- band the other night that it is feared she will not recover. There does not seem to have been any specific cause of quarrel. Husband and wife had gone home after drinking together, and they "stopped up" talking. Duggan after- wards became bad tempered, and beat his wife within an inch of her life. He behaved like a madman; he was maddened with drink.

A miner named Rabbitt, employed at the Hay- dock Collieries, left work because he was told that he could not have his lamp unless he signed, as the other men had done, a document contracting to pay for sharpening tools, for the club, and for oil. He sued the firm for a fortnight's wages in lieu of notice, and would have carried his point had it not happened that, after the first day, he was told he could resume work. Messrs. Evans and Co. set themselves right by paying for one day, and Rab- bat had his claim dismissed. The case is an interesting one as revealing the niceties of the law.

From a paper road before the conference of School Board Clerks, it appears that over £lO,OOO were deposited last year in the 139 banks con- nected with the Manchester Board schools. This is one way of training up a child in the way he should go. It seems that at holiday time it is customary to draw on the bank for new clothes, &c. How would it be if banks were instituted in connection with all the schools in Warrington? In this -way, it might be possible to make provision for Walking Day without having to go round with the book so much. Self-help is, after all, the best help.

The poet Browning once asked, "What's become of Waring s"; but the question put by the "Finan- cial News" is—" What's become of Walker's Brewery scheme P" There seems to have been a row with Messrs. Baring Brothers about the terms on which it should be floated; and it is thought not unlikely that something will yet be heard of the matter in the law courts. It would be in- teresting, by-the-by, to know whether, if the com- pany were now promoted there would be the old rush for shares—in view of the agitation against compensation.

Mr. Chamberlain seems in the way of cutting off his nose in order to spite his face. While Mr. Gladstone is exposing the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill, the member for West Birmingham tells the licensed victuallers that he is disposed to stand by them. He does not, he says, care about the legal aspect of the question. That is the usual cry of man when the law is against him. Laws, however, are made to be obeyed, so Mr. Chamberlain has told us. But perhaps he means that they are to be obeyed by Nationalists only; and that Brewers are to be allowed to disregard the law, or have it altered to suit their convenience.

Lord Harting-ton stands where he did;, and Coercion lives, moves, and has its being in him. He is not going to commit himself to Mr. Chamber- lain's scheme of local government for Ireland, or to any other scheme of the kind—just yet. Writ- ing to the Liberal Unionists of Dublin, he asks them not to shut their eyes to the danger of plac- ing new weapons in the hands of their opponents, until the authority and supremacy of the law have been established beyond the possibility of dispute." This is the "Coercion for ever cry. Lord Hartington apparently believes that force 'is a remedy.

The destruction of the Spanish Armada in 588 is to be celebrated this year. In some parts of the country the celebration has already commenced. For instance, at St. Nathaniel's Church, Liver- pool, on Sunday, it was celebrated by the church choir singing "Rule Britannia," with—it is stated —'• splendid effect." When the feeling gets a little higher at St. Nathaniel's, as it will during the year, they will perhaps take to rendering that other warlike song We don't want to fight, But by Jingo !if we do, &c. And then, of course, the effect will be glorious.

The New York "Evening Post," referring to the General Conference of the Methodist Epis- copal Church held in that city, says :—" At nine o'clock the chaplain, the Rev. Mr. M'Cabe, stepped to the front of the platform and said, 'I wish some delegate would go into the lobbies and ask the members of the Conference to come in to prayers.' There was a general laugh at this, and a delegate said that it reminded him of another General Con- ference, when Bishop James said, after the devo- tional exercises had been held, that he wished somebody would step to the door and tell the brethren to come in, as prayers were over." This may seem very spry on the part of the American preachers; but what if their congregations should follow the cue fth to sermons, and thus "better the instruction?"

THE RAINFALL.-Dr. Gornall furnishes us with the following interesting particulars P-The five' months of the year already passed have been per- haps the driest on record, the amount registered at the Fever Hospital-only 5-1- inches-being nearly ,1 three-quarters of an inch less than the dry season of 1 1887. The average amount registered during the 7 years (18812-7), in the corresponding months, was 9.6 inches. The largest amount registered was in wet season of 1886, when 14.1; inches were recorded. SOUTH-WEST LINCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARS.— The quarterly session of the South-west Lanca- shire District Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Mission Hall, Atherton, on Saturday afternoon, Brother J. B. Collings, D.C.T., presiding. He was supported by the officers of the district, and there was a good attendance of lodge representatives. The report of the D. Sec. (Bro. M. Tones),showed an in- creo.,a inemoership, and that an active work had been carried on during the past guar- ter. The juvenile branch of the order, accord- ing to the report of the D.S.J.T. (Brother A. Newall) had wonderfully improved, there being an increase of over 300 members, and preparations were leeing made for an active campaign throughout the district, in promoting prize schemes, &c. The D. Treasures (Brother R. W. Kurkus's) report showed the finances to be in a satisfactory position. The business was afterwards proceeded with, and it was decided to hold the next quarterly session at Liver- pool. A public procession was afterwards formed headed by the Lowton Brass Band, and the splendid banner of the City of Refuge Lodge, Chowbent. The principal streets were paraded, and a crowded meet- ing was held under the presidency of Mr. Caleb Wright, M.P. Addresses were given by Bros. J. B. Collings, A. E. Eccles, and others.
