div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchase all kinds of in- ferior manufacteree spectacles, which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, and 44, Market-st., Manchester' 143, Lord-st., Southport, and 60, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his " Per-1 fection " Spectacles, which he adapts at either of the above addresses at 7s 6d per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on application.—Advt Mr. G. E. QUIRK, of Deacon-road, has been appoin- ted secretary and curator of Bootle Liberal Club. He recently held the office of the steward of the Widnes Liberal Club. MERIT RIDGES AT WlDNlS.—Constables Thompson and Worsfold have recently had conferred upon them the badge of merit for good conduct, and the vigilant execu- tion of their duties. HOLY TRINITY Cnuncn, RUNCORN.—In aid of the fund for the restoration of the organ of this church special services were held on Sunday last. The preacher was the Rev. W. K. Ormsby. formerly curate of the Parish Church, Runcorn, and there were crowded congregations at each service.

SHOCKING MISAGLT AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. H. Gas- kell, junr., at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Moran, apparently about 40 years of age, was charged with indecently assaulting Alice Ditchfield, aged 13years' who lives with her parents at 30. Water-st.—lt appeared that on Sunday the girl was engaged by Mrs Moran to help her in her household work, and the girl stayed at the house all day. About nine o'clock the prisoner and two other men were drinking in the kitchen. His com- panions happening to leave the room it was alleged that the prisoner committed the offence complained of. After ,the the evidence his Worship committed the prisoner for trial.

CRUELTY TO A CAT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Enoch Abraham, a flatman, of Weston Point, was summoned for having on the 6th May cruelly illtreated a cat, belonging to Alexander McLean, also of Weston Point. Inspector Aplin, R.S.P.C.A., pro- secuted. The evidence showed that the defendant's do,g made several attacks on the cat, and then the defendant savagely kicked the cat, breaking its leg, and causing it to fall into the canal. Upon being brought from the water the cat was in such agony from the injuries it had sustained that an end was put to its life.—The defendant alleged that the cat " flew " at a puppy he had by his side; he " merely " kicked it away and it rolled into the canal.—He was ordered to pay a fine of 20s, and costs, 14s. A LIVELY NEIGHBOURHOOD IN WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Ann Noon pleaded guilty to having on the 26th May been drunk and disorderly, and with doing damage to the house in Water-st. occupied by Margaret Taylor. P.C. Thompson proved the drunk and disorderly conduct, and Mr. Barnett Dut- ton, auctioneer, Oakland-st., said he was the owner of the property in Water-st. There were six panes of glass broken and the shutters were damaged. The stun of El. 2s Od would be required to repair the damage. There was a great deal of damage done in this,street. There were several families who made it a rule when any feel- ing was created to smash one anothers windows, and his (Mr. Dutton's) tenants had become so terrified that they dare not lay information against them. The street had become almost unfit to live in. Last year he paid £5 for damage done to this property and other owners had suffered in a like degree.—The prisoner was fined 5s and costs in each case, and ordered to pay the damage. THE DISAPPOINTED WIDOW AT RUNCORN.—John Walms- ley, who was described as a wholesale and retail green- grocer, was summoaed before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of the illegitimate child of Annie Hulme, a widow.—Mr. J. Burton was for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Linaker for the defendant.—Mrs. Hulme alleged that the defendant was the father of her child, and that he had promised 'to marry her. He had told her that he had some shares in an industrial society, and some money in a bank at Liverpool. When he promised to marry her he had a scheme for building a house, and carrying on the business of a wholesale greengrocer. He had, however, married another woman, and lived at Blackburn.—For the defence it was contended that the defendant was not possessed of the means described. The business belonged to his wife and what money lie had was allowed to him as pockeemoney. The defendant said 2s 6d per week was as much as he could afford.— The Bench made an order for the payment of 3s per week.

RAILWAY TRESPASS BY COLLIERS Ar BOLD—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. J. Brock, a collier named Robert Phoenix was charged with having, on the 17th April, trespassed on the line of the London and North-Western Railway Co. He pleaded guilty. Mr. Ferrand, who prosecuted, said the men employed at the Bold Colliery had made it a practice to frequent the railway as a public highway. They had been repeatedly warned, but without effect.— Joseph Sands and John Mattinson, also colliers, were charged with committing a similar offence on the 20th April. Each defendant was fined lOs and costs.— Richard Barton, John Lowe, and Samuel Fleming pleaded guilty to trespassing on the railway at Bold. Mr. Ferrand said the circumstances in this case were dif- ___.

ferent to the others. The defendants reside at Wigan, 1 and theyhad been engaged repairing an engine and boiler at Collins Green Colliery. As they were anxious to catch ' a train home they inquired the nearest Way to the sta- tion, and the colliers directed them along the line. Per- i haps their worships would be satisfied with asking the i defendants to pay costs. The magistrates agreed, and each defendant had to pay 7s 6d. WIDNES LIBERAL COUNCIL.—On Thursday evening a meeting of the Widnes District Council of the divisional Liberal Association was held in the Lacey-st. School for 1 the purpose of electing officers. There was a very fair attendance. Mr. J. Morrison presided during the early ' part of the meeting. After a few remarks from the Chairman, a hehrty vote of thanks was accorded to 1 Mr. E. Carey (chairman of the District Council), and Mr. T. Sutton Timmis (honorary secretary) for the ser- vices they had rendered during the past year, on the motion of IIV. Frank Cave.—Mr. Carey responded on be- half of himself and Mr. Timmis Cwho was not present), and said that he had only done his duty; any other man would have done as well.—On the motion of Messrs. J. Taylor and J. Morrison, Mr. Carey was unanimously re- elected chairman for the ensuii g twelve months; and on the motion of Messrs. Cave and Robinson, Mr.Timmis was unanimously re-elected hon. secretary. Several vacancies on the new committee were then filled; Mr. Morrison and Major Wareing were re-appointed to re- present the district on the registration committee of the division: and subsequently the meeting discussed the County Electors (England and Wales) Bill EXTENSIVE DAMAGE AT WID,NES.—Thomas Tansey, a young man, was brought before Mr. H. Gaskell, at Wid- hes Police Court, on Monday, charged with having on the 19th May committed wilful damage upon the White Star Hotel, Dock-st., occupied by T. John Gerrard. From the evidence it appeared that on Saturday night, the 12th May, the prisoner was at the bar of the public- house and wanted to make a disturbance. The landlord refused to serve him with drink, and ordered him to leave the house. The prisoner struck the landlord, and attempted to throw a half-pint glass at his wife. The following Saturday the prisonelswas lounging about the house all day, and at night a youth named James Bees- ley, who lives at 25, Pear-st., heard the prisoner say "I have a good mind to throw my pipe through the win- dows." The prisoner walked towards the house as though he would carry out his threat, but Beesley pre- vented him. About two o'clock in the morning three boys named Patrick Hughes, William Carr, and William Dodd, who were taking part in a " wake " at the house of Mrs. Billinge, opposite the White Star Hotel, heard ; the sound of breaking glass, and ran to the door. They saw five plate-glass windows of the public house broken, , and also saw the prisoner walking quickly down the street towards his house. He was carrying what ap- peared to be a brush. The damage amounts to £l2 12s. - The prisoner, when apprehended by P.C. Thompson, ) denied his guilt, and now said he knew nothing about the windows. He was committed to the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT.-011 Wednesday, Michael Connor, who had been 17 times previously convicted, was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial on a charge of having, on the 19th May, stolen a pair of boots from the shop of Mr. Croley, Bridge-st , and also two shawls from the shop of Mr. Marsh, pawnbroker, Church- st.--On Thursday, James Walsh was sentenced to seven days' hard labour in default of paying a fine of 5s and costs for having been drunk on the previous night. —Thomas Byrom, a loafer, was charged with sleeping on the works of the Runcorn Soap and °Alkali Company. He was discharged with a caution. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—An Abusive Pedlar : Yester- day, before Major Hazlehurst, Dennis Murray, a young man from Ashton-under-Lyne, was sent to gaol for seven days in default of paying a.fine of lOs and costs, 7s 4d. On the previous evening be went into the shop of Mr. Davies, pawnbroker, High-st., and because the latter would not purchase some letter paper he was hawking lie used abusive language, and threatened to break into the shop during the night.—Superintendent Honing- worth said the prisoner was in possession of a pedlar's certificate, which was used as a cover for begging.— Drunk, 4-e. : John McCormick, a stranger, was convicted of being drunk and begging in High-st. on the previous night.—lnspector O'Donnell proved the case. The pri- soner had annoyed Mr. James Lea, furniture dealer. He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour in default of pay- ing a fine.--John Delaney, a middle-aged man, was fined 5s and costs, 5s 4d, or in default seven days' hard labour for being drunk in Brunswick-st. ELOPEMENT AT GOLBORNE.—There has been quite a stir during the past week or so about an elope- ment in low life. A young married woman, a weaver, had, it is stated, formed an acquaintance with a young miner, who lodged not far from her residence. The young woman a husband, it may be mentioned, has been an invalid for some time. The neighbours were, however, astonished to find that the faithless spouse had disappeared without giving any sort of warning. It was soon afterwards ascer- tained that the collier had also vanished, the infer- ence being that they had gone away together, the husband being "left lamenting." A correspondent who gives us particulars sums the case up in the following rhyme Oh 'Bob," had you known How deceitful she'd have grown You would have surrendered the chick, And done then, I vow, What you cannot do now, And handed her over to Dick. DEATH OF •A PRESTON CENTENARIAN.—OR Sat- urday Mrs. Shackleton, of Dawson-st., Preston, ex- pired after an illness lasting for about three months. The eld lady, who celebrated her 100th birthday on Monday, the 7th ult. was the aunt of Mr. R. Shackleton, billposter, iVarrington. She was born at Blackburn, and shortly after her marriage she went to Preston with her husband, a cotton spinner, who obtained work at one of the mills. The old woman had many difficulties to contend against, owing to her husband being thrown out of work by the strikes, and she about twelve months ago gave some interesting reminiscencea which we published. When a Press correspondent saw her to congratu- late her on the attainment of her 100th year, she was in bed, attended by Dr. Holden, but she was in full possession of all her faculties, and she chatted very cheerfully for some time. It appears she gradually sank, and expired on Saturday, aged 100 years and 3 weeks, He husband died some years ago. BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN.-011 Monday a bowling match for 1:20a-side, between Mr. W. Dain- teth, of Widnes, and Mr. W. Rhodes, of Runcorn, took place at the green of the Bridge Hotel, Run- corn. Much interest was taken in the event, which proved to be of a most exciting description. The game was 101 up. Rhodes, who had the advan- tage of playing on "his own green," went off with the lead, but Dainteth gradually crept up, and the game was called out "28 all." Again Rhodes drew to the front, but Dainteth drew level and passed his opponent, the game standing—Dainteth .53, Rhodes 44. At half-time the scores were—Dainteth 55. Rhodes 51. From now to the end of the game first one and then the other had the lead, but towards the finish Rhodes played well and had to his credit 97 points, whilst Dainteth had only scored 91. By splendid play Dainteth drew level at 97, and amid great excitement the gams was afterwards called 100 each. Rhodes just scored the last end and won by one point.. Messrs. R. Wright and S. Marwood were the referees.

MESSRS. BOSTOCE AND WOMBWELL'S MENAGERIE is en route through this district, and wid visit War- rington next week, as per advertising, columns. We understand that this famous show is considerably enlarged since its last visit to this neighbourhood, and that in addition to its former splendid collec- tion of animals there is now to be seen a monstre Patagonian sea lion, a pair of ferocious emzellas from the Transvaal, and the royal jubilee dwarf elephants, " Victoria " and "Jubilee." Another attraction is the presence at each representation of Captain Martin, the lion hunter, who will perform with the lions, tigers, bears, wolves, hyranas, and elephants. The very latest additions to the men- agerie are a litter of baby lions, and "Big Ben," a monster North American Bison, purchased from "Buffalo Bill." The exhibition comprises 16 ponder- ous carriages, which find accommodation for 600 beasts, birds, and reptiles, and are drawn by 50 powerful horses. We are given to understand that the collection is far superior to anything previously exhibited.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. —On the arrival of a train from Manchester to Liverpool, due at St. Helens Junction a few minutes after eight o'clock, on Monday night, a young Irish- man was found suspended to the rack of a third- class carriage by his pocket handkerchief. It ap- pears that the attention of a porter named Tyrer was first called to the carriage by a door being open, and he at once saw the man hanging. Tyrer called the attention of the guard, Henry Partington, and the two men.got into the carriage and cut him down. The man was then in an insensible condi- tion, and black in the face, with all his muscles contracted. A messenger was despatched for Dr. Casey, and on his arrival it was found that the man was in a dangerous condition, the throat bay- ing been injured, and there being imminent danger of suffocation. It was then decided to take him to the St. Helens Providence Hospital, and he was placed on a stretcher and conveyed by train to St. Helens, attended by Dr. Casey. Part of an envelope with the words "Whitehead, Victoria-terrace, King- ston-on-Hull," and a letter. addressed "My dear Henry." leads to the supposition that the mans name is Henry Whitehead, of the above address'. The hat he wore bore the name of a Hull tradosman, but in the trunk there was an old hat of Yankee shape, giving the idea that he had recently arrived from the States. During Monday night the young man recovered consciousness and told the Sister Superior of the institution that his name was Henry Whitehead; that lie had been travelling about tbe States; but had determined to return to England for a while to see his parents. who live in Manches- ter. He said he did not remember anything of the occurrence. On Tuesday night he was removed from the hospital to the Town Hall, and was on Wed- nesday brought before Dr. Gaskell charged with at- tempting to commit suicide. Tie prisoner said— I reached Dublin at half-past nine on Monday morn- ing, and I had a lot of drink. I remember nothing after leaving Chester. Prisoner was remanded to gaol for a week. WEST LANCASHIRE RUGHT FOOTBALL UNION.— The annual general meeting of the above Union was held on Thursday evening, at the Goat Hotel, Peter's Lane, Liverpool; Mr. W. S. Rawcliffe, vice-presi- dent, occupying the chair; and there was a fair attendance of representatives of clubs comprised in the Union. Mr. F. T. Parry first read his annual secretarial report, which was passed; and the state- ment of accounts, -Which was taken as read, showed that the Union was in a flourishing condition, hav- ing a balance of £B4 14s 3cl to its credit. The re- ceipts included £25 2s 2d, the proceeds of the junior final at Warrington; £lB, the takings at the West- moreland match at Aspull ; and £157 14s 9d, the proceeds of the senior final at Warrington. The total receipts amounted to £2BO Os 10d, and the ex- penditure to £195 6s 7d. The Earl of Lathom was unanimously re-elected as president, and Messrs. W. Eckersley (Tyldesley) and W. S. France (Wigan) were added to the Tice-presidents. Messrs. B. Wilcock and F. T. Parry were re-elected hon. treasurer and secretary res?ectively, without dissent.—lt was proposed, seconded, and carried, that the Wilcock and Parry testimonial funds should receive £l5 each from the union funds, and the chairman generously proffered £5 to each of the funds.—The election of auditors was then made, and the following gentle- men were appointed :—Messrs. R. Slack (Southport Olympic) and A. Houghton (St. Helens.)—The re- presentatives of the following clubs were next elec- ted as the committee :—Tyldesley, Aspull, St. Helens, St. Helens Recreation, Wigan, Warrington, Widnes,l Litherland, Southport Olympic, Leigh, Widnes St. Mary's, 4th L.A.V., Blundellsands, Liverpool Hor- nets, Ince Conservative Athletic, and Wigan Rovers. —lt was proposed that Thatto Heath should be allowed to join the union, and the motion was as- sented to.—A presentation was made, after the meeting, of a gold watch, albert, and illuminated address, to Mr. F. T. Parry, in recognition of his services as hon. secretary, ard as the principal founder of the union; and a very enjoyable evening was spent.

Moonz WESLEYAN SUNDAY ScHoor,.—On Sunday the anniversary sermons in connection with this school were preached in Moore Chapel by the Rev. John Howell Jones, of Stockton-on-Tees, and for- merly of Warrington, to crowded congregations. The collections, which were in aid of the school funds, realized £l7 Ss.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon. Mr. E. Carey presided. and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. D. Wright, B. Brown, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood, H. Cook, F. Liddell, J. Taylor, H. Gaskell, unr., J. Houghton, S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), and

I. Carr (gas engineer). THE DISTRICT RATE.-0/1 the proposition of Mr. W. W. Gossage. seconded by Mr. R. Cook, the seal of the Board was affixed to a general district rate of is Id in the pound for the half-yearending September 29th next.. ADJOURNED.—Consideration of the proposal to adopt the new scheme of the Dinsmore Gas Company for mak- ing gas was deferred. The question of the easement through land belonging to the trustees of the late Mr. E. Bibby, for the Moss Bank sewer, was also deferred. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. A letter was read from Mr. Fred C Hulton, clerk to the County Justices, Preston, informing the Local Board that the President of the Local Government Board had consented to receive a deputation from Lancashire on Tuesday next. The chief object of the deputation was to call Mr. Ritchie's atten- tion to the main road question, and It was proposed to hold a preliminary meeting at the Westminster Palace Hotel for the purpose of agreeing upon such amendments , to be submitted to him as would place the question upon a fair and equitable basis. He need hardly point out that this was a matter of grave importance to the rate- payers of Widnes and the County Justices hoped to have the support of the Widnes Local Board in their endea- vours to obtain the insertion of the amendments in the Bill.—Mr. Gaskell moved that the Local Board send a deputation as requested; and explained that un- der the Bill as proposed about one half of the population would be excused from all payment towards the County roads, and the other half would have to pay the entire cost. The cost was estimated by the committee of the justices to be about £B,OOO per annum, which would be equal to about 2d in the £ to those upon whom the charge would fall. It seemed to him unjust and hard that Widnes should have to pay 2d in the £ towards the maintenance of county roads, whilst their neighbours in St. Helens would pay nothing at all.— Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which was unanim- ously carried.—lt was afterwards resolved that Mr. T. Handley. Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. Allen (the clerk), form the deputation.

div.head: TERRIBLE ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDNES.
div.p: TERRIBLE ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDNES.

Widnes is in a fair way for justifying the term of the "black spot on the Mersey," which is often be- stowed upon it. During the past few months the number of crimes of violence have been gently on the increase, and ma Monday. Mr. Gaskell was en- gaged in inquiring into a case in which a fatal ter- mination is anticipated. James Duggan, a labourer, of 14, High-st., was charged with having on the 26th of May unlawfully and felunously wounded his wife, Julia, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. Superintendent Johnstone said the woman was in extreme danger of her life, and on the pre- vious day her deposition was taken. She said she was perfectly aware of the danger she was in. She had lived with the prisoner as his wife for six years. ()n Friday night the 25th ult., the prisoner was drunk. He had been drinkingthe whole of the week. She had several drinks with him up to eleven o'clock at night. When they left the public house they were quitefrienclly-, and went to a fish shop in Waterloo-road. After they arrived home they "stopped up" talking after mid-night until morning. The prisoner became bad ,tempered and violent like a madman. He struck her on the head with his fist, and she ran into the kitchen. He made her go upstairs before him, and told her to get into bed. She replied "all right Jetn." He then knocked her down with the boots he wore. He used her so violently that all her clothes were torn off and she was naked. She be- came unconscious and did not remember anything until morning. She was then bleeding from the head, and her husband was crying and he asked her to forgive him. He bathed her head" and washed her face. She felt a severe pain in her stomach, which was much swollen, , and she had severe pains in the head. There was only , three little children in the house, the eldest being five years. She did not strike her husband, but refused to carry the child to bed. He had assaulted her before but not often. Cross-exatnined by the prisoner, the woman ! said she remembered falling in the street that night, but! she did not see any blood then. He did kick her in the stomach once.—Dr. Hutchinson, who is in attendance upon the woman, certified that he did not think she would recover. The prisoner was remanded for a week.

On inquiry last night our representative was informed that the injured woman had slightly improved, and there are now hopes that she may recover. She is still, however, in a very weak and precarious condition.

div.head: FRODSHAM. POLICE. NEWS.
div.p: FRODSHAM. POLICE. NEWS.
At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following cases were heard :

" ONE DnumEEN Do "—John Starkey, a small farmer, of Kingsley, was charged with two offences of drunken- ness and disorderly conduct, first at Norley on the 11th May, and second at Kingsley on the 15th Defend- ant pleaded guilty. He said it was all one drunken do. Defendant was fined 5s and costs in each case. PITCH AND Toss.—Alfred Dimelow' Frederick Worrall, Walter Lee, Frederick Darlington, George Carter, and Isaac Carter (all boys), and Edward Antrobus (a young man of about 21 or 28), were charged with playing at pitch and toss at Frodsham, on Sunday, the 29th ult.— P.C. Pearson proved the offence, and Antrobus was fined 2s 6d and 83 6d costs; and the other defendants ordered to pay 4s 6d before the next meeting. Worrm-an TRAVELLERS. Henry Dilke and Frederick Parsons, the former of whom did not appear, were charged with unlawfully being on licensed premises dur- ing prohibited hours, at the Railway Inn, Dunham, on Sunday, the 29th April.—Parsons pleaded guilty, saying that he was a stranger to these parts, and did not know the rules. The defendants lived about one mile and a quarter from the public-house.—Parsons was fined lOs and costs, and Dilke 15s and costs.

HUSBAND AND WIFE AT VAIIIANCE.—Edwin Holland, a bricksetter, of Frodsham Lordship, was charged on a warrant with failing to pay £1 12s, arrears of an order made upon him on the 26th of March last, to contribute 8s a week towards the support of his wife. Mrs Hol- land said the prisoner had paid nothing. Prisoner said he understood that the order was that if he provided a house for his wife there would be no necessity for him to pay the money. This he had done. Complainant said he had not. The Chairman said they would have nothing to do but commit prisoner to gaol. Prisoner said this would neither do him any good, them any good, nor his wife any good. Prisoner was ultimately committed to gaol for one month. SERIOUS ASSAULT.—SamueI Barkhill, a labourer, of Five Crosses, was summoned for assaulting William Sharpes, at Frodsham, on the 19th instant.—Complain- ant said he found the defendant in one of his fields about five o'clock oh the day in question. He was accompanied a woman. He ordered him out, but he would not go, and because he persisted in him being turned out he put himself in, a fighting attitude. He then desisted in his attempts to get him out, when defendant struck him several times, and knocked him down. He had seen Dr. Robinson since, and he had told him that in addition to other injuries one of his ribs was broken. He could hardly walk, and had hard work to dress himself. De- fendant said he was acting in self-defence.—Defendant was fined 40s and costs.

div.head: CATHOLIC BISHOPS AND THE PAPAL
div.p: CATHOLIC BISHOPS AND THE PAPAL

DECREE. At the meeting of tte Roman Catholic archbishops and bishops of Ireland, herd on Wednesday in Clonliffe Col- lege,the following resolutions were unanimously adopted and ordered to be published : "1. In obedience to the commands of the Holy See, and in willing discharge of the duty thus placed upon us, we desire to put on public record that the re- cent decree of the Holy Office addressed to the Irish hierarchy was intended to affect the domain of morals alone, and in no way to interfere with politics, as such, in this country., "2. Even this very day we have had from our Holy Father the Pope direct and unequivocal assurances of his deep and paternal interest in the temporal welfare of our country, and that, so tar from intending by this decree to injure our National movement, it was the hope and purpose of his Holiness to remove those things which he judged might in the long run be obstacles to its ad- vancement and ultimate success.

"3. With these facts thus clearly before us, apart altogether fitin his other numerous titles to our filial affection and respect, we must warn our people against the use of any hasty or irreve- rent language with reference to the Sovereign Pontiff or to any of the Sacred Congregations through which he usually issues his decrees to the faithful. "4. While expressing our deep and lasting gratitude to the leaders of the National movement for the signal services they had rendered to religion and country, we deem it our duty, at the same time, to remind them and our flocks, as we most emphatically do, that the Roman Pontiff has an inalienable and divine right to speak with authority on all questions appertaining to faith and morals."

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY "Alum."
I hear that the Runcorn branch of the Sons of

Temperance have got up a petition against the coni--- pensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. The petition is 12 yards long. I believe that with- out exception the ministers of religion in the town have added their names to the long list. But ought they not to do something more th4n lodge a silent protest against the objectionable clauses? In other parts of the country ministers have given their views with no uncertain sound, and have greatly aided in forming public opinion on a most impor- tant subject, but neither in Runcorn nor in Widnes have I heard of a single parson lifting up his voice to guide his fellow men aright on this question of compensation. Apparently they would prefer to give a disquisition from their pulpits on how the Children of Israel crossed the Red Sea rather than to follow in the footsteps of the Great Teacher and enter into the ordinary affairs of man, remembering that "the life of religion is to de good." For the past few months silence has once more been preserved by the Runcorn Board of Commis- sinners as to how matters• are progressing with regard to the much-needed improvement of Water- loo Bridge. At the rate negotiations are proceeding the present generation will have departed for their "long home" before anything whatever is done, and the money borrowed for the purpose of altering the Bridge will have been repaid, and the interest lost The Commissioners appear to have forgotten the old adage that "delays are dangerous." Per- haps Mr. Pritchard, as the Chairman of the Com- mittee most concerned, will enlighten the rate- payers at the meeting of the Board next Thursday Apropos of the Weaver Trust agitation, I hope that Mr. Aaron will not be contented until he has carried the resolution he has drafted, and the river Weaver is managed by the representatives of the ratepayers It would be idle to expect that Mr. Linaker will answer the questions asked at the last meeting of the Runcorn Guardians, considering the votes that were given. It may be interesting to know, therefore, that in consequence of the Weaver Trust not having for years previously handed over any money to the county funds, the Runcorn Guar- dians raised a most vigorous protest in the year 1873. with the result that in 1874 the Trustees paid £15,000 to the County Treasurer. In 1876, the sum of £lO,OOO was contributell to the county, but in 1877 and 1878 not a penny was paid. I have been unable, so far. to see the record for the succeeding years. but these facts are sufficient to show that the Trustees consider they are in no wise bound to aid the county rates. Once let the ratepayers obtain control of the Weaver, and the county, and the de- pressed salt industry, which contributes the greater part of the revenue of the Weaver Trust, and both will be benefited. Mr. Brunner, I am confident, will not let the matter rest where it is at the pre- sent time. The trustees of Widnes Parish Church have again been to Ireland for a vicar, and they are indeed to be congratulated if they have found a successor to Mr. Wright Williams, who will work with the energy and good will that gentleman did for a period of eight years. The Rev. Geo. Henry St. Patrick Garrett, 8.D., will come to Widnes with the highest recommendations, and he will, I doubt not, receive a hearty welcome from his numerous and hard-workingparishioners.

div.head: RETIREMENT OF MR. PATERSON.
div.p: THE RETIREMENT OF MR. PATERSON.

Mr. Jas. Paterson, manager of the Warrington Gas- works, has reported to the Gas Committee that he considers it necessary to tender his resignation. In his letter to the committee, Mr. Paterson says that it is not without a sense of pain that he feels it to be for the interests of the Corporation that a younger and more active man should be placed over the works. On this ground, combined with his failing physical powers, he purposes to retire, with the consent of the committee, at the end of the present month. The committee, in accepting the resignation, have prepared a report te be submitted to next Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council, in which reference is made to the long and faith- ful services of Mr. Paterson. The committee consider it desirable, in the interests of the rate- payers, to retain the services of Mr. Paterson as consulting engineer, and they propose to pay him a. salary of .£lOO per annum for his services. This position he is willing to accept. He will attend at the works as often as may be necessary, and will be at the services of the committee for the purposes of consultation and advice, so long as it may be deemed advisable that this arrangement be con- tinued. He will also report to the committee at least once a month on the condition of the works. The committee, after careful consideration, recom- mend the appointment of Mr. William Spence Haddock as gas engineer to the Corporation. Mr. Haddock served his articles under Mr. Paterson, and has held the appointment of assist- ant manager of the works, at a salary of £l5O per annum, since the 2nd of August. 1881. It is now proposed to pay him £3OO per annum. It is further recommended that Mr. Frederick Taylor, who has been in the employ of the Corporation and the old gas company for 30 years, have the manage- ment of the secretarial department, and that his salary be increased from .£lO5 to £220 per annum. In consideration of extra duties it is proposed to raise the salary oi Mr. W. S. Howard from .£lO4 to to .Cl2O per annum. The committee point out that these changes do not involve any additional expen- diture, but, on the contrary, effect a saving of .£209 per annum in the salaries paid to the several officers.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.

The following extracts are from the annual re-. port of this valuable institution :—Two events make the year 1887 a memorable one in the annals of this College. On January 31st, the new Practising Schools were opened; and on October 28th, the Chapel was dedicated by the- Right Reverend the Lord Bishop of Liverpool. The pressing wants of the College have thus been supplied. The Chapel has been built by the subscriptions of the friends ef the College and of the Clergy Daughters' School, by the pupils of which institution it is also used. Your committee are glad to be able to announce that the whole amount of the cost has been raised and that several handsome gifts of furniture have been added by kind friends. The number of students in residence during the year 1887 was one hundred and one, viz. :—Fifty-one seniors, and forty-nine juniors. One First Year student did not return to college after the summer holidays, owing to an illness contracted during those holidays. With this single exception the health of the students has been very good. The result of the Govern- ment examination for certificates, held in December, was as follows :—Seniors, lit class 13, 2nd class 37, 3rd class 1. Juniors, lit class 5, 2nd class 32, 3rd class 12. One of the five prizes offered by the Royal Geographical So- ciety for proficiency in geography to the students in Female Training Colleges was gained by Isabel Innes, a Second Year student. At the drawiqg examinations in October, eighteen students obtained their full drawing certificates. Thirty-nine passed in freehand, forty-five in geometry, forty-two in perspective, twenty-two in model, and thirty-three in blackboard, making a total of of one hundred and eighty-one. Sixty-two students passed in physiography, the science taken up for this year. An examination in the theory and practice of cookery was held in the college by a South Kensington Examiner. Thirteen students obtained the diploma, which entitles them to become teachers of cookery. The Annual Inspection by her Majesty's Inspector, J. G. Pitch, Esq., took place on June 28th and following days. He was assisted by W. S. Coward, Esq., 11. E. B. Harrison, Esq., and C. F. Harrison, Esq. Mr. Fitch af- terwards met the Committee. He reported that the premises were in excellent order, congratulated the Corn mittee on the acquisition cf a Chapel. and advocated the' building of a Recreation Room for the Students. Hlt commented very favourably on the tone and demeanour of the Students, but wished that the calibre of the can- didates for admission could be raised. The staff he con- sidered very valuable. The weak point in the work was the reading. The teaehing was also below the average, but a distinct improvement was observed in the notes of lessons. Ile was much pleased with the new practising schools. The senior students were examined in music by Dr. Stainer, on September 29th. All passed his examination, and thirty-five out of fifty were classed excellent. In the evening the students sang Sternelale Bennett's "May QIIPRI1," and Dr. Stainer expressed himself much pleased with it. Several gentle- men kindly gave their services in the choruses and to form a band. The Queen's Scholarship Examination was held, as usual, in the first week of July. There were one hundred and twenty-five candidates. No change took place in the resident staff during the year, but your committee, finding that the principal needed more help, sanctioned the appointment of a clerical lecturer, who should devote almost the whole of his time to the College instead of the four hours a week, formerly given by the clerical principal of the Clergy Daughters' School. The Rev. Oswald P. Whalley, 8.A., has been appointed to the post. Very satisfactory accounts of the work done by former students have been received, and 60 former students have obtained their parchments in the course of 1887. Your committee are glad to be able to state that the Finances of the College are in a satisfactory con- dition. It has not been necessary to apply to the Diocesan Boards for any subsidy this year.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Sexuanax.—Before Alderman Burgess. AN UNticricsmi HAvrxra.—Arthur Bryant, labourer, from London, was charged with being lan idle and dis- orderly person, acting as a pedlar without a license. A box- containing laces, ribbons, etc., was produced, which it was stated was carried by the prisoner. Alderman Burgess remarked. that he did not think it possible for any person to get a living in that way. It was onlyan ex- cuse for begging. Prisoner would be seat to the House of Correction for 14 days' ESCAPE FROM AN INDVSYRIAL SCROOL.—Frallk Church- man, 16, was charged with having absconded from the Barns House Industrial School, at Heaton Mersey. He was ordered to be sent back in charge of an officer. MoNnay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alderman Harrison, and Councillors Greening and J. Pierpoint. DauNNENNNss.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—James Wilkinson, in Bank Park. on Saturday, fined 5s including costs; John Taylor, in Win- wick-St., on Saturday, fined 5s and costs; Thomas Lamb in Winwick-at., on Saturday, fined 5s includint,a costs; Jane Runcorn, in Nicholson-st., on Saturday night, fined 5s including costs; Edward Lloyd, in Scotland-road, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs ; Patrick Moore, in Bewsey-road' on Sunday, fined lOs and costs; Winifred Conway, in Scotland-road, on the 19th ult, dismissed with a reprimand; Daniel Crosby, in Buttermarket-st., on the 19th ult., fined 56 and costs; Mary Knockton, in Wilderspool-road, on the 22nd ult, sent to prison for fourteen days. • Fusions DRIYING.—A young man named Joseph Had- land, was summoned for having furiously driven a horse in Winwick-road on the 16th ult. He,told the magistrates that the reins had broken, and that he had no intention of driving furiously. The case was dismissed. WIFE ASSAULT.—John Kane, for having been drunk and disorderly in Rose-yard on Sunday, and for having also assaulted his wife, was fined lOs and costa. MiscemANtous.—William Collier and John Smith, for baying disturbed the peace by fighting in Mersey-st., on the 19th ult., were each bound Over to be of good beha- viour for the ensuing six months, in their own recogni- sances of £s.—Patrick McLoughlin, who keeps a lodging house in Rose and Crown-st., was fined lOs including costs, for having neglected to lime-wash the walls and ceilings of his house, and to sweep the floor before a given hour in the morning.—William Looker, Cockhedge- lane, for selling milk without having been registered as a milk-seller, was ordered to pay 8s and costs. He pleaded that he had acted in ignorance. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough and Councillor John Pierpoint. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Martin Scanlan was charged with having assaulted Ann Hart, in Haydock-st., on the 20th of May. Defendant pleaded not guilty. After hearing evidence the magistrates ordered him to be bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of £lO, and one surety of £5, and to pay 17s 6dt the costs. In default he was to go to prison for

14 days. TimnsDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and Councillors Francomb and Platt. .—Catherine Taylor, who was brought up for having been drunk and disorderly in Hill-st., was dismissed on promising to leave the town. Michael Dowd was fined lOs and costs for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-st. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Dr. Gomall, and Alderman Harrison. A DESERTER.—George Burrows, a deserter from H.M. East Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Newry, was re- manded to await escort. A WOMAN'S DEFENCE.—Deborah Galin summoned her husband, Edwin Gaunt, for having assaulted her on the 28th ult. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. In cross-examination complainant admitted having on one occasion stabbed her husband on the nose with a table knife, and acknowledged that she was "free with her tongue,", as that was a woman's only defence. The case was adjourned for a week to give the parties time to ' come to some arrangement.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall (in the chair), W. Long. J. C. Parr, and H. Marson. Switut FRI7E/Z.—John Kirkham, innkeeper, Hatton,was charged with having unlawfully failed to report the existence of swine fever on his premises as required by the Contagious Diseases Act. Mr. Browne, of Warring- ton, appeared for the defence. It was stated that de- fendant sold two pigs to Mrs. Rowland, of Grimsditch Hall, on the 6th April, which were afterwards found to be suffering from swine fever, and had to be destroyed on the 21st April. After two or three witnesses had been heard on both sides, the case was dismissed.—Peter Woodward, for carrying pigs through swine fever infec- ted areas at Stretton and Appleton contrary to orders, was fined is for each pig and costs. DRUNKENNESS —John Allen, for having been drunk on the sth May at Grappenhall, was fined 5s and costs.— James Mullen was charged with having been drunk at Walton on the 18th March, and he was further charged with having assaulted P.C. Dutton at Moore. It ap- peared that, when arrested, the prisoner was very vio- lent and kicked, and otherwise assaulted the officer. For the drunkenness it was directed that the prisoner be sent to gaol for 21 days without the option of a fine, and a further 21 days' imprisonment for the assault. POACHING.—Joseph Tomlinson, a worker on the Ship • Canal, and William Thompson were charged with poach- ing at Acton Grange on the sth May, and each of them were fined Ss and costs or fourteen days' imprisonment. . Doe CASES.—Thomas Basnett for having kept a dog 'without a license, at Newton, Lei the 16th April, was ordered to pay costs 5s 6d ; Charles Purslow, for a simi- lar offence at Appletim on the 18th April, was fined 2s 6d and costs, lOs in all ; Thomas Holland was charged with having allowed a dog to be at large at Grappenhall on the 21st inst. in contravention of the rabies' order, and was ordered to pay costs, 3s 6d. CARELESS DRIVER.—For not having proper control 'Of dray and two horses at Stretton on the sth May, Wm. Hunt was fined 5s and costs; Robert Mellor, for having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Sevenoaks on the 3rd of April, was fined 2s 6d and Casts. THE STAG INN, LOWER WALTON.—On behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., plans were submitted to the bench showing a proposed alteration at the Stag Inn,l Lower Walton. It was stated that legally the alterations could be done without submitting the matter to the bench, but they (Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.) did net like to go about it in that way.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said that if it were intended to make in- ternal communication with premises not already licensed they were bound to submit the matter to the bench, but the proper time would be the general annual licensing meeting.—The Chairman said the Bench could not give any expression of opinion as to the matter on that occa- sion. THE ASSISTANT-OVERSEERSHIP OF APPLETON. Mr. Thomas Hall, one of the overseers for Appleton, applied to have a rate made for that township on the 27th April cancelled, and to have a new one allowed; also for the appointment of Mr. John Ellison, Stretton School, as assistant overseer, in place of Mr. C. J. Calvert. —ln re- ply to the Bench, !Mr. Hall said the overseers called a meeting of the ratepayers on the 17th May to ask Mr. Calvert to resign or revoke his appointment, as he had done his work very inefficiently. Mr. Calvert accord- ingly resigned, and ,at the poll, on the same day, Mr. Ellison was selected as his successor. The salary was £4O per annum.—The Bench acceded to the application, the Chairman expressing a hope that the overseers would be more successful in the new appoint- ment.

The Australians are not having all their own way this season, and the Gentlemen of England managed to make a draw of it in the game against them at Lord's on Tues- day. It will be remembered that the match between Lancashire and the Australians, which was concluded on Friday in last week, resulted in a victory for Lancashire. In this match, by the way, S. M. Crosfield, a Warrington player, did good service by securing three catches. In their first innings against the Gentlenlan the Australians totalled 179 and, the Gentlemen going in, W. G. Grace delighted everybody by running up a score of 165. The total of the innings amounted to 490, towards which W. W. Read got 109. When play was resumed on Tuesday, the Australians again went in, and scored 213 for the loss of one wicket, when the game was drawn. The two " not:outs " were Bannerman (30) and Jones (51), and Bonner, before being stumped out had put on 119 runs to his credit.

The huts in this neighliourhood are now neatly all occupied, and are beginning to have a homely look. A couple of ponderous navvies of the American type are vigorously making a way in. the 'direction of WilderspoOl, and it is surprising what a difference a few days' cutting snakes in the distance traversed. Where these navvies are now working is at a spot in the mea- dows nearly opposite Walton Lea, and the activity that is going on, can be seen by people passing on the Walton-road. A narrow cutting has been made for a short distance beyond the larger cutting, and the two navvies are working opposite each ,other, almost side byside, widening it. The close proximity to each othgr of the huge machines makes the scene at the bottom of the cutting one of unusnal bustle, as the excavators are both at the same time filling trains of waggons, which are constantly going and coming as they are loaded and unloaded. On the occasion of our last visit, there icarcely seemed to be a moment when one or the other of the trains was not in motion, and the horses were cons antly engaged in dragging away the filled waggons to make up the trains, and returning with the empties." Tho horses are fine, well-condi- tioned roadsters, and the way in which they go about their rather difficult business speaks Well for their docility as well as their training They take no notice of the clamour of the machinery, and pick their way among rails and sleepers as though to the manner born. A little preparatory work in the way of marking out the route, and removing surface' earth, is being carried on further forward in the direction of Wllderspool, and in a field that slopes, down towards the canal near Twenty- step bridge.

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
O. 20.-RUNCORN.

The Ship Canal is, for the purposes of the Act of Parliament, divided into three parts, or "works." Number one work extends from the foreshore of the estuary of the Mersey at Eastham to the west end of the north pier of the Old Quay Docks at Run- corn: number two work begins at the Old Quay Docks, Runcorn, and terminates at the intended Latchford Locks to the east of Warrington; and number three work commences at Latchford Locks, and end with the canal at Manchester. In this article we propose to forecast, as far as pos- sible, the alterations that are to be made near the termination of work number one, and the beginning of work number two at Runcorn. At the present time the Runcorn and Latchford Canal runs close past the southern side of the Old Quay Works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, but in the future its , channel will here and onwards to its termination ' at Old Quay Docks, practically be absorbed in the greater bed of the Ship Canal. The Old Quay piers. tidal basins, and wharves will be swept away, and the water of the new canal will flow over their sites. Amongst other buildings which at present stand directly in the intended course of the canal are the mortar works, which until lately belonged to the Bridgewater, Mersey, and Irwell Navigation, but now owned by the Ship Canal Company . them- selves, and the pottery works, offices, &c., In the occupation of the executors of the late Mr. Thomas Norman.

div.head: -AN EMBANKMENT AND A LOCK.
div.p: -AN EMBANKMENT AND A LOCK.

As it runs past Runcorn the southern banks of the canal will be pretty nearly the same as the present i south bank of the river, but as the canal sto be parcelled out of the river at this point it is evident that an artificial embankment will be needed to separate the channels of the natural and artificial waterways. This embankment will commence near the north-eastern or upper end of the island known as No Man's Land, and will extend up to the termi- nation of work number one, near the end of Irwell- lane. In order that a vessel, say from Widnes docks, may pass into the canal from the river, the embankment—which will be something like fifteen feet in height above the intended water level of the canal—will be pierced by a lock, the position of the lock being about two hundred yards above or to the east of Runcorn bridge. LIMITS Or DEVIATION.

In addition to what lies in the direct course o 1 the canal, the Canal Company have powers to ac- quire compulsorily if they like a good deal of house and other property lying along the southern bank of the Mersey at Runcorn, and which is included in what are known as the "limits of deviation:' It may not be without interest if we mention in some detail what lie* within these "limits of deviation," first premising that the property referred to was "scheduled" three or four years ago, and therefore doubtless in some cases has changed hands in the meantime. Commencing at Runcorn Bridge and going eastwards towards the Old Quay Works, we find amongst the scheduled property a boat-building yard with offices and workshops in the occupation of Messrs. Philip Speakman and W. Clucas ; a house, yard, footpath, outbuilding. &c., in the occupation of Mr. Wm. Leeson and Mr. T. Knight. The ferry and landing steps belonging to the London and North- Western Railway Co., and the old baths, which may have been a busy place when Runcorn was a health resort, but which have been long unoccupied and unused, at least for their original purpose, are also included. Next we have boat-building slips, one of I which was formerly the property of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, and the other of Mr. Philip Speakman; a flour mill, storehouse, stable, and wharf belonging to Mr. Geo. Lewis; houses, &c., marked as being in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Cawley, Mr. T. EvansoMr. Jos. Firtdlow, and Ellen Barker; and the workshop and premises of Messrs. John Brundritt, Wm. Hayes, and John Higson. Fol- lowing these we have houses and premises occu- pied by Mrs. Mercer and Mr. Henry Eaton, a wharf and retaining wall,, the property of the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners, a timber yard occupied by Messrs.Brundritt, Hayes,& Higson, and a shipbuild- ing yard in the possession of the same gentlemen. It should be mentioned that All Saints Church, which stands near to the river side hereabouts is not in- cluded in the "limits of deviation," nor are an part of its grounds. A public highway and foot- path belonging to the Runcorn Commissioners will, or rather may, be encroached upon; and the gra- Vitig dock, timber yards, and smithy set down as in the occupation of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation and Mr. George Lewis, come within the scope of the Canal Company's demands. Further on are the 'house, greenhouse, and outbuildings, the property of Mr. Joseoh Littler, and several cottages belong- ing to Mr/Philip Speakman, and in the occupation of various tenants. After these are a number of dwelling-houses and their appurtenances at present or formerly in the occupation of Messrs. Henry Hankinson, John Yates, Andrew Matthews, John Ball, R. Wilson, and the Rev. Father Fennelly. On the west side of Irwell-lane the old smithy may or may not, as circumstances require, continue to exist, and on the east side of Irwell-lane—which itself partly comes within the limits of deviation—there are about a dozen cottages formerly belonging to the Mersey and Irwell Navigation and Bridgewater Trustees and duly scheduled. Near the Old Quay Works some fields belonging to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, may be taken, besides a variety of outbuildings. To the westward of Runcorn Bridge the limits of deviation include a quantity of buildingland, which, as being part of the property of the Bridgewater undertaking, will no doubt now be in the possession of the Ship Canal Company, and also the block of nearly twenty cottages nearest the bridge,. The houses in Suffolk-st, Cawdor-st., Portland-rt., Ben- tinck-st, and Leinster-st. are not indicated as being within the limits.' ANOTHER EMBANKMENT AND LOCK.

As we have mentioned the embankment which terminates near the Old Quay works begins at the upper end of the island:known as "No Man's Land" on the other side of Runcorn Bridge. The canal, after passing under this bridge, runs through what is known as "The Gut.," that is the channel be- tween the mainland and "No Man's Land," and at this point this latter-named island will take the place of the embankment as the northern boundary of the canal. The lower end of "No Man's Land will be the terminating point of another embank- ment which will begin on Frodsham Score, and through this embankment there will be no fewer than three locks. The nearest of these locks will be opposite the Bridgewater docks, and until this lock is constructed and open for the passage of traffic between the docks and the estuary of the Mersey, all traffic destined for or coming from the docks is to be allowed to pass up and down so much of the canal between Runcorn and Eastham as shall for the time being be open and available free of any ship dues, or canal, or lockage tolls. After the opening of the lock referred to for Runcorn traffic the Canal Company are to afford such facilities for all vessels and barges which shall, on any tide, be ready to leave the docks, and which, but for the construction of the canal, could have left Runcorn over the existing sills and proceeded down the estuary on the same tide, as will enable the vessels and barges to cross the canal and pass into the estuary on the same tide. In case vessels and barges have not these facilities afforded them by the Canal Company they will have the right to pass down and out of the canal free of any ship dues or canal and lockage tolls. (To be Continued.)

div.head: EASTHAM.
div.p: EASTHAM.

The cottages that have been built at Eastham for the navvies have now very prettily laid out gardens, and numerous visitors are rather surprised at the air of com- fort that there is about them. At Pool Hall brook an object of much speculation has bean unearthed. A foot- path has been laid bare, composed of boulders, and edged with red sandstone about three feet wide, and leading in a south-east direction; some of the trees immediately above it are of great ago, and the clay has become stra- tified. The excavations in the lock pits have now been carried down a second lift, making a depth of about 35 feet. The clay is extremely hard, and the steam navvy has difficulty in forcing its teeth through it. It is ex- pected that rock will very soon be struck in this lift. Hundreds of stone-dressers will be set on as they arrive here in search of work, as there are miles of dressed stone embankments to be made on this section. MOORE AND DISTRICT.

The progress that is so characteristic- a- feature of the Ship Canal undertaking is shown in a marked degree at Moore, Acton Grange, and Walton, though..there is very little this week to be recorded beyond a general advance in the various departments of the work. The workshops and offices that have for some time now occupied a posi- tion at Acton Grange are beginning to lose their new appearance, and are gradually assuming a darker hue in

div.head: ECCLES AND BARTON.
div.p: ECCLES AND BARTON.

The works in the Eccles and Barton districts are being pushed forward at every point with the utmost expedi- tion. At Stiggin's Island, half a mile below Barton bridge, a new cutting isbeing made to divert the river, and thus afford tipping accommodation in the old bed of the Irwell, 'which runs round the !gland. A Freribli steam navvy has been got to work on the island; and the cut- ting has begun at Flixton, near Hulme's bridge. There are seven locomotive. and 1,009 men at work on the Eccles and Barton sections. TELEPHOIC COMMUNICATION. The telephone that is being placed along the route of the canal has been completed for a distance extending from Eastham to a little beyond midway on the section between Latchford and Warburtou. div.head: NEW BILL.
div.p: THE NEW BILL.

On Thursday the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill deposited a petition in the Examiner's Office for leave to bring in a bill to alter certain authOri,sed works in Salford. Mr. Coates, Mr. Leader Williams, and Mr. Saxon proved that the necessary notice had been served. It was stated that the works to be abandoned were estimated at £1,041,574 15s 7d, and that the sub- stituted works would cost £1,028,586 7s Bd., the inten- tion being to expend the saving on the new docks and nothing else. The Examiner doubted whether the 4 per cent, already deposited under the original Act applied to the proposed substituted works, and after some discus- sion he expressed the opinion that the rule had been complied with. Though the Standing Orders were de- clared not complied with, it is only a formal matter, as the bill will now come before the Standing Orders Corn. mitten of the House of Commons on the questionof time. No difficulty is anticipated on this point, as the bill is not opposed.

div.head: TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.

FIVE WOMEN BURNED TO DEATH. A fire broke out on Wednesday morning on the premises of Messrs. Garrould, milliners and drapers, ' in Edgware-road and Queen-at., London, which re- sulted in five persons being burned to death; whilst five young women who were sleeping on the pre- mises were severely injured by burns and by jump- ing from the second and third floor windows. The alarm was first given at a quarter past six by the porter on the premises. The fire broke out on the ground floor in 58, Queen-st., and spread with such rapidity thst within half an hour the Queen-st. pre- mises were burned out, and the Edgware-road shops were burned out within a very short time after- wards. There were sleeping on the premises 22 female assistants and six servants, besides 15 young men. On the alarm being given the inmates were aroused, but were unable to escape by the staircases on account of the flames and smoke. The young women appeared at the windows at both the front and the rear of the premises, and one named Jane Fletcher, remarking to her companions that she was not going to stay to be burned, jumped from the second floor window in the rear, and falling through a skylight sustained severe injuries. A large crowd of people had assembled, and shouted to the inmates to wait until ladders were brought. This was soon done. A party of painters who were working in Newman-st., close by, hurried to the scene with their ladders, and placing them to the windows, succeeded with the aid of the police in rescuing several of the young women. The flames, however, were spreading so quickly, that it it was evident that all could not be rescued in this way. A tarpaulin was brought, and held stretched out in the roadway by a number of police, who called upon the occupants of the buildings to jump into it. Several of the girls did so and escaped more or less uninjured; but one named Annie Webb, striking the side of the sheet, fell violently upon the ground. Meantime the men of the Metro- politan Fire Brigade, who had arrived upon the scene with their usual promptitude, were pouring water upon the burning block, but with little effect, the fire having got complete hold of the building. So rapidly indeed had the fire, gained that though the fire escapes were almost inimediately at hand, there was no possibility of making use of them. At the top of 58, Queen-st., the house in which the fire originated, the housekeeper, Hannah Glew, slept with her niece. They were both seen at the window, which they did not open, although they were urged to do so by the firemen and police, who held.another tarpaulin for them to jump into. This was the only means of ,escape, as the window was surrounded by the flames. Mrs. Glow and her niece, however, were apparently paralysed with fear, and were presently seen to fall upon the floor. They were not observed again alive; but subsequently their charred bodies were found close together. An heroic rescue was effected by David Buchanan, a labourer. He ascended one of the ladders in Edg- ware-road, and finding it was too short to reach to the upper storey climbed upon the coping of a win- dow and succeeded in placing one of the girls in safety on the ladder. The feat, which was attended with great risk, was loudly cheered by the crowd. In addition to Mrs. Glew and her niece, three other of the inmates lost their lives in the flames, and their bodies were afterwards found and conveyed to the Marylebone mortuary. The names of the dead are :—Hannah Glew, 55, housekeeper; her niece, 20: Mary W. Berry, 25, of 29, Carlton-road, Manor Park; Emma Margaret Edwards' 35, of TivertonNon-Avon, Bath; Agnes 1171 and, 24, of 87, Coldharbour-lane, Camberwell. Five persons who were injured were removed to St. Mary's Hospital, two of them suffering from burns and the others from Injuries sustained in jumping from the windows. An affecting incident in con- nection with the fire is the death of a young lady, ' not one of the employ i 6s, who was staying n the ' house. She arrived in London on Tuesday to attend the wedding, which was fixed for Wednesday, of her friend, who was one of the assistants. , Both lost their lives. The loss is estimated at £130,000. This, 1, however, is covered by insurance. A fund has been opened for the relief of the sufferers. Lord Randolph Churchill, whose town residence is near the scene of the tire, and Mr. John Aird, M.P., head the list of subscribers with .f5O each. Funds are stated to be urgently needed.
Dregsmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's. which for strength is unequalled.—Advt.

EXPLOSION AT STEEL WORKS.—Four men were badly burnt at Messrs. William Jessop & Sons' Brightside Steel Works, Sheffield, on Wednesday night, by an explosion of steel. An ingot was being cast in a crucible furnace when the ladle burst, causing the molten metal to fly. Three of the men were removed to the Infirmary, and are in a critical condition. A Winow's BRRAar OF PROMISE ACTION.—The action for breach of promise of marriage brought by Ada Dunderdale, widow, Gwendor-road, West Kensington, against Captain Cadell, Calcutta, was again before the Middlesex Sheriff's Court, on Thursday. Plaintiff on the previous occasion claimed £5,000 damages, and as the defendant did not appear judgment went by default. The jury were not asked to assess damages. Mr. Dickins, however, for the plaintiff, said the case had keen arranged, and judgment was entered for £420 and costs.
