, pOIitTISATION TO BREWERS.

MEETING-AT WARRINGTON: On Tuesday evening a well-attended public meeting, convened by the Warrington Temperance Federation,. was held in the Co-operative Hall, to protest' against the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill now befere Parliament. In the absence of the president (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), the chair was taken by the Rev. J. Yonge. Among those present were the Revs. J. J. Langham, G. D. Wray, J. Warnock, E. C, E. Carleton. E. H. Jack- son; Councillors J. Greening and H. Roberts, Dr. Gornall, Messrs. J. Walker, W. Twiss, J. B. Isaac, W. Roberts, T. Birchall, &c. , The Rev. J. J. LA.Nallel4f read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. R. Garnett, the Rev. W. Graham, and the Rev. E. Moore.. Mr. Garnett, who wrote from London, hoped to heat of a good meeting; and the Rev. W. Graham trusted that they would have a good meeting, and emphatically condemn the compensation clauses of the Bill now before the House. The Rev. E. Moore wrote : From the standpoint of public policy, as well as from a moral point of view, I think these compen- sation clauses very objectionable. 'lle CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, hav- ing referred to the objects of the Warrington Temper- ance Federation, went on to say that the committee of the federation were strongly of opinion that the time had come just at.present when the public temperance senti- ment of this town should find emphatic and unmistak- able expression in reference to the proposals now before the House of Commons on the part of the Government with respect to compensating publicans who may, if the new bill passes into law, be called upon to surrender their licenses. These compensation clauses, as they were called, were exciting a very large and intense opposition through the length and breadth of the country, and he thought that was a matter upon which they might fairly congratulate themselves. He thought there could be very little doubt that it was the feeling with reference to these particular proposals which had something and per- haps a great deal to do with the recent election in the town of Southampton. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With regard t 9 the eiettSes they were seeking to protest against, he did het know whether any gentleman in the room had seen a printed copy of the Local Government Bill. If they had they would have been impressed by the bigness Of the measure; by the vastness of its provisions, and its scope,' and there could be no doubt whatever that it contemplated a very big work. (Hear, hear.) The compensation clauses sought, as he understood them— and he thought that it was very necessary for any one speaking of a bill before Parliament to put in a saving clause like that, for next to the proper understanding of Bradshaw's railway guide he did not know anything much more perplexing than bill before the House of Commons. (Laughter.) Well, as he understood the present proposals of the Govern- ment, the power to give licenses had to be vested in licensing committees selected from the county councils which the bill would call into existence, and it seemed to be intended that these licensing committees should have. power to refuse to renew licenses if, in the opinion of the committees it was for the interest of the particular dis- trict that the license sqould be withdrawn. Then the bill went on to provide that such refusal to renew lic,eir sea must be confirmed by the County Council, and when that had been done the license holder yeas to receive a money compensation for the loss of his license. With regard to that, the essence of a publican's license was that it was for the good of the public, and moreover that it was distinctly and unmistakeably ,an annual license granted year by year. (Applause.) They must remember also that publicans who took out those licenses were perfectly well aware of the conditions on Which they held them. They knew that licensee had been made annual by Act of Parliament in the interests of the public welfare, yet notwithstanding that fact it was proposed to compensate publicans whose licenses were, in the in- terests of the public welfare, withdrawn from them. The bill specified that compensation was to be paid in the first instance out of the county fund, but ultimately such compensation for renewal of licenses was to be paid, as he understood, out of the rates of the licensing division in whichthe licensed house was situate. The Local Government Bill so managed the licenses that the county ratepayer loses by every public house that was extin- guished, and gained by every license whith was given. He thought they could foresee that the County Council would have before them in all these questions a supreme regard to the interests of the ratepayers, meaning by that the pecuniary interests of the ratepayers; they would not always be so particularly anxious for the moral welfare of the ratepayers. (Hear hear.) Some of them would remember that he had at one time the privi- lege of serving on the Board of Guardians, and he noticed very frequently the greater interest of the Guardians was to guard the pockets of the ratepayers than to be "guardians" of the poor, and he often thought that the "guardians of the poor" was a remarkable misnomer; it ought to have been "guardians of the ratepayers." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He fancied also that the County Council would care infinitely more for the money interest of the ratepayers than for the sobriety of the public. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to know why publicans should be compensated when their licenses were withdrawn for the welfare of the public. This had not been the case in days gone by. When, for instance, free trade came in farmers suffered, but they were never compensated. When the Irish landlords suffered reduc- tions through the action of the Land Acts they did not get any compensation. When Parliament sanctioned the introduction of railways into this country coach pro- prietors suffered a tremendous loss, but they were not compensated. (Applause). He saw in the "Daily News" that day a somewhat remarkable letter from a medical man, who said that the introduction of the new bill meant the extinction of many salaried appointments. The holders of these appointments had at any rate an equal claim to compensation with the brewer and the publican. In all, the medical officers of health number 1,300, and it was estimated that 'their numbers would be reduced to 200. But Mr. Ritchie breathed no word of compensasion for them. But why not ? Their tenure was identical with the tenure of the license holder. Like him they had their license on appointment renewed yearly, and like him felt entitled to expect such renewal except in the case cff misbehaviour. If there was a difference, surely the medical officers of health might claim to have done more for the community than the license holder. Either compensate all who were injured alike or don't compensate at all. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) Let them ask what that compensation really meant as a matter of money for the ratepayers of the , country. Mr. Caine, who had worked up the calcula- tion, had no hesitation in placing the amount with which the Government proposed to endow, the liquor trade at from £200,000,000 to £250,000,000. The great bulk of this sum would go into the pockets of monopo- list distillers and brewers, and not into the pockets of the publicans. (Hear, hear.) •He should like them as ratepayers of the county to consider whether they felt disposed to pay large sums of money to firms like those of Messrs. Bass, Guinness and allsopp, or even to those very estimable gentlemen whom they all knew—Sir Andrew Walker and Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) The Rev. J. J. LANGIHAM moved "That in the opinion of this meeting those portions of the Local Government Bill Which provide for a change of the licensing autho- rity, without conferring upon the inhabitants the power of preventing the issue or renewal of licenses, and which would assign compensation to the holders of annual licenses when such licenses were not renewed, are open to the gravest objection; and this meeting most strongly urges the removal of the clauses relating to compensa- teen and the insertion of others giving power to the in- habitants themselves to veto the issue or renewal of licenses in their respective districts having a direct popu- lar vote." (Applause.) Whatever, he said, might be the result of the great contest that was now taking place in reference to the licensing clauses he felt very strongly that as temperance workers they owed the present Go- vernment, and Mr. Ritchie in particular, a great. debt of gratitude. He would tell them why. Never had tem- perance sentiment been so much to the fore as it was at the present time, and never was the 'question more ripe for settlement, fnd never, therefore, were they in a better positidn to demand what they meant to have some day with the hope of success. (Applause). Why, even Mr. Gladstone had at length declared himself on their side. They had not had very much to thank him for in days gone by in the matter of temperance. It was to his instrumentality they owed those off-licenses which he (Mr. Langham) considered one of the greatest banes of the country; but Mr. Glad- stone had at last declared himself on their side, and right glad he was to hear it, and to welcome him in future as a worker in the cause. (Applause). He could not help speaking most hopefully on the question that night, for if Mr. -Gladstone declared himself in favour of local option—and he took it that his recent speeches .meant that if they meant anything—his followers would be on their side too. He wished he had come to that conclusion sometime ago, but no doubt the Southampton election had opened his eyes, and he very earnestly hoped it would not be long before other expressions of opinion had the effect of waking up the present Govern- ment too. It was, indeed, only a matter of time. They might have opposition now, but truth was on their side, and in the end it would prevail. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause). There was much in the Local Government Bill with which he cordially agreed, even in the matter of the iie.eeetere clauses, and there were certain aspects which commendeu to his reason and to his sense of justice. First of all the neekelee ss.vises pro- posed to transfer the licensing authority. With tnat was entirely in harmony, as nothing could be more un- just than the present mode in which licenses were granted. At present, public houses were planted in a locality presumably for the benefit of that locality, yet the people most concerned hadnovoice whatever as to the way in which their wants should be supplied. But that was a style of things which must come to an end, and the licensing clauses recognised the fact that the people whose wants are supposed to be supplied should have a hearing and should be allowed to say what they want and what they do not want. (Hear, hear). But coming to the exact proposals that were before Parliament they found that it was proposed to hand the question of licensing over to the County Council. The members of these County Councils would be elected not

only to decide licensing questions but a variety of other matters. That, he thought, was a source of grave ob- jection to them all, for the reason that they might be perfectly certain that the members would not look upon the question upon its merits. They would be elected members by people who had entrusted to them a num- ber ef other interests, and they would not look upon the licensing question as it should be looked upon. What they wanted was a body who should decide the temper- ance question, and that question alone—(litar, hear, and applause)—as it was the gravest and the most import- ant question before the country at the present time. (Hear, hear.) With regard to compensation he could not admit for a moment that the publicans had any right to it, either legally or equitably. (Hear, hear.) bealing with the moral aspects of the question, he said the pro- posal of the Government was simply a specious and underhand way of endowing the liquor traffic throughi out the country. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Government had, he said, started with the best inten- tions, and they no doubt thought they were about to do a clever thing and please both parties—the publietins and the temperance party—but as a natural result be- tween the two stools they had come to the ground, or, rather, they would come to the ground—(hear, hear, and laughter)—unless they learnt better,for the question was one which could not be put off any longer, They who had worked in the temperance cause had been trifled with too long. The country had been ripe for local option for years, and it was only an equitable way of dealing with the question to give the people a direct popular veto in the matter. (Applause.) This was not a question of party. It was a question of truth, equity, and righteousaess, and he fer one as a clergyman knew no politics except so far as they had to do with the ele, vation of the people. (Applause.) The Rev. G. D. WRAY, in secOnding the motion, said that this was a matter which ootieerned the moral well- being of the people of the cOlintry, and, therefore, must be of far greater moilleat than politics, and ought to be fully discussed by n*ii. of an shades of political feeling. Ho must admit that be a certain extent he rejoiced in the clauses 14.1 the Bill, because they recognised for the first time the principle of local option. It was very round- about•aad indirect, but he felt convinced that something must come of it. They had met together that evening to protest against the manner in which it was wished to give them local option,' and also to the clauses of com- pensation. They would not like their members of Par- liament to be returned by a council appointed by them- selves. They preferred to vote directly for them, and why should they not vote directly on the most important Question of public morals? (Hear, hear, and applause.) He thought they might take a hint from the colonies. He saw from the "Alliance News" that at Melbourne they had had the direct popular veto, and there the tem- perance party had won their cause by a large majority-, and the public-houses in Melbourne were to be reduced from 48 to 28. (Applause.) And last week he read a letter from his brother, who lives in Ballarat, in which he said the temperance party had, just won a great vic- tory, and the public-houses, which numbered 72, were to be reduced to 27. (Applause.) With regard to com- pensation, if a man entered into a business without understanding that business, why should he have com- pensation ? It was a publican's duty to know how long his license did extend, and if he chose to think that his license was permanent that was no reason why he should be compensated for his voluntary ignorance. The pro- position was absurd in the extreme, and not to be con- sidered for a moment. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN. having invited discussion, Mr. W. H. BUTLER said that he was not in favour of making local option the point for which temperance re- formers ought to work. If they wished to deal effec- tually- with the liquor traffic they must take a higher platform. With respect to the question of compensa- tion, he was altogether against it. He denied that the license-holders, publicans, and brewers had an equitable right to compensation; there was no basis for compen- sation, either on legal, moral, or seatimental grounds, (Hear, hear). The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETbN said he thought the way in which the licensing system of this country had been administered was such as to give the publican a reason- able ground of belief that if he conducted his house in a respectable manner his license would not be taken from him. A publican engaged in the drink traffic, as other people engaged in their businesses, on the faith that the existing order of things would continue, to a certain ex- tent; certainly that there would beno violent stoppage which would bring immediate ruin on him. He con- sidered it rather unfair to treat the publican as if he alone was to blame for the existing state of things.. The truth was they were all to blame and were all respon- sible; and, therefore, to ask the publican 'to bear the sole blame and pay the penalty was rather too much. The publican had not made the law; it was made by the people of this country, and they it was who were entrusted with its administration. He thought their temperance friends ought to be prepared like others to make some sacrifice for their principles. He did not admire some men of strong .opinions who took precious good eare that their convictions should not cost them anything, and he doubted the wisdom of taking up the ground of earnest moral reformers, and at the same,. time saddling the publican with a big share of the burden, and expecting him to bear the expense of the movement. (Hear, hear.) He thought they should, as earnest, strong, and religious reformers be prepared to share the cost and the suffering which the triumph of their cause might necessitate. (Applause.) Of course he did not wish it to be understood that he approved of all that was contained in those compensation clauses, and he had no doubt the 'Government would give con- sideration to the various amendments which had been
placed upon the bpi*. He should certainly think tile; foolish if they sought to pass the bill as it stood, in the face of the great opposition which had arisen. (Ap- plause). . . _

, Dr. GORNALL said that he should like to quote two opinions on this question, one from either side of the House. The first was by Sir H. Selwin Ibbetson, who held office in one of L.ord Beaconsfield's Administrations, and who said :—" With regard to the licensing question, he admitted that publicans had no legal claim to com- pensation. He had been concerned in the passing of some of the Licensing Acts, and ft was understood at the . . _

, time that there was no legal claim." The second opinion was from the Liberal side of the House, Sir William Ver- non Harcourt being the speaker. He said : "Now, in 1883, when that was a Cabinet question, it was his duty to make a statement, and he then said that there was an unquestionable power on the part of the magistrates with discretion to refuse the renewal of licenses. He stated that without any referenceto compensation whatever, and the representation was made on behalf of the whole Gov- ernment, of which the right hon. gentleman, the member far West Birmingham, was a member. That was the at- titude which the present Opposition took up in 1883, and that was the position to which they had ever since ad- hered. He hoped the Liberal part3r would adhere to the course the Liberal Government took in 1883, and support local option without any compensation clauses." (Ap- plause.) Apropos of the occasion, the Chairman had read a letter from a Medical Officer of Ffealth, and as one who had occupied a similar post. he might say a word on that subject. He held the position of Medical Officer of Health for the Rural Sanitary District for a period of ten years and without any reason whatever was die- charged—discharged for no other reason, perhaps, than lbecause he had the interest of the poor at heart. Some of his medical friends took an interest in the mat- ter, and appealed in his behalf to the Local Government Board. A certain Mr. Jesse Collings was then the Secre- tary to the Local Government Board, and he wrote in reply saying that as his alepointment was merely a yearly one he had no claim. (Laughter.) Why should he have worse treatment--(laughter)—than the promo- I ters of a traffic which had degraded this town to the ut- most extent? (Applau4.) Mr. JOHN WALKER then replied on the discussion. With regard to the question of the slave trade, men- tioned by Mr. Carleton, he said they would all admit I that the traffic was inhuman, but it was none the less a fact that the law did recognise an estate in slaves. ("Shame.") He wished them to understand that, as distinguished from the fact that the law did not recog- nise an estate in lidenses That was the broad distinc- tion in law, and in argument. He understood Mr. Carleton to suggest that they on their side were a little too prone to advocate the question on purely moral grounds: Mr. CARLETON : You do not admit the sacrifice; that's what I mean. Mr. WALKER. continuing, said that teetotallers were prepared to make some sacrifice in the matter, but they were not disposed to make the mad and tremendous sac- rifice that the Government had proposed they should make. (Applause.) Mr. Butler had said that, even if it wasP determined that compens'ation was legal, that would not satisfy him. Mr. Carleton seemed to be en- tirely at issue with him there, and they on the platform were at issue with him as well. He, Radical as some people would call him, considered himself a law-abiding citizen, and if the highest courts in this country had de- cided that a claim for compensation was really legal—if by our negligence we had allowed an estate in licenses to be made—he should be ready to say—" We have blundered in this mattes, but we must pay the piper." (Hear, hear.) But they had not blundered. the point was that no such estate had ever been created It thus fepowed that, legally, at any rate, no claim could be set up for licensing compensation. The Lord Chief Justice would be recognised as a high authority in such a matter. He said: "There is no vested interest in the trade. It has been tested again and again, and laid down that the discretion of the licensing justices is absolute. Magistrates have the absolute power in cutting short publicans' interests." his opinion, entirely disposed of the, contention raised by o had pleaded that publicans had some undentatruYAY7.ll `.4""7 would be abi. t 4, tinue their licensee. _ Mr. CARLETON : Expectation; that was it-. If the State was to set about trying to satisfy all the oxpecta- tions that people had, he thought that nine-teaths of the tradesmen of Warrington—he was certain aoeut some of the newspaper proprietors—would have a claim to make. stand Mr. Butler, as a temperance man, objecting to' local option. far-reaching influences of that kind were, he might tell them that to-day, in the far-off city of Chicago, perhaps one of the most powerful influences for good, a sworn enemy of the drinking and gambling saloon, a man always foremost to raise the fallen, was proud to say that he gained many of his practical ideas," and his enthusiasm in good work, within those walls. About 27 or 28 years ago the great co-operative move- ment had been commenced, and what he believed was to-day perhaps one of the most substantial institutions in Warrington, and one of the most sound co-operative societies in England, was the result of work that went on at that school. That society was now distributing arriongst tile" poor working people of this town at 'least £B,OOO per annum. He was glad to see that as the old ones fell by the way the young men seemed to take up the work with renewed courage and vigour, and he had never known in the history of the school more earn- est workers amongst their young men than they had at the present time. (Applause.) Mr: W. Lox° said that he looked forward to the future position of the Sunday school with great hope, and thought that in the hands of the . present superintendent it wouldincrease in usefulness. He then proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. Drummond for his services on Sunday, and to the various speakers who had addressed that meeting. (Applause.) • Mr. C. TRAVERS seconded the proposition, which was cordially carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close. PRESENTATION TO MR. C. TRAVERS. A social gathering in connection with the centen- ary celebration was held in Cairo-st. schoolroom on Thursday evening, when occasion was taken of the opportunity to present Mr. Charles Travers, the secretary of the Sunday school,' with a handsome writing desk, as a token of the esteem of his fellow workers at the school, and as a mark of the manner in which they , appreciated his services. Mr. Travers, who is leaving Warrington to take an ap- pointment at Newcastle-on-Tyne, has been secretary of the 'Sunday school for the past five years, prior to which time he was for abo•tt eighteen months the assistant secretary. He has also for a long period been a teacher at the school. The arrangements for the pre- sentation had been left in the hands of a committee composed of Messrs. T. Birchall, T. Knowles, John Chalmers, Alfred Hampson, and S. Wellings (secretary). The writing desk, which is made of oak and handsomely mounted, bears on a silver plate the following inscrip- tion :—" Presented to Mr. Charles Travers by the teachers and friends of Cairo-street Sunday school, Warrington, in grateful recognition of his services as secretary, with the earnest hope that his future career may be happy and prosperous. May 31st, 1888." The position of secretary rendered vacant by the retirement of Mr. Travers will, it may be mentioned, be now filled by Mr. S. Wettings. The pro- ceedings commenced with a tea, to which about 75 per- sons sat down, and at which the wants of those present were looked afterby Mrs.Chamberlain,Miss Hill, and Mrs. Jefferson, assisted by various friends. Subsequently there was dancing, and musical selections were given at intervals. Mr. T. Birchen was MC., and Mr. T. Ford officiated at the piano, as well as rendering solos on the harp and concertina. Mr. T. Stirk gave eornet solos, Miss F.tlith Birchall a solo on the pianoforte, and a duet was contributed by Mr. Edwin Wright and Mr. Harry Wright. The presentation was made at about nine o'clock by Mr.T. BIRCILLLI, who said that his duty was a very pleas- ing one. Though a pleasing one it was in some respects a sad one. It was pleasant to offer something to some- one they respected, esteemed, and loved, but when it was but the prelude for that someone's departure, for a time at least, there was always a tinge of sadness about it. Mr. Travers was on the point of leaving Warrington for a new sphere of work, and the teachers, scholars, and friends thought the would not like him to go without giving him some slight token of their regard—something that would in the future remind him of the kind feelings that they entertained towards him. Mr. Travers was a young man for whom he had always felt great respect; he had seen him grow up from scholar to teacher, and had always considered him a valuable acquisition to their ranks. He believed that the principles Mr. Travers had imbibed in that school, and his sturdy :determination of character, would ensure his success in the future. (Applause.) He then made the presentation. In reply Mr. TRAVERS said that the friendships he had formed at Cairo-st. Sunday School were friendships that he Oaould never forgct ; wherever fortune might place him in the future he should never forget the kind friends that he had worked with in that school. He should never think that one day spent in the school had been wasted, for he had learned some of the truest and best lessons of his life in it. Although he was leaving War- rington, he hoped that in the town he was going to he i might work amongst those who were helping n the cause of Unitarianism there. (Applause). Mr. CHALMERS then presented Mr. Travers. on behalf of Mr. F. Buckley Mellor, harmoniumist at the school, with a handsomely bound copy of the" Vicar of Wake- field." In doing so he said that the sincerest wish of the teachers of the school was that Mr.Traversmight prosper in his new sphere of labour, as he had prospered in the past. Mr. TRAVERS having replied, the presentation proceed- ings terminated.

WIDNES RATEPAYERS AND THEIR SERVANTS. Sir —A few years ago some stir was made about Mr. Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, having earned an odd day's remuneration as poll clerk during an elec- tion contest in the town. It would be interesting to learn how many of the Local Board officials hold per- manent dual-appointments at fixed annual salaries at the present time. The salaries paid by the Board are presumably for a full day's work, and require that the whole of an officer's time shall be devoted to the duties assigned him, but from a document which has came into my possession to-day, I notice that one of our rate collectors is also the assistant overseer and rate col- lector, at an annual salary of £3O, to a neighbouring authority in whose township he resides. Should not such amounts, if allowed to be receivable, be taken in part payment of, and deducted from, the salary paid by the ratepayers of Widnes? There is room for economy here.—Yours, A RATEPAYER. P..—Are all the officials allowed to reside outside the township?

div.head: " CADMUS ALIVE AGAIN.
div.p: " CADMUS ALIVE AGAIN.

Sir,—A " Marciful Providence, who fashioned him hol- ler." has restored "Cadmus "to us, when I was deplor- ing his loss. I am, for one, very thankful, because I really did not want to miss his mental twistings, Which are nothing if not absurdly comic! I assume, from "Cadmus' " last epistle that he has only attended one church, and one needs to seek no further for the " knifey narrowness" of his views. If his knowledge of men and things had been gained in a wider field, the ludicrous as- sertions he hasjust made would neverave appeared, and he would not stand, as he most assuredly does now, a laughing-stock for his brother scribes. What on earth is the meaning of this phrase? "To commit a theft is to take something from somebody that one has no legal right to." It takes my breath away! and only " Cad- mus " can explain. May the explanation be no more fogging than the phrase! For guidance to a correct view of what is theft, I say : A publican, or tailor, or cobbler, or even a parson, who has bought a living, has acquired a tangible, and inalienable right to call it his own; and the man (or men), who, by act or deed, takes it from him is an unmitigated thief. No subterfuge can evade this fact, and I say, with all humility, to "Cad- mus," that if he holds contrary views, he.must not come visiting to my house without due notice, so that I may have spoons and other small valuables stored away! I hope I have explained how I came to my "extraordin- ary conclusions ; " if not, I can only say that it is be- cause my antagonist is, what all bigoted teetotallers are, " one:eyed " in argument; luminosity itself where there is a plausible chance of injuring a tradesman as legally constituted as himself; but "blind as a mole" to any arguments on the opposite side. They are as like as two peas, what one of our greatest poets wrote of a narrow-minded, and not too honest, genius of seventy years ago : " Sepulchral Grahame. pours his notes sublime In mangled prose, nor e'en aspires to rhyme; Breaks into blank the Gospel of St. Luke, And boldly pilfers from the Pentateuch; And, undisturbed by conscientious qualms, Perverts the Prophets, and purloins the Psalms." BELLEROPHON. Warrington, 29, 5, 1888.

THE TEMPERANCE PARTY AND THE LICENSING QUESTION. Sir,—lt is not easy to understand the position which was taken up by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton with regard to this compensation to publicans' question at the meet- ing on Tuesday night. So far as one could gather from his not very emphatic declarations, he seemed to identify himself with those temperance reformers who are seek- ing to lessen the opportunities and incitements to drun- kenness by reducing the number of public-houses, and yet at the same time to advocate compensation to dis- possessed publicans. Now, sir, just as it is impossible for one moan to stand on his feet and his head at the same time, so it is impossible for any one individual to be both an effective friend of temperance and an advocate of such compensation as we have proposed. Not even the most sanguine teetotaller can disguise from hinseelf that, if the compensation clauses pass, the liquor trade will hold a stronger and less assailable position than it has , ever held before—a position in fact, so long as the clauses stand, of impregnable strength. Were the clauses once law all the efforts of temperance reformers would have to be diverted from the direct attack on the liquor traffic and concentrated upon an agitation for securing the repeal of the clauses. Gentlemen like Mr. Carleton should, therefore, define their position. They cannot run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. If they support the compensation clauses they are not en- titled to use the language of temperance reformers. The temperance party are striving to reach a certain goal, and whoever helps to place an unscalable barrier between them and that goal is certainly not a friend of the tem- perance cause. Mr. Carleton put forward the extraordinary conten- tion that reformers ought to be ready to bear the costs of reform. Consider for a moment what this means. A man is suffering from some insidious disease, which, if allowed to grow unchecked, may rapidly eat away his vital powers, and perhaps bring about a premature death. A friend anxious for his welfare urges upon him, and at length persuades him of, the need for a remedy, which, though more or less expensive, he re- solves upon trying. Is the friend under a special ro • • Lion to pay the expenses of the cure? Accord;. F Carleton's style of reasoning, he is, h•-' r. people it would seem that the obl: ....a th most other other side. The temp.,- ...gatioh WAS all on the for many years - „..estleQ 'Arty hate been urging the . vast that the Hoot traffic was mapping —O4 powers of this Fratton., tind riow that they have Almost perstiade4 tht We Of the remedy, we have rem- Ang tok*aid itehtlemen—who in the past may have ren- dered no active assistance, and, even if they did cot op- pose, probably stood aside in cynical, sneering indiffer- ence—to say that temperance reformers are under a special obligation to pay for the remedy. For myself, I consider the temperance party of this country have acted a noble and patriotic part, and that even in the matter of pecuniary sacrifice for their opinions they stand far ahead of most of their critics.—Yours, Bcc., , CADMUS. , Warrington, May 30, 1888. THE REV. E. C. E. CARLETON ON COMPENSATION AND THE SLAVE TRADE. Sir,—At the Meeting BM On Tuesday evening to cp. Eider the licensing clauses of the proposed Local Govern. ment Bill, I rehired to the manner in which the country dealt with the question of the Slave Trade as a precedent worthy of consideration in dealing with the ;qllestion of compensation to the publican for loss of liktrise through no fault of his own. It is well known that the country at that time made a considerable sacrifice in order to put an end to the immoral traffic, the Government voting no less than twenty millions sterling to satisfy the vested interests of the owners; and in support of their claims to compensation Mr. Gladstone made one of his earliest speeches. Mr. Walker, who spoke after me at the meet- ing, endeavoured to meet my contention by saying, that the case of the slave-owner was different to that of the publican inasmuch as the slave-owner's property was an • estate that had legal recognition, and that therefore the vested interests had to be provided for, which was not the case with the publican, as his license was only granted from year to year. I cannot accept this statement of Mr. Walker. The slave-owner's property, though it might be recognised as an estate in the colonies, was not recognised by English law. Slavery is, and was then, unknown to the British constitution, and so far from its being recognised as an estate in this country, even though it might be an estate elsewhere, if transferred to British soil it became non- existant. There was a decision given to this effect in 1772, obtained by Granville Sharp, that as soon as a slave sets foot on English ground he becomes free. The truth is that the nation at that time, to put an end to an immoral traffic in her colonies, was content to recog- nise the property of the slave-owners as an estate, and to pay the compensation claimed, though it might well have been denied that there was any such moral claim upon the mother country. Mr. Gladstone, however, advocated such compensation, and his family received some of the money voted to satisfy the claims of the slave-owners.—l am, yours, &c., E. C. E. CARLETON. June Ist, 1888.

Our reverend correspondent states his point fairly; but he will see that the analogy between the two cases does not hold good, when he draws a distinction be- tween an estate recognised in the colonies, but not recognised in this country. Neither in the colonies nor in England does the law recognise an estate in licenses. If the Government at home were to insist on the drink traffic being abolished in the colonies, and if at the same time the colonial law recognised an estate in licenses, it would certainly be the duty of the mother country to grant compensation. But we are dealing with a traffic at home, where, because there is no estate in the license for such traffic, no compensa- tion should be granted.—ED.

div.p: THE LICENSING CLAUSES.

Sir,—l am a-Scotchman, and reside pretty far north, and that may perhaps be the reason why I am so ignor- ant as to have been much astonished at the letter of " Bellerophon " in last Saturday's issue. In Scotland we are not accustomed to read letters characterized by the beautiful frankness of " Bellerophon's," or adorned with such classical poetical quotations, as for example— "He wot takes wot isn't his'n, When he's cotched he goes to prison." He who proposes to take what "isn't his'n " is we are assured, he who objects to paying compensation to liquor dealers. "Bellerophon" says—" If I were on a County Council, as proposed by the present Government, and by my casting vote turned a publican out of his house, and thus robbed his family of their daily bread, I Should regard myself as an unmitigated scoundrel, and as deserving a thief's fate, and in my humble opinion, whoever else perpetrates this offence, either by word or
deed, is just as bad as I should be under the same cir- cumstances; and no amount of Local Option sophistry, or any other pious fraud on his own conscience can get him out of it." • _

Sir, my idea was that publicans held their licenses from year to year, and that there was never any guaran- tee given that these would be renewed. In fact it has been over and over again declared that when the Jaw or the people (when lawfully empowered) shall decide against the issue of a succeeding license, such decision leaves no claim for compensation for the loss of a prospective trade, the continuance of which was never guaranteed by law. In 1877 Meldon's Act raised the rateable qualifications of Irish beer-houses, and this closed 557 beer-houses in Dublin. During the same year Ireland secured the boon of Sunday closing, and Wales got the same blessing in 1881. No compensa- tion was given in any of these cases, nor is compensation being paid now, when three-quarters of the Scotch license holiers have to close at ten p.m. The license holder has been allowed to possess a profitable, eagerly sought, special privilege, which he has oftimes—in Scot- land, at least—secured against the expressed wish of the community. In taking this special privilege from the drink seller, society takes but what it gave, and puts him, as regards the power to make money by vending intoxicants, just on a level with his fellow citizens. Where, then, is the robbery in taking back a privi- lege that was given to certain parties for a limited period? The hand-loom weavers got no compensation when more improved machinery knocked their business effec- tually on the head, and horse-hirers got no compensation when railways stopped their business. If the publican has a landlord, the landlord will eject him at the end of his lease if it suits him to do so, and why should the state show more ?onsideration ? I for one have all my life objected to licenses being granted, and the " thief 'is "Bellerophon," and those who would dare to make me pay compensation to the publicans when I never wished to have a publican in proxi- mity to my abode, and when he has been placed there in defiance of the wishes of myself and others. Compensa- tion, forsooth! As well frighten a vampire from thevic- tim he sucks, and then talk of compensation for disturb- ing it. Morally, I have been told—since not legally—the publicans are entitled to compensation ; but I deny that there is any morality in the business at all. The publi- cans tell us with a snivel that if some of their customers meet with an untimely death through the influence of drink ; that if some of them beat and starve their wives and children, and occasionally commit a murder, that they (the publicans) are sorry for it, and are not to blame.- Still, they go on contributing to these results, and by the fruits of the trade it stands condemned Inthe eyes of every right-thinking man. If the average warm- hearted Lancashire man is not better educated on the temperance question than " Bellerophon," then perhaps the Good Templars will allow the S.D. for Banffshire to say that he hopes they will take energetic means at 'once to spread knowledge on the subject. Apologising. Mr. Editor, for taking up so muchof your space, I am, &c., G. H. _ . _
Buckie, 29th May, 1888.

THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.—IMPORTANT LICENSING FACTS. Sus,—The popular delusion—that a publican would receive, as a matter of course, a renewal of his license so long as the house was properly conducted, and that magistrates have not refused to renew a liquor license because there was no longer any public necessity for it, but only when the holder had committed some breach of the law—is so widespread, and arguments for com- pensation to superfluous publicans are so frequently founded upon this false assumption that the presenta- tion of a few facts known by practical experience or re- corded in blue and other books will be useful in dis- pelling the general misapprehension. Refusals to renew the licenses of old-established public-houses are not nearly so rare as is sometimes stated by those who have given little attention to the subject, for actually both law and custom are against the contention of a publican having any right to demand a renewal of his license. Whole columns of declarations by barristers, statesmen, magistrates' clerks, licensing justices, and the judges of the superior law courts might be cited to the effect that there is no vested interest in or right to a license, but the latest must suffice, that of the highest legal authority in England, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, who said on April 25th, 1838 : "There is no vested interest in the trade. It has been tested again and again and laid down that the discretion of the licensing justices is absolute, Magistrates have the absolute power In cutting short publicans' irltereStrl," Facts confirm this learned dictum. I have myself used a reading-room which was formerly the bar of one of the five public-houses in a southern village. The license of this house was, like another house in the same place, refused renewal by the justices, without any conviction of the holder, simply because, in the opinion of the bench, there were too many public-houses for the legiti- mate needs pf the inhabitants. As I write, a photograph lies befom me of another licensed house with its sign painted out because the magistrates, after giving the I hoider a year's notice that they should not again re- license the house, refused on the next licensing day to renewal the annual permit. In the year 1871 five P.Zeniks (three full public-house Itcenses and two l'erhouses) were refused renewal by tAB Uominster Bench. No misconduct was alleged ' I,e;ainst any of them. There was no appeal and the licenses were not restored. In the year 1883 a magis- trate wrote me:—" In our district the clerk to the justices tells us that we have no discretion in the grant of renewals of publicans' licenses, and the majority of the bench believe him, in spite of what the superior courts have ruled, or I may say, of what you and others may write, and the determining authority being thus led on by the nose nothing is done, although nobody de- nies that the public-houses are far too numerous." Long standing licenses were refused renewal by this Very bench at the 1884 Brewster Sessions, amongst them being that attached to the oldest public-house in the district. REDUCTIONS IN tICINSES ON PtIBL/0 OntINDS. The liquor licenses at Bristol Were reduced by 111 In two years—from 1,350 in 1882 to 1,230 in 1884. Many ' of these licenses were quite free from endorsements, the grounds of objection being "house not wanted." Appeals to the Quarter Sessions only brought confirma- tion of the refusal to renew. In the Knutsford district the licenses were 40 less one year than in its pre- deteseet, 4nd at NeweaStle-upon-Tyne there were 103 Year': licenses in three years. A public-house bearing a irnortgage of 200 years' duration was, with others, on the action of a local ratepayer, refused renewal by the Dorsetshire justices a year or two ago, and the refusal sustained by the Quarter Sessions. In the year 1884 the magistrates of Derby, in the exercise of a general and absolute discretion, refused again to re-license a house which had been occupied for 100 years by wine merchants with a full public-house license. The Court of Queen's Bench held the discretion of the magistrates to be absolute, and declared that "the notion that there was a property of the landlord in a license was not sound law." In the same year the Dorsetshire justices refused the renewal of two public. house licenses on the grounds that "the house was not required for the wants of the public," the neighbours having objected to one as a "nuisance." About the same time, amongst many other licenses refused renewal, were 5 " full " licenses at Llandudno because "the house not required ;" at Aber- dare 10 " full " licenses, 2 beerhouses ; Bradford, 38 "off" licenses, 1 innkeeper, 3 beerhouses—grounds, "the necessity for the house no longer existed :" Crewe— "hog and Partridge Inn," "Golden Lion Inn "—ground of opposition, "the licence not required," the Bench saying "the objection was not to the man or the house, that was very narrow grounds to take:" Llanelly, 4 " full " licenses; 'Merthyr, 12 licenses, some because "house not wanted." "public accommodation supplied without them ;" Bridlington, 2 hotels. 1 "off," &a. The notice of objection which caused these refusals of renewal was sometimes served by the police, and sometimes by a rival publican or by a local ratepayer.

LICENSES WITH° II tIVN WITHOUT COMPENSATION. The withdrawal of " off " licenses was quite common in 1882, the numbers being reduced all over the country. Magistrates in some districts have carried their con- trplling authority up to the point of total prohibition of all such licenses. Of 384 " off ' licenses refused renewal for no offence by the holder, but because they were no longer thought to be necessary, 84 were situated in Yorkshire, 59 in Lancashire, 11 in Surrey, 8 at Warring- ton, 14 at Bradford, 35 at Over Darwen, 5 at Birming- ham, 21 at Manchester, 16 at Bristol, 24 at Sunderland, &c. In no case was compensation paid. The law gives magistrates exactly the same absolute power to refuse "full" licenses as " off " beer licenses, yet by the pro- visions of the proposed County Government Bill, if the new authority were in the public interest to refuse to renew 384 full" licenses the holders would be entitled to claim as a first charge upon the rates a sum—esti- mating the value of the licenses at far below that officially claimed by the publicans—exceeding half-a- million sterling. The abolition of these 381 licenses cost the ratepayers nothing. REFUSALS TO RE-LICENSE OLD PUBLIC-HOUSES. 3,570 old established victuallers, beer-house, and " off " licenses were refused renewal between the years 1875-82, in addition to 15,080 new applicants. Of these old licenses, 801 were victuallers, 1,957 beer and wine houses, and 812 other beer licenses, taken from every county in England, and without any endorsement. The location and number of these licenses (excluding those under a total of 6) refused to be renewed after proper notice had been given to the holders, are abstracted from an extensive and voluminous Government Return as follows :—Lancashire, 222; Staffordshire, 144; War- wic ksh i re, 46: Surrey, 160; Beds., 26; Cheshire, 57; Cumberland, 42; Berks, 16; Bucks, 11; Cornwall, 12; Derbyshire, 19; Devon. 39; Dorset, 24; Durham, 39; Essex, 11; Gloucester, 48; Herts., 25 Leicestershire, 17; Lincoln, 40; Middlesex, 17; Monmouth. 22; Norfolk, 13; Notts, 9; Northumberland, 15; Oxon., 13; Somerset, 32; Hants, 7; Wilts, 16; Suffolk, 7; Worcestershire, 14; Anglesea, 6; Breckon, 32; Cardigan, 9; Carmarthen, 20; Carnarvon, 16; Denbigh, 12: Montgomery, 8; Glamor- gan, 69; Salop, 53; Kent. 82; YOrkshire, 288; and in Boroughs: Liverpool, 263; Bristol. 315; Birmingham. 18; Wolverhampton, 28; Dudley, 27; Salford, 58; Sun- derland, 61; Luton, 7; Reading, 10; Birkenhead, 17; Carlisle, 15; Gateshead, 8; Stockton-on-Tees, 11;

Gloucester, 12; St. Albans, 8; Dover, AL, Margate, 18; Bolton, 9; Over Darwen, 35: Preston, -19; Warrington, 8; Newport, 21; Norwich, 26: Northampton, 10; New- castle-on-Tyne, 86; Tynemouth, 16; Portsmouth, 18; Longton, 25; Bradford, 33; Kidderminster, 12; Hull, 6: Middlesbro', 8; Dewsbury, 14; Sheffield, 29; Aberyst- with, 6; Carnarvoo, 6; Leeds, 7; Cardiff, 18; Swansea, 17; Ashton-under-Lyne, 86; London City, 105; and Manchester, 200. Similar reductions might now be made anywhere without loading the rates with Coln- pensation, for the absolute right of magistrates to refuse to renew the license of any house that they may think unnecessary, although there may be no complaint against the holder, has been recently again confirmed by two Judges in the High Court. A later Government return shows that there were no less than 1,182 fewer public-houses and beerhouses in 1885 than in 1884. This diminution has been going on since at a similar rate and at no cost to the ratepayers, and, presumably, would continue to do so, did not Mr. Ritchie's Bill, by interposing the brand new block of compensation, stop this steady reduction in the number of what a Conservative Lord High Chancellor once styled "traps and pitfalls for the working-classes."— Yours, kc., W. C. AMERY. 287, Stratford-road, Birmingham.

SALFORD AND BARTON. Already in some parts the level of the foundations has been reached at Salford. The concrete work preparatory to the laying of the foundations for the dock walls is ex- pected to commence at no distant period. At the tem- porary wharf on the bank of the Irwell flats laden with material, chiefly timber for building purposes, are be- ing lighted from morning till night. In the work- shops that have been erected here men are busy making wagons for the removal of "the spoil." The Navvy Mission Society is pushing its work in this quarter, and on Wednesday night the men were enter- tained to a service of sacred song in the Mission Room which has been erected by the children of the Ragged Schools.

INCE.

Between Ellesmere Port and Inge Hall nothing of a harder nature than clay nas yet been met with. At Stanlow Point, about twelve of the new huts are occu- pied, and many others are being erected. A mission room is also being erected. Last Sunday afternoon, the missionary (Mr. Cleverley) held a Sunday school at Stanlow, and his services are conducted as usual in the National Schools on Sunday and Thursday evenings. He hopes shortly to be in residence at Stanlow Point, in the midst of the men, when the schools will be dispensed with. Five locomotives are employed between the Gowey and Ellesmere Port.____

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

After many weeks of preparation actual operations have this week been commenced on the Weston sectionby orders of Mr. T. A. Walker, the great contractor. Mr. John Weston, the agent in charge of the section, has at present about 250 nien employed under ' him, but this number will shortly be largely increased. At the river- side on Frodsham Marsh about 150 piles have been driven in the sand, and have been used in the partial formation of a stage at which to load and unload the necessary material. The stage would doubtless have been com- pleted ere this, but the Mersey Conservancy Board have in the exercise of their powers stopped the work: and the labourers engaged on the job are for the present out of employment. In many quarters it is considered that the Mersey Board are carrying red tapeism too far, and are i acting n a manner that is not in accordance with the interests of those concerned. It should be stated that the Weston section starts at the Pumping Engine at the end of the Runcorn Docks and continues along the river wall, and across the mouth of the Weaver, and then along Frodsham Marsh to the Gunpowder Magazines, where the Ince section joins. Over 200 men are engaged in taking off the top soil on the marsh, and already upwards of 12,000 square yards of soil have been removed. This soil is being used to form a spoil bank between the river and the line of the canal. It is imperatively necessary that there should be such a bank, as at high tides, and when the stormy winds do blow, the water inundates a great portion of the marsh. From the half-finished stage previously mentioned, sleepers have been laid for a considerable distance for the purpose of making a railway, and a couple of loco- motives are expected in a few days. An American navvy, a German navvy, and a French navvy are also expected soon to be on the scene, and busily at work carving out the canal. The " Frenchman "is a new in- vention in the science of navvying, and is the first in- troduced on the Ship Canal works. It is specially adap- ted for working in a damp soil, such as will be met with on Frodsham Marsh, and it is confidently expected that excellent results will be obtained. Five of the huts erected on the Weaver Wharf at Wes- ton Point are occupied, and the sixth is re- served for use as a hospital until a proper hospital is constructed near the "Old Folly." The three huts in course of erection at this spot are rapidly approaching completion under Mr. Kirkham's superintendence. Al- ready the men employed on the section have experienced the greatest difficulty in obtaining lodgings. About 60 ,or 70 live in Weston, and are rowed across the river to their labours at the marsh every morning, and are brOugiit WA in the same manner in the evening. Frod- sham cannot Ana ateem&s4ttl9l3 fer the remainder, and many are put to sore straits to find a place to lay their • heads. Mr. Walker is, however, dealing with the mat- ter in his usual thorough fashion and has let a contract f to our townsman, Mr. Thomas Kirkham, for the erection of 36 workmen's huts in the centre of the marsh. There will also be a mission house. In the same neighbourhood Mr. Kirkham has also undertaken to build a depot, con- sisting of Oleos, joiners' shops, smithies, &c.

RUNCORN. Capital progress continues to be made on this section, , The cuttings become perceptibly longer each day. The excavation which commences at the depot at Norton is now about a mile in length, and the lower excavation has extended as far as the works of Messrs. Wigg Eros. and Steele. The depth of the excavation is about 20 feet. The water which accumulates is drained into the Old Quay Canal. In a few weeks the two cuttings will meet, and it is surmised that the steam navvies will then return to the depot and commence to make the ex- cavation 20 feet deeper. The spoil bank on the marsh has now assumed enormous proportions, and Mr. Greg- son, the agent, has thought it necessary to commence laying another bank nearer to the river in order that the Old Quay Canal may not be prejudici- ally affected by the shifting ground. Formerly the marsh sank under the tremendous weight; it has now begun to rise. Since the commencement of the formation of the second spoil bank, the marsh land that lies between the two has become elevated to a height of 15 feet above the former level, and its rise was go rapid that it is said the men eA work on the job could plainly see the land uplifted. For the accommodation of the numerous horses that are employed on the Mellon, Mr. T. Kirkham has just erected a fine block tlf gables with stalls for eixteen horses. There is a capital house at- tached, and here the ostler and the drivels take up their residence, and are therefore always at hand to attend to their charges. On Thursday a few of the directors visited the section and made a thorough inspection of the works, and expressed themselves highly gratified by the pro- gress that had been made. One of the gentlemen, who occupies a high social position, had a brief experience of the labour the men perform. Taking hold of a barrow, piled to a considerable height with blocks of turf, he cleverly wheeled it along a plank and tipped the contents into the required spot. This feat created considerable merriment amongst the gentleman's co-directors. THELWALL AND LYMM.

Steam navvies are getting tobe plentiful on the ground between Morris-brook and the river at Thelwall. There are already three busy at work—two of the so-called "American" type and the other the" Jubilee" navvy of the make of Messrs. Whittaker Bros., Horsforth, near Leeds. In addition to these, there is in course of erec- tion near the bend of the Mersey at Thelwall, another "patent excavator" of a fresh type, the production of Smith, of Rodley, near Leeds. To an unpractised eye this latest specimen of the steam navvy seems to have some of the characteristics of both the " American " and "Jubilee" types, though in many respects it is different to both. The parts of another steam navvy have been within the last few days taken upon the canal works near Morris Brook, and when this has been erected it will be the fifth on a compara- tively short length of ground. In the course of this week, the work of excavation has been extended into the fields opposite Morris Brook farm buildings, and no doubt one of the new navvies will be put in operation at this point before long. Between Morris Brook and Cedar Lawn, the late residence of Alderman Pickmere, excavation will be conducted on the most extensive scale, as here lies the site of the future Latchford Locks.

Over the river from Thelwall the labour of making the new bed for the Mersey is continued with great energy, and it is evidently intended to bring this one of the numerous incidental works to a completion as quickly as possible. To a spectator the making of this river bed is, as we have mentioned before, one of the most interesting spectacles on the canal, owing to the methods adopted for raising the displaced soil on to the huge spoil heaps. Between Thelwall and Statham there is little that is fresh to be mentioned, though it is to be noted that the steam navvy, the parts of which have been on the ground near Thelwall for some time, has now been erected, but not yet put to use. At Statham the steam navvies there also still stand idle, though in this district a good deal of hand labour is busily engaged.

div.head: 'WAitIiURTON.
div.p: 'WAitIiURTON.

Owing to a re-arrangement of the sections the works at Warburton are now included in the Latchford section, thus reducing the number of sections to eight instead of nine. This division of the work now extends from a point almost immediately south of Warrington to the village of Warburton. At present only three steam navvies are at work on this section, but menarepreparing breast- works for three others to commence operations, and these will be engaged in the second lift. Gangs of men are busily employed in taking off the top soil in various places along the section, Two pulsometer engines and a centrifugal engine are at work pumping out the water from wells which have been sunk to the depth of fifty feet, for the purpose of draining the canal cutting. Piles are being driven into the bed of the river, close to the mouth of the river Bollin. preparatory to constructing a trestle bridge, which will connect the two sections of Warburton and 'Thelwall. Work is carried on night and day. ECCLES.

At Eccies a bridge has just been commenced, which, when conpleted, will span the Bridgewater Canal to Trafford Park. The new French navvy, whose advent on the cutting has been looked forward to with in- terest,-is now at work. On the Eccles and Barton divi- sions there are now working 1,000 men and seven loco- motives. Near Irwell Park the cutting operations are being pursued with vigour.

div.head: VICARAGE OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE VICARAGE OF WIDNES.

The trustees of this living have been most un- wearied in their efforts to get a suitable successor to the Rev. J. W. Williams, who was appointed to Rainford some time since. The work is, because of the vast population, most important. There were many candidates. local as well as distant. The trustees have at last been encouraged to offer the appointment to the Rev. George Henry St. l'atrick Garrett, 8.D., curate of Christ Church, Leeson-park, in the city of Dublin. The rev, gentleman has, it is believed, against the wish of many of his friends, decided to accept the appointment, solely through the attractiveness of the work amongst men. Mr. Garrett is one of the most brilliant scholars of his year in the Dublin University. He won a classical scholarship in 1877. He carried off two gold medals as senior moderator in classics, and senior modera- tor in moral and mental philosophy in 1878. He won a classical studentship in the same year, as well as Archbishop Ring's Divinity Prize and Bishop Forster's Divinity Prize in 1878. In the following year he carried off the Church Formulary Prize, Biblical Greek Prize, and Divinity Testimonium. In the next year he won the Theological Exhibition, and, what is peculiar to the Dublin University, the B.D. degree by examination. Mr. Garrett is but 31 years old. He is a man of the, highest character, and regarded with affection in the University and beyond it. The trustees and the people of Widnes are to he congratulated upon such an appointment

div.head: ILLNESS OF MR. BRIGHT.
div.p: ILLNESS OF MR. BRIGHT.
Mr. John Bright is lyinz at One Ash, Rochdale, suffering from an attack of congestion of the lungs.

The expressions of regret at Mr. John Bright's illness are very numerous, and many sympathetic messages have been received at One Ash, among them being a telegram from the Prince of Wales. On Tuesday night Mr. Bright's condition was con- sidered more satisfactory. Refreshed by sleep, he was not so feverish, and though weak his symp- toms were far less alarming than on the previous night.

Under the most favourable conditions Mr. Bright will be confined to bed for several weeks. For a fortnight he has taken but little food. His present nourishment is chiefly milk, which he takes readily. Although suffering no actual pain, he is troubled with coughing. Mr. Bright has throughout his long life, at any rate since his boyhood, enjoyed good health, and had little call for medical attention. His habits have been simple, and ordinary colds have been his chief complaints, caught probably enough during his fishing excursions. Some years ago, while in London, he had an attack somewhat similar to the present, but he was then stronger. Dr. flayle says Mr. Bright's fever has disappeared. The left lung is still congested, but the acute stage is passed. Mr. Bright had seven hours' sleep on Wednesday night, and is progressing favourably. At ten o'clock the doctor found his patient much im- proved, and his temperature normal, 984. His breathing was better, and he continued to take nourishment more readily. Mr. Bright spent a restless night on Wednesday, but dozed on Thursday forenoon, and at ten o'clock appeared better. Mrs. Cash, Mr. Bright's youngest daughter, arrived at One Ash on Thursday from Warwickshire. Dr. Hayle visited Mr. Bright shortly tatu nc9ll Thursday, and found him improving, the temperature bein normal, The Queen has sent a telegram from Balmoral by Major Begge inquiring as to the health of Mr. Bright, and it was promptly answered. Dr. Ifayle visited Mr. Bright at eleven o'clock on Friday morning, and found him a little stronger, but his general health is so poor that he must remain in his room some time.

div.head: PRINCE -OF IDLERS.
div.p: A PRINCE -OF IDLERS.

There is a man well-known to the Warrington police who seems to have a fixed determination to pass through life without putting himself to much exertion in the way of earning a living. His name is Thomas Miskell, and, when in trouble, he is usually described on the police charge sheet as being of "no settled abode. He is a man in the prime of life, strong and healthy-looking, but anything in the shape of work is his aversion. Rather than earn his bread by labour, he would prefer to be in the Workhouse; and, in preference to the Workhouse, he would choose the gaol. This will appear to be a remarkable attoment, but Miskell's own conduct, atid, indeed, his own words, confirm it. The reason map be that he has the bad fortune—or, to his way of thinking, the good fortune—to suffer from an infirmity .to one of his hands, which prevents him being put to the usual task of " hard " allotted to the general run of prisoners. This infirmity, it may be presumed, will also make his life when in the " Big Flouse" somewhat easier than that of the rest of the inmates who are not so conveniently afflicted. He is described as being a carter, and it is to be borne in mind that his affliction does not hinder him in gaining a liveli- hood by carting. On more than two score occasions he , has made an appearance on various charges, principally of drunkenness and assault, before the borough justices, and on Thursday morning he was brought up in custody to answer a charge of a character that has notpreviously formed the subject of inquiry by the local magistrates. Proceedings had been taken at the instance of the Board of Guardians, and the charge agaiast him read to the effect that he, being a person able to work or otherwise to maintain himself, did neglect to do se, and in conse- quence became chargeable to the common fund of the Workhouse.. The unusual nature of the charge led to an inquiry from Major Litton, who was in the chair, in answer to which the Clerk to the Magistrates (Mr. H. B. White) said that it was intended to meet cases where people would not work. The particulars of the case were then narrated to the Court by Mr. Basil Shearer, Inquiry Officer, who said that Miskell, who was a single man, had since October in 1885 spent 54 weeks in the Workhouse, he had been in and out no less than ten times. All last winter, with the exception of three terms of imprisonment that he served, he was in the Workhouse. On the sth of last month he took his dis- charge, and secured work from Mr. Buckley, contractor, as a carter. He worked until yesterday week, when he got some drink. As he did not turn up to work en Satur- day, or to attend to the horse on Sunday? another man was taken on. On Tuesday he made application for ad- mission to the workhouse, stating that his money was all gone, and that he was destitute. Mr. Shearer added that that was the first time that they had to prosecute a person for neglecting to maintain himself.—Major Litton: You must keep them too well in the Workhouse.—Mr. Shearer: We give them all the work that we can.—major Litton: Can you give us any idea of the difference between the living in the Work- house and the living in the prison P—Mr. Shearer: I believe the prison is equally as good as the Workhouse. This man would just as soon be in prison as in the Work- house. There is something the matter with one of his hands, and I believe he is not put to the same hard labour as other people.—Major Litton: I suppose he has the privilege of the treadmill at Walton Gaol ?—Mr. Shearer : I do not think he is given much of that.—Mr. Hunt (the Chief Constable) : He is in gaol very often, but he has some infirmity in his hand, and he is never put to hard labour, but to light work. Consequently, he does not know what hard labour or work is —The magistrates sent Miskell to prison for a month.— Prisoner: I had rather be in prison than in the Work- house.

SUCCESS OF A NEWTONIAN.-Mr. Alfred Caldwell, assistant surveyor in the Commissioners Office at the Newton Town Hall, has secured appointment to the post of Surveyor to the Reddish Local Board, near Stockport. Mr. Caldwell, who has served un- der Mr. R. Brierley, for the past eight years, was selected from a large number of applicants, and he is to be complimented upon his appointment. He will start upon his new duties towards the end of June.
