div.head: RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.

The new Rector of Warrington, the Rev. Frederic William Willis (Corpus Christi College, Oxford), was on Tuesday instituted to the Rectory and Parish Church of Warrington, at the Diocesan Registry Office, Lord-st., Liverpool, by the Right Rev. Dr. Ryle, Bishop of the Diocese of Liverpool, in succession to the late Rev. W. Quekett, who had held the living from 1854 until his recent decease. Mr. Willis, who comes from Wellingborough, and is a brother of Captain H. Rcelolph d'Anyers Willis, of Halsnead Hall, near Prescot, was presented to to the living by the Right Hon. Thomas Lyttleton Powys (Lord Lilford), the patron. Mr. Willis came to Warrington on Wednesday. and, accom- panied by Messrs. It. W. Francomb and N. B. Per- cival, in the morning made an inspection of the Rectory and the church. In the afternoon he attended at the church to go through the ceremony of induc- tion, so that he is now Rector of Warrington, al- though he will not take actual possession until the commencement of the month of August, the Rev. J. A.. Drummond remaining in his capacity of curate- in-charge of the parish anti' the last Sunday in next month. Among the gentlemen who were in i attendance at the church when the induction cere- mony was carried out were the Rev. S. Wilkinson (the vicar of St. Paul's), Messrs. N. B. Percival and R. W. Francomb (the churchwardens), J.E. Wright. Thomas Moores, F. Taylor, and Leigh. The Bis- hop's mandate, formally appointing Mr. W illis the rector, was read in the main isle of the church. Those present then left the building. The key hav- ing been handed to Mr. Willis the reverend gentle- man unlocked the principal door of the church, and, accompanied by an atttendant, he proceeded to the belfry, where he several times tolled the bells. He then returned to the entrance of the church, and admitted the company of gentlemen who had re- mained standing outside, and received their hearty congratulations. The ceremony over, the new rec- tor, accompanied by the vicar of St. Paul's, entered the vestry and signed the necessary papers. Mr. Willis was again in town yesterday, and in the morning he was at the Rectory. In the after- noon he met the churchwardens to inquire into various matters concerning the parish. In reply to inquiries, Mr. Willis said that he was only in War- rington for the day. He intended in the evening to go to his brother's place near Prescott and then to- day (Saturday) to proceed to Wellingborough,where he will conduct services as usual in the church the charge of which he is relinquishing. It was also his intention to be in Warrington, if possible, on Walking Day, but he should not take part in any service at the church until the first Sunday in August, when he will " read himself in " in the morning, and preach the sermon at the evening service. Mr. Willis further said that he had been once or twice in Warrington, and was favourably impressed with what he had seen of the town. He could see that there was plenty of work to be done ; but he was only too glad to perceive that. The six or seven thousand parishioners amongst whom he had been labouring at Welling- borough were principally composed of railway guards, drivers, and shoemakers, so that he was used to being among a working population such as there is in Warrington. The new Rector will bring with him from Wel- lingborough, as curate. the Rev. T. A. Easter- ling, who went to Wellingborough from St Michael's, Teignmo uth, Devonshire, a short time ago, with good credentials. The term of the 'engagement of the Rev. J. A. Drum- mond, 8.A., who has been curate at the War- rington Parish Church for the past four years, ter- minates at the end of July, and, judging from the fact that the reverend gentleman has already re- signed the post of secretary to the Warrington Photographic Society, it would seem that he does not contemplate having to remain here. Mr. Drum- mond has, during his residence in Warrington, made many warm friends among the parishioners, and if the prospect of his departure becomes a cer- tainty, his final removal will be felt by a large circle. For some little time past there has been a con- siderable amount of speculation amongst the towns-

people as to the High Church doctrines of the new Rector, and an impression prevails in some quar- ters that if the services are altered in any very material degree in that direction, unpleasantness will almost of a certainty result. Mr. Willis, how- ever, in reply to a question regarding that matter, told our representative that he should make no changes that he could possibly avoid. He did not care at present to express any more decided opinion on that point. The reverendt gentleman hhs pre- viously declared himself to be "most distinctly and decidedly a thorough High Churchman, but a most considerate one." It is hoped that his consideration will be such as to meet the wishes of the par- ishioners in this matter.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The loomers' and drawers' strike at Blackburn still continues. The masters are employing strangers. The cricket match, Players versus Australians, resulted. yesterday afternoon, in a victory for the players by ten wickets.

Mr. Pyne, M.P., was released from Clonmel Gaol on Friday, after six weeks' imprisonment. He was greeted by a crowd of sympathisers. The body of Superintendent Scott, who was murdered at Durham on Thursday, was on Friday removed to Jarrow for interment on Sunday. Fourteen hundred shipbuilders and boilermakers struck work at Hartlepool on Friday. their notice for 121 per cent, increase having expired on Thursday night. Yesterday the whole of the underground men em- ployed by the Trede,"bar Iron and Coal Company, Limi- ted, refused to work as protest against certain new rules. The strike throws out of employment 2,500 men. SIR H. JAMES AND THE COMPENSATION CLAUSES.—Re- plying to a resolution condemning compensation to pub- licans, passed at Bury, Sir Henry James says he desires to retain his freedom of action unfettered until the ques- tion is practically dealt with. ANOTHER MURDER OF A WARDER.—A convict in the prison of Riggio d'Emilia, Rome, during a fit of madness, on Thursday, killed a warder with a knife and also severely wounded the governor, the assistant-governor, four warders, and a fellow-prisoner. A JUBILEE KNIGHT.—Mr. Alderman J. J. Harwood, Mayor of Manchester, has received a letter from Lord Salisbury informing him that her Majesty the Queen, in recognition of the services he has rendered as Mayor of Manchester, has been pleased to confer upon him the dignity of knighthood. FATAL COLLISION ON THE THAMES.—EarIy On Friday morning the sailing barge Europa, laden with Condy's fluid, was proceeding down the river, and when off the Eagle Flour Mills at Peckham she came into violent col- lision with a screw steamer, and immediately sank. The three men on board jumped into the water, and two of them were drowned. CHARGE OF MURDERING A POLICEMAN.—At Westmins- ter, on Friday, Frederick Wood, 23, a carman, was re- manded, charged with causing the death of Constable Michael Lewis, at Chelsea, on Thursday evening, by in- jury by resisting arrest. The accused was arrested for la eft, but struggled violently, and threw Lewis, who flied from internal injuries. ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.—At Sheffield, on Friday morning, a retired soldier named Richards, who is between 50 and 60 years of age, attacked his wife with a razor. The woman ran out of the house, escaping without serious injuries, but immediately after she left Richards appears to have used the weapon upon him- self. He was found a few minutes after lying on the kitchen floor with a great gash in his throat. He ex- pired shortly afterwards. It is said he frequently threa- tened his wife, and that jealousy was the cause of the outrage.

THE MANCHESTER MURDER. Arrests continue to be made in various places, but all efforts to capture the murderer have as yet proved futile. From various parts of the country so many reports have been received aud published regarding the apprehension and ultimate discharge of men resembling Jackson or Firth, that any fresh accounts short of the actual arrest and identification of the man must now be received with considerable doubt. A Sittingbourne telegram says that the Kentish railway stations are being watched, in the belief that Jackson has passed through London for the Continent. THE CONVICT VISITS HIS NATIVE PLACE. In spite of the vigilance of the police, it is stated that Firth visited his native place, Birstall, near Bradford, on Wednesday. He called at a shop, bought a bottle of aerated water and a newspaper, and afterwards inquired from the woman the whereabouts of an acquaintance, who was away from home. The woman recognised him, and he at first denied his identity, but afterwards admitted it. She urged him to leave for his parents' sake, and after inquiries as to their health he disap- peared.
THE EMPEROR FREDERICK. The Emperor passed an excellent night on Thursday. His Majesty left Charlottenburg for Potsdam at a quarter to eleven on Friday morning. NEW CATHOLIC BISHOPS.

Rome, FRIDAY AFTE"—a-WOON.LAFii;;—&-ms. istory, held to-day, the Pope appointed Monsignor Ullathorne, for- merly Bishop of Birmingham, to be bishop in Rartibus. Monsignor Ilsley was appointed Bishop of Birmingham; Rev. Father O'Donnell, Bishop of Raphoe; Rev. Father Lyster, Bishop of Achonry ; and Rev. Father Macgennis, Bishop of Kilznore.

div.head: LIST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSI OF COMMONS.
div.p: LIST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSI OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past three o'clock. The attendance of members was again very small.

LOTTERIES.—MT. BRADLAIMII asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether his attention had been drawn to the great increase during the past few years in the prac- tice of gambling by means of lotteries, and whether it was true that the various Governments had rarely en- 'forced the lottery law, except against petty offenders.— Mr. W. H. SMITH said in a great many cases the local authorities had themselves taken action against lotteries, i and the Government did not hesitate n those cases where lotteries appeared to be distinctly illegal to order inquiries to be made with a view to instituting a pro- secution.
THE WINE DITTIES.—The CHANCELLOR of the Ex- cmgcaumt intimated that on Monday next he would make a statement respecting the Nine duties. - TRUSTEE SAVINGS BANKS. -

------- On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. HOWELL called attention to the position of Trustee Savings Banks. He moved a resolution stating that the present relationship between these banks and the State required revision ;that banks should not make it appear that they gave Government security; and that trustees and managers should be made responsible for the safe custody of deposits committed to their case. He cited the cases of the Seven Oaks and Cardiff Savings Banks in support of the resolution.—Sir A. RoLLET, as trustee of the Hull Savings Bank, welcomed the discussion. He suggested the appointment of Select Committee to in- quire into the subject.—Mr. BARTLEY thought the time had arrived when the subject should be inquired into, but he trusted nothing would be done by the Government which would compel the present Trustee Savings Banks to collapse. He also ad- vocated an inquiry.—The CHANCELLOB of the EXCHE- QUER was afraid no regulations could be framed that would entirely prevent fraud. He suggested the omis- sion of that part of the resolution regarding the liability of trustees. If that was done, the Government would, or the hon. member could, move for the committee to in- quire into the whole of the matters raised in his resolu- tion.—The discussion was continued by sir E. Reed, Mr. Whitley, Mr. Tomlinson, and Sir J. Lubbock.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. Row- lands, said he would at once communicate with the Na- tional Debt Commissioners with the view to prevent Trustee Savings Banks representing themselves as Government institutions.—Mr. HOWELL, however, ac- cepted the proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and his resolution was negatived. SMALLPDX AT bHEFFIELD —Mr. rwrox then suggested an inquiry into the circumstances of the epidemic of smallpox at Sheffield and the surrounding districts in or- der to ascertain whether its origin is to be traced to de- fective vaccination, or insufficient sanitary precautions and other causes.—Mr. Cm-max, Dr. FAuntatenson, and Dr. CAMERON also urged an inquiry.—Mr. RITCHIE said that the Local Government Department was holding a searching inquiry on the spot. He did not think there was a more complete case in favour of Avaccination than that of Sheffield. Only two per cent, of the vaccinated children attacked died, while the percentage of deaths of unvaccinated children was 48. He could not assent to the special inquiry suggested. Mussel, BEDS.—Mr. ANDERSON afterwards called at- tention to the extent of private rights in mussel-beds in tidal waters of Scotland. He wished for the appoint- ment of Royal Commission.—After observations from the Lord Advocate, Mr. Sutherland, Mr. Rowntree, and Mr. Coleridge, the House went into Committee of Supply. CLEFT SITTING.)

PRESENTALTIONB TO Mn. GEORGE BURGESS.— Mr. George Burgess, the respected headmaster of the Wesleyan day schools, Barlestown, has been the recipient of a handsome gift as a mark of esteem on the occasion of his forthcoming marriage. The teachers of both the mixed school and the infants' department subscribed for a handsome full china tea service and a splendid glass flower stand, and these were handed over to Mr. /Burgess at the close of the school last Friday afternoon. Miss Tate, assistant mistress, made the presentation, and in doing so expressed the esteem and respect which the teaches had for Mr. Burgess, and wished him much happiness in his new sphere. Mr. Burgess, who was taken by surprise, acknowledged the gift. The girls in the 6th standard also presented a break- fast cruet and an inkstand to Mr. Burgess in the preceding week.

LYMM. THEFT.—At Altrincham Police Court, on Wednes3l John Rinksky, of Widnes, was charged with ha'° stolen a set of dominoes and a pint pot from the te, house of William Millyard, at Lymni, on the prey'. day. The ease was remanded in order that MVO might be made. SUDDEN DEATEL—On Monday, Sarah Clare, a virian: aged 85 years, died suddenly at her residence, Warn° ton-lane, Statham. She had suffered from an attack spasms on the previous day. The coroner was conirS nicated with in regard to the event, but it WO thought necessary to hold an inquest. CONFIRMATION AT Lrst3l.—On Monday last, the I'S Bishop of Chester (Dr. Stubbs) conducted a confirms service at which forty candidates were nwiln firmed, 38 from Lymm and two from High Legli• Rev. G. W. Guest, rector of Lymni : the Rev. 117• Lomas, curate; and the Rev. H. A. D. Surridge, of High Legh, were present. Appropriate hymns sung during the service, Mr. James Blakemore officials' at the organ. LYMM VOLUNTEERS.—Having been under canvaSsl Tatton Park for the week previous, the H Company V.B.C.R. arrived home on Saturday evening in spiels, condition. The men seemed to have benefited great. by their week's training at Knutsford, the weather ha ing been all that could be desired. This was in marlf, contrast to last year, when, owing to the excessive rail the camp had to be struck on the Friday. Through°, the week, the company has been up to its full streng" showing a better average attendance than any oth company in the battalion. On arriving at the Drill 01 the men were thanked by Captain T. A. Jones for the behaviour during the week, and for their great efficiea when on parade. Cheers were afterwards given fort captain, for Lieutenant Cookson, and for the sergeaS of the company. A LOST CRILD.—On Saturday Sergeant Rogerson, Bridgewater-st., on getting home from Tatton Pal found his youngest child, a girl about five years missing. Search was made all over the village on, after midnight on Saturday by friends assisted by police, but no trace of the missing child could be foull When last seen the girl was playing with some childre who had come to Lymrn on a trip up the canal from t direction of Manchester. Inquiries were made early ' Sunday morning at Manchester, and also at allthe pla4 from which boats had come the preceding day to Lyyal After a very fruitless and tiring journey through Wrol ley, Patricroft, Barton, &c., the search party came INT to Lymm by the last train, when they were agrees' surprised to hear that the child had been brought Igg during the day, having been taken good care of at Pat croft. It appears that the child was playing in the Is° at Lymm with other children, and in the hurry to get the teachers had not discovered her presence Ufl a considerable portion of the journey had been accOl plished.
